docs.title: Welcome to
docs.text:
Surfquake has been designed to processing seismic traces and to streamline the workflow of estimating seismic source parameters. The signal processing toolbox is extended with a lage variety of numerical methods while the comprehensive set of workflow toolboxes automates the determination of arrival times, event locations, event magnitudes , attenuation, and moment tensor inversion. The software is programmed in Python 3 and offers the users the possibility of three programming levels for flexibility and customization.

  • The Core Library allows users to integrate the core of surfQuake into their preexisting scripts, giving advanced users full control.

  • The Command Line Interface gives users access to an upper layer that simplifies the use of the core, enabling task execution through simple commands.

  • The Graphical User Interface (GUI): Now SurfQuake user-friendly interface is fully included in Integrated Seismic Program, making it accessible to users who prefer visual interaction.

docs.title: Ambient Noise Processing
docs.text:
Ambient Noise Processing is a passive seismic technique based on the cross-correlation of continuous background seismic noise between station pairs. SurfQuake provides a complete workflow including:

  1. Building a waveform dictionary from traces files
  2. Creating frequency-domain spectral matrices
  3. Cross-correlating and stacking station pairs
  4. Optional rotation of horizontal components

The ANT module is designed for large-scale continuous seismic datasets and supports parallel processing, spectral whitening, time normalization, instrument response removal, and multiple stacking strategies.

References



Ambient Noise Processing workflow:

Bensen, G. D., et al. Processing seismic ambient noise data to obtain reliable broad-band surface wave dispersion measurements. Geophysical journal international, 2007, vol. 169, no 3, p. 1239-1260.

Special signal processing. Phase Wave Stack and phase Cross-correlation

Schimmel, M. Phase cross-correlations: Design, comparisons, and applications. Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America, 1999, vol. 89, no 5, p. 1366-1378.

Clock Synchronization:

Cabieces, R., et al. Clock drift corrections for large aperture ocean bottom seismometer arrays: application to the UPFLOW array in the mid-Atlantic Ocean, Geophysical Journal International, Volume 239, Issue 3, December 2024, Pages 1709–1728.

Fast Horizontal Components Rotation:

Lin F.-C., Moschetti M.P., Ritzwoller M.H., 2008. Surface wave tomography of the western United States from ambient seismic noise: Rayleigh and Love wave phase velocity maps, Geophys. J. Int., 173, 281–298. doi: 10.1111/j.1365-246X.2008.03720.x 10.1111/j.1365-246X.2008.03720.x

docs.title: ANT Create Dictionary CLI
docs.text:
This command scans a MiniSEED archive recursively and builds a dictionary-based project file containing waveform paths organized by network, station and channel.

The generated pickle file is later used as input for the ANT processing pipeline.

        Key Arguments:
            -d,  --data_path         [REQUIRED] Root directory containing MiniSEED files
            -i,  --inventory_file    [REQUIRED] Path to StationXML inventory file
            -s,  --save_file         [REQUIRED] Path to save the ANT dictionary pickle
            -nt, --net               [OPTIONAL] Network filter, wildcards allowed (default: *)
            -st, --station           [OPTIONAL] Station filter, wildcards allowed (default: *)
            -ch, --channel           [OPTIONAL] Channel filter, wildcards allowed (default: *)
            -w,  --workers           [OPTIONAL] Number of parallel workers

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: >> surfquake ant_create_dict -d [data_path] -i [inventory_file] -s [save_file]

docs.title: Interactive help
docs.text: >> surfquake ant_create_dict -h

docs.title: Examples CLI
docs.text:
# Process all stations and channels
>> surfquake ant_create_dict -d ./mseed -i ./meta/inventory.xml -s ./output/data_dict.pkl

# Process only BHZ channels for network II
>> surfquake ant_create_dict -d ./mseed -i ./meta/inventory.xml \
-s ./output/data_dict.pkl -nt II -ch BHZ

# Use wildcard filters and multiple workers
>> surfquake ant_create_dict -d ./mseed -i ./meta/inventory.xml \
-s ./output/data_dict.pkl -nt "IU" "II" -ch "BH*" -w 8

docs.title: ANT Process Matrix CLI
docs.text:
This command processes the waveform dictionary created by ant_create_dict and generates frequency-domain spectral matrices for each station/channel.

The workflow includes:

  1. Reading continuous waveform files
  2. Gap checking and merging
  3. Optional instrument response removal
  4. Optional decimation
  5. Time-domain normalization
  6. Spectral whitening
  7. FFT transformation into frequency-domain matrices

Results are stored as pickle files and later used by the cross-correlation stage.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: >> surfquake ant_process_matrix -c [config.json]

docs.title: Generate template configuration
docs.text: >> surfquake ant_process_matrix --generate config_process_matrix.json

docs.title: Interactive help
docs.text: >> surfquake ant_process_matrix -h

docs.title: Example configuration
docs.text:
{
    "project_file": "./output/data_dict.pkl",
    "inventory_file": "./meta/inventory.xml",
    "output_path": "./output/matrices",
    "processing_window": 900,
    "remove_response": true,
    "units": "VEL",
    "waterlevel": 90,
    "decimate": true,
    "factor": 5,
    "time_norm": true,
    "method": "running avarage",
    "timewindow": 25,
    "whiten": true,
    "freqbandwidth": 0.02,
    "prefilter": true,
    "filter_freqmin": 0.01,
    "filter_freqmax": 0.4,
    "filter_corners": 4
}

processing window: (int) Noise time window in seconds. It is important to keep a long window to be able to capture the longest period of the EGFs. Be into account your minimum interstation distance to correctly select this parameter.

units: (str: DISP, ACC and VEL are available). The instrument response is removed and seismograms converted the physical unit output. This is important when you are mixing different types of instruments, because EGFs can have phase shifts.

waterlevel (int). Basically this parameter controls the deconvolution in the intrument response removal. Set to 90 is safe!

decimate: (bool). It is recommended to decimate your waveforms due to the later RAM memory usage and because computational efficiency.

factor: (int). Target sampling rate in Hz after decimation, if decimate is set to True.

time_norm: Apply time normalisation (see method). This is necassary in many cases due to seismogram noise use to be contaminated of transient signals.

method: (str: running avarage, 1 Bit and PCC). Time normalization methods or special phase cross correlation. If PCC is applied then whitening is skipped (because it is not totally necessary to equilibrate noise frequency band power).

whiten: (str). Apply spectral whitening using a moving avarage in the spectral domain.

prefilter: (bool). Apply a zero-phase bandpass pre-filter before noise cross correlation. recommended.

filter_freqmin: (float). Min frequency of pre-filter.

filter_freqmax: (float). Max frequency of pre-filter.

docs.title: filter_corners: (int). Number of poles of the pre-filter.
Examples CLI
docs.text:
# Generate template config
>> surfquake ant_process_matrix --generate config_process_matrix.json

# Run ANT spectral matrix processing
>> surfquake ant_process_matrix -c config_process_matrix.json

docs.title: ANT Cross Stack CLI
docs.text:
This command reads the spectral matrices generated by ant_process_matrix and computes cross-correlations between station pairs.

The processing workflow includes:

  1. Identification of common days between stations
  2. Frequency-domain cross-correlation
  3. Inverse FFT transformation
  4. Daily and full stacking
  5. Optional horizontal rotation

The resulting cross-correlations are stored in HDF5 format.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: >> surfquake ant_cross_stack -c [config.json]

docs.title: Generate template configuration
docs.text: >> surfquake ant_cross_stack --generate config_cross_stack.json

docs.title: Interactive help
docs.text: >> surfquake ant_cross_stack -h

docs.title: Example configuration
docs.text:
{
    "input_path": "./output/matrices",
    "output_path": "./output/stacks",
    "channels": ["Z"],
    "stations": [],
    "stack": "Linear",
    "power": 2.0,
    "autocorr": false,
    "min_distance": 1000.0,
    "daily_stacks": false,
    "overlap": 50.0,
    "workers": null,
    "rotate": false,
    "rotate_daily": false
}

input_path (str), path to the folder where the storaged matrix files from the pre-processing steps are saved.

output_path (str), path to the folder where stack files will be saved.

channels: (list), Channels list to effectuate the cross correlation and stacking. Example ["N", "E", "Z"].

stations: (list), Stations list to effectuate the cross correlation and stacking. Example ["STA1", "STA2"]. If empty ALL stations will be processed.

stack: Stacking methods: Linear, PWS, nrooth.

power: Exponent for PWS or nrooth stacking.

autocorr: if user want to compute autocorrelations. This is mandatory if user wants to get Radial (RR) and transversal (TT) EGFs.

min_distance: Threshold interstation distance to compute the cross and stacking.

daily_stacks: If you want to also compute partial stacks. Very useful for Synchronize clocks. (20 days stack).

overlap: Shift in time daily stacks. Example, if set to 50.0 the shift will be 0.5*20, then every 10 days.

workers: Number of parallel worker processes (default: null = cpu_count - 1).

rotate: Run ZNE rotation after stacking. User will obtain RR and TT components, used for Rayleigh and Love waves.

rotate_daily: If user wants to rotate daily stacks.

docs.title: Examples CLI
docs.text:
# Generate template config
>> surfquake ant_cross_stack --generate config_cross_stack.json

# Run cross-correlation and stacking
>> surfquake ant_cross_stack -c config_cross_stack.json

docs.title: Plotting EGFs
docs.text:
It is possible now to plot the EGFs with command quick. We show how to plot it as record section. Moreover ISP can also plot the output EGFs using the ANT module.

# Plotting EGFs in a record section
>> surfquake quick -w "./output/stacks/*ZZ*" --plot_config "./plot_conf.yaml"
It is mportant to add the option record_option: egf, so that plot the EGFs as a record section

plotting:
  traces_per_fig: 3
  sort_by: distance
  vspace: 0.05
  show_legend: true
  title_fontsize: 9
  plot_type: record
  record_option: egf
  sharey: False
  show_arrivals: False
  pick_output_file: ./picks.csv

docs.title: Rapid Earthquake Association and Location (REAL)
docs.text: The main goal of this tool is to associate the arrival times of different P- and S-waves to the their corresponding events. The associator algorythm used in surfquake is REAL (Zhang et al., 2019). The user needs to set the input parameters and point to the folder where the picks have been storaged. In th following sections it will be describe the surfquake imprementation of REAL, for a full description of the parameters visit REAL cookbook

docs.title: Events Associator from CLI
docs.text:
Key Arguments:
        -i, --inventory_file     [REQUIRED] Path to station metadata (XML or RESP)
        -p, --picks_folder       [REQUIRED] Folder containing station pick files
        -c, --config_file        [REQUIRED] Path to REAL .ini configuration file
        -w, --work_dir           [REQUIRED] Working directory for REAL intermediate output
        -s, --save_dir           [REQUIRED] Output directory for associated pick results
        -v, --verbose            [OPTIONAL] Enable detailed logging

docs.title: Interactive help
docs.text: >> surfquake associate -h

docs.title: Run Phase Picker from CLI
docs.text: >> surfquake associate -i /surfquake_test/metadata/inv_all.xml -p /surfquake_test/test_picking_final -c /surfquake_test/config_files/real_config.ini

docs.title: Config files
docs.text: The parametrization of the Event Assocciator tool can be storaged in a file.ini. An example of this file is as follows:

docs.title: Create a template config file
docs.text:
Key Arguments:
            -c, --config_type    [REQUIRED]         Config type 
            -o, --output_folder  [REQUIRED]         Output_folder for saving configuration

>> surfquake make_config -c real_config -o ./configs


[GEOGRAPHIC_FRAME]
LAT_REF_MAX = 43.0000
LAT_REF_MIN = 42.0000
LON_REF_MIN = 0.8000
LON_REF_MAX = 2.2000
DEPTH = 20.00
#
[GRID_SEARCH_PARAMETERS]
HORIZONTAL_SEARCH_RANGE = 4.80
DEPTH_SEARCH_RANGE = 50.00
EVENT_TIME_WINDOW = 120.00
HORIZONTAL_SEARCH_GRID_SIZE = 0.60
DEPTH_SEARCH_GRID_SIZE = 10.00
#
[TRAVEL_TIME_GRID_SEARCH]
HORIZONTAL_RANGE = 5.00
DEPTH_RANGE = 50.00
DEPTH_GRID_RESOLUTION_SIZE = 2.00
HORIZONTAL_GRID_RESOLUTION_SIZE = 0.01
#
[THRESHOLD_PICKS]
MIN_NUM_P_WAVE_PICKS = 3
MIN_NUM_S_WAVE_PICKS = 1
NUM_STATIONS_RECORDED = 1
The performance of REAL depends critically on parameter tuning. These parameters control: 1) Search geometry 2) Grid resolution 3) Time tolerance 4) Pick thresholds

docs.title: Parametrization Details
docs.text: The parameters in the configuration file define the geographic limits of the study area, the search volume used by REAL, the resolution of the travel-time grid, and the minimum number of picks required to accept an association. A good configuration should cover the target region and the seismic network while avoiding search windows that are unnecessarily large.

docs.title: Geographic frame
docs.text:
The GEOGRAPHIC_FRAME section defines the spatial limits used by the associator.

  • LAT_REF_MAX / LAT_REF_MIN: Maximum and minimum latitude of the study area.
  • LON_REF_MAX / LON_REF_MIN: Maximum and minimum longitude of the study area.
  • DEPTH: Maximum depth, in kilometres, considered during the association.

The geographic frame should include the complete station network and the expected seismicity area. It is recommended to add a small margin around the network, usually around 0.5–1.0°. If the area is too large, REAL can generate more false associations. If it is too small, events located close to the borders may be missed.

docs.title: Grid search parameters
docs.text:
The GRID_SEARCH_PARAMETERS section controls the event search volume and the time window used to group picks.

  • HORIZONTAL_SEARCH_RANGE: Horizontal distance, in degrees, used during the event search.
  • DEPTH_SEARCH_RANGE: Maximum depth range, in kilometres, used during the event search.
  • EVENT_TIME_WINDOW: Time window, in seconds, used to associate picks that may belong to the same event.
  • HORIZONTAL_SEARCH_GRID_SIZE: Horizontal spacing, in degrees, of the search grid.
  • DEPTH_SEARCH_GRID_SIZE: Vertical spacing, in kilometres, of the search grid.

As a general rule, the horizontal search range should be larger than twice the average station spacing. Dense networks can usually work with values around 0.5–1.0°, medium-density networks with 1–2°, and sparse networks with 2–4°.

The grid size defines the precision and computational cost of the search. Smaller values improve the resolution but increase the execution time. Typical values for HORIZONTAL_SEARCH_GRID_SIZE are 0.02–0.05° for production runs and 0.05–0.1° for testing. Values larger than 0.2° should normally be avoided. For DEPTH_SEARCH_GRID_SIZE, common values are 2–5 km.

The EVENT_TIME_WINDOW should be adapted to the seismicity rate. Low-seismicity regions can use wider windows, such as 90–120 s. For swarms or regions with many close events, shorter windows, such as 30–60 s, usually reduce false associations.

docs.title: Travel-time grid search
docs.text:
The TRAVEL_TIME_GRID_SEARCH section defines the grid used to compute and store travel times.

  • HORIZONTAL_RANGE: Maximum horizontal distance, in degrees, covered by the travel-time grid.
  • DEPTH_RANGE: Maximum depth, in kilometres, covered by the travel-time grid.
  • HORIZONTAL_GRID_RESOLUTION_SIZE: Horizontal resolution, in degrees, of the travel-time grid.
  • DEPTH_GRID_RESOLUTION_SIZE: Depth resolution, in kilometres, of the travel-time grid.

The travel-time grid must cover the maximum expected distance between stations and possible events. It is recommended to add a margin of approximately 20–30%. If the travel-time grid is too small, REAL may not associate any events. Typical resolution values are 0.01° horizontally and 1–2 km in depth.

docs.title: Pick thresholds
docs.text:
The THRESHOLD_PICKS section defines the minimum number of observations required to accept an event candidate.

  • MIN_NUM_P_WAVE_PICKS: Minimum number of P-wave picks required.
  • MIN_NUM_S_WAVE_PICKS: Minimum number of S-wave picks required.
  • NUM_STATIONS_RECORDED: Minimum number of stations that must record the event.

For small networks with 5–8 stations, a good starting value for MIN_NUM_P_WAVE_PICKS is usually 2–3. For networks with 10–15 stations, values around 3–4 are commonly used. The MIN_NUM_S_WAVE_PICKS parameter can initially be set to 0 and increased later if S-wave picks are reliable. For NUM_STATIONS_RECORDED, dense networks can use 3–5, while sparse networks may require 2–3.

docs.title: Parameter interactions
docs.text:
The parameters should be tuned together rather than independently. Large search ranges combined with wide time windows can increase the number of false associations. Smaller grid sizes improve precision but increase computation time. Narrow search ranges and short time windows reduce noise, but they can also miss events if the expected event location or origin time is not well constrained.

A practical workflow is to begin with permissive values, inspect the resulting associations, and then progressively tighten the thresholds, search ranges, and time windows until the number of false associations is reduced without losing valid events.

docs.title: Bash Scripts with SurfQuake
docs.text:
SurfQuake is used from the terminal, by typing commands. That is perfect to explore a few files, but when you have to repeat the same steps many times (every day, for every event, for every station), typing them again and again is slow and error-prone. A bash script solves this: you write the commands once in a text file, and run them all with a single command.

This page is for beginners: no previous experience with bash is needed.

docs.title: What is bash?
docs.text:
• The terminal (or console) is the window where you type commands instead of clicking.
  • Bash is the program inside the terminal that reads your commands and runs them. It is the standard on Linux and macOS (on recent macOS the default is zsh, which understands the same commands used here).
  • A bash script is a plain text file (usually ending in .sh) containing a list of commands. Bash runs them one after the other, from top to bottom, exactly as if you had typed them.

So, if you can run a SurfQuake command in the terminal, you can already write a bash script: just put the commands in a file.

Windows users

Bash is not the default on Windows. You can use it through WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) or Git Bash. Alternatively, write the same commands in a PowerShell or .bat file, one per line.

docs.title: 1. Create the file
docs.text:
Open any text editor (VS Code, gedit, nano, TextEdit in plain-text mode...) and create a file named run_surfquake.sh in your working folder:

#!/bin/bash
# My first SurfQuake script

surfquake explore -w "./data/*"
surfquake quick -w "./data/*" -c ./configs/typical_config.yaml -o ./output -a
  • The first line, #!/bin/bash, tells the system that this file must be run with bash. Always keep it as the first line.
  • Lines starting with # are comments: they are ignored, and you can use them to explain what each part does.
  • The other lines are normal SurfQuake commands.

docs.title: 2. Make it executable
docs.text:
The first time, give the file permission to be run:

chmod u+x run_surfquake.sh

docs.title: 3. Run it
docs.text:
From the folder where the script is:

./run_surfquake.sh

You can also run it with bash run_surfquake.sh. Avoid sh run_surfquake.sh: on many Linux systems sh is not bash, and some lines may fail.

docs.title: Activating your environment
docs.text:
If you installed SurfQuake in a conda environment, the script must activate it before using surfquake, otherwise the command will not be found. Inside scripts, conda needs one extra line:

#!/bin/bash

# Activate the conda environment where SurfQuake is installed
eval "$(conda shell.bash hook)"
conda activate surfquake        # replace 'surfquake' with the name of your environment

surfquake quick -w "./data/*" -c ./configs/typical_config.yaml -o ./output -a

If you use a Python virtual environment instead, replace those two lines with:

source /path/to/your/venv/bin/activate

docs.title: Basic tools to write better scripts
Long commands on several lines
docs.text:
A command can be split over several lines by ending each line with a backslash \. It is much easier to read. The backslash must be the last character of the line (no spaces after it):

surfquake quick \
  -w "./data/*" \
  -c ./configs/typical_config.yaml \
  -o ./output \
  -a

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
A variable stores a value (often a path) that you can reuse. Define it with NAME=value (no spaces around =) and use it with $NAME. If you change your data folder, you only change one line:

DATA=./data
CONFIGS=./configs
OUTPUT=./output

surfquake quick -w "$DATA/*" -c "$CONFIGS/typical_config.yaml" -o "$OUTPUT" -a

docs.title: Quotes around paths and wildcards
docs.text: Always write paths with wildcards between quotes: "./data/*". Without them, bash expands the * itself and passes a long list of files to SurfQuake, which may fail or be slow. With quotes, SurfQuake receives the pattern and finds the files itself. Quotes also protect paths that contain spaces.

docs.title: Stop on the first error
docs.text:
By default, bash continues with the next line even if a command fails. Add this line after #!/bin/bash to stop the script as soon as a command fails, so a broken step does not produce wrong results downstream:

set -e

docs.title: Keep a log
docs.text:
To save everything the script prints (messages, warnings, errors) in a file, run it like this:

./run_surfquake.sh > run.log 2>&1

docs.title: Running without questions: automatic mode
docs.text:
In a script nobody is watching the screen, so SurfQuake must not open plot windows or ask questions. Use the option -a (--auto) with quick, processing and processing_daily:

  • The traces are processed and written to the output folder (-o) in HDF5 format.
  • No interactive window is opened.
  • If you also want the figures saved automatically, set show_plot: false and a plot_output_path in your plotting configuration (see Plotting).

docs.title: Example: a complete workflow
docs.text:
This script chains two SurfQuake steps: it processes some waveform files with your own Python script, and then cuts and processes the waveforms of a list of events from a project.

#!/bin/bash
set -e

# --- Environment
eval "$(conda shell.bash hook)"
conda activate surfquake

# --- Paths (change them once here)
BASE=/home/user/surf_test
CONFIG=$BASE/config/config.yaml

# --- Step 1: process waveform files, with your own post-processing script
surfquake quick \
  -w "$BASE/nuclear/cut_event/*" \
  -c "$CONFIG" \
  --post_script "$BASE/scripts/my_script.py" \
  --plot_config "$BASE/config/plot.yaml" \
  -o "$BASE/output" \
  -a

# --- Step 2: cut and process the waveforms of a list of events
surfquake processing \
  -p "$BASE/project.pkl" \
  -i "$BASE/metadata/inv_all.xml" \
  -e "$BASE/events/events.txt" \
  -c "$CONFIG" \
  -o "$BASE/processed_events" \
  -a

echo "Workflow finished"

docs.title: The options used
docs.text:
Option Description -w Path or wildcard pattern of the waveform files (MiniSEED, HDF5, ...). Always in quotes. -c Processing configuration file (YAML): detrend, taper, filter... See Processing. --post_script Your own Python script, applied to each stream. See Scripts. --plot_config Plotting configuration file (YAML). -o Output folder for the processed traces (HDF5). -p A SurfQuake project file (.pkl). See Project. -i Station metadata (StationXML or dataless): station coordinates and instrument response. -e Event file (date, time, latitude, longitude, depth, magnitude). See Processing. -a Automatic mode: no plots, no questions.

echo simply prints a message on the screen.

docs.title: Repeating a task: loops
docs.text:
A for loop repeats commands for every item of a list. For example, to process every event folder separately:

#!/bin/bash
eval "$(conda shell.bash hook)"
conda activate surfquake

for folder in /data/events/event_*; do
    echo "Processing $folder"
    surfquake quick -w "$folder/*" -c ./configs/typical_config.yaml -o "$folder/processed" -a
done
  • folder takes, one by one, the value of every folder whose name starts with event_.
  • The commands between do and done run once for each folder.

Another example: save an image of every spectrogram in a folder.

for file in ./time_freq/*.spec; do
    surfquake specplot -f "$file" --split -d --save_path ./figures
done

docs.title: Running a script automatically: cron
docs.text:
On Linux and macOS, cron runs a script at fixed times, for example every night, without you being there. Open your cron table with:

crontab -e

and add a line like this one, which runs the script every day at 02:00 and saves the messages in a log file:

0 2 * * * /home/user/surf_test/run_surfquake.sh >> /home/user/surf_test/run.log 2>&1

The five fields are: minute, hour, day of the month, month and day of the week (* = every).

Paths in scheduled scripts

Cron does not start in your working folder, so relative paths like ./data point somewhere else. In scripts run by cron, use absolute paths (starting with /), or add cd /home/user/surf_test at the beginning of the script.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Test first: run each command by hand on a few files, and only then put it in the script.
  • Use -a in scripts, so nothing waits for an answer.
  • Quote paths with wildcards or spaces: "./data/*".
  • Activate the environment at the beginning of every script.
  • Use variables for the paths you repeat.
  • Use set -e to stop at the first error, and keep a log of long runs.
  • Use absolute paths in scripts run by cron or from another folder.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A seismic array is a group of stations close enough to record the same wavefront, but far enough apart to see it arrive at different times. From those small delays, beamforming measures two properties of each wave that crosses the array:

  • Back-azimuth (BAz): the direction the wave comes from, in degrees clockwise from North (station → source).
  • Apparent slowness (s): how fast the wavefront sweeps across the surface, in s/km. Its inverse is the apparent velocity.

Together they identify the wave: where it comes from, and which phase it is (a steep teleseismic P crosses the array almost at once and has a small slowness, while a crustal Lg travels along the surface and has a large one). With them you can detect and locate events with a single array, separate phases arriving at the same time from different directions, and improve the signal-to-noise ratio by stacking.

SurfQuake computes the beamforming over sliding time windows, so you follow how power, slowness and back-azimuth evolve along the record, and lets you open the slowness map of any window with four different estimators: FK, Capon, Multitaper Coherence and MUSIC.

Scientific Reference:

Rost, S., & Thomas, C. (2002). Array seismology: Methods and applications. Reviews of Geophysics, 40(3).

A complete worked example is the Beamforming Tutorial (North Korea nuclear test, ILAR array).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Far from the source, the wavefront that crosses an array is approximately a plane. It is described by the horizontal slowness vector \(\mathbf{s} = (s_x, s_y)\): its length is the slowness and its direction points along the propagation. A station at position \(\mathbf{r}_i\) (relative to the array centre) records the wave with a delay

\[\tau_i = \mathbf{s} \cdot \mathbf{r}_i\]

Beamforming tests a grid of slowness vectors between \(-s_{max}\) and \(+s_{max}\) in both directions. For each one, the traces are shifted by their delays and stacked (in practice this is done in the frequency domain, with phase shifts). If the tested vector matches the real wave, the traces add up in phase and the beam power is maximal; otherwise they partially cancel. The grid point with the maximum power gives the slowness and the back-azimuth of the dominant wave:

\[s = \sqrt{s_x^2 + s_y^2}, \qquad \text{BAz} = \operatorname{atan2}(s_x, s_y) \;(\text{towards the source})\]

The power of all grid points forms the slowness map: a picture of where the energy comes from in a time window.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Idea When to use it FK (conventional, Bartlett) Delay-and-sum in the frequency domain. Every direction is weighted the same. Robust, the reference method. Its resolution is limited by the array aperture: a broad peak and side lobes given by the array response. CAPON (minimum variance) Adaptive weights: for each direction, it minimises the power coming from all other directions. Sharper peaks, better separation of close arrivals. More sensitive to noise and to errors in station positions. MTP.COHERENCE Multitaper estimate of the coherence between stations instead of power. Low-variance estimate, insensitive to amplitude differences between stations (site effects, gains). MUSIC Subspace method: separates the cross-spectral matrix into a signal subspace (1, 2 or 3 signals) and a noise subspace. Highest resolution, can resolve several simultaneous waves. You must choose the number of signals; the values are a pseudo-spectrum, not a power.

The time evolution (sliding windows) is computed with FK or CAPON. The slowness maps can be computed with any of the four methods.

docs.title: What the array can resolve
docs.text:
• Aperture (largest distance between stations): the larger the aperture compared with the wavelength, the sharper the slowness peak. Small arrays resolve high frequencies well but give broad peaks at low frequencies.
  • Station spacing: if the stations are further apart than half a wavelength, the slowness map shows aliases (several peaks of equal power). The minimum spacing sets the highest usable frequency.
  • Geometry: irregular, two-dimensional layouts give cleaner array responses than lines or regular grids.

This is why the frequency band (fmin, fmax) must be chosen for your array: a band where the wavelengths are comparable to the aperture, but longer than about twice the station spacing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• An ObsPy Stream with one trace per station, usually the vertical components, with the same sampling rate.
  • An inventory (StationXML or dataless) with the coordinates of every station (-i).
  • The traces are cut to their common time window (padding with zeros where needed).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description How to choose it method FK or CAPON. FK by default. timewindow Length of each sliding window (s). It must contain at least a few cycles of fmin (e.g. 3 s at 1 Hz). Shorter windows follow fast changes but give noisier estimates. overlap Step between consecutive windows, as a fraction of timewindow. 0.05 moves the window by 5 % of its length (95 % overlap). 1.0 gives contiguous windows without overlap. Small values give a dense, smooth time evolution but take longer. 0.05–0.2 is usual. fmin, fmax Frequency band of the analysis (Hz). Only the frequencies in this band enter the cross-spectral computation. The band where your signal is above the noise, adapted to the array size (see above). smax Maximum slowness of the grid (s/km). The grid covers \(-s_{max}\) to \(+s_{max}\) in \(s_x\) and \(s_y\). Larger than the slowest phase you want to see. 0.3–0.4 s/km covers body waves and Lg. slow_grid Spacing of the slowness grid (s/km). Fine enough to separate the phases you are interested in: 0.01 s/km for teleseismic P, 0.02–0.05 s/km for regional phases. Computation time grows with \((2 s_{max} / \text{slow\_grid})^2\). output_folder Folder where the result is saved.

docs.title: Typical apparent slowness of seismic phases
docs.text:
Use these values to choose smax and slow_grid, and to interpret your results (they vary with distance and with the Earth structure under the array):

Phase Apparent velocity (km/s) Slowness (s/km) Teleseismic P (30°–90°) 12–25 0.04–0.08 PKP (core phases) > 25 < 0.04 Pn ~8 ~0.12–0.13 Pg ~6–6.5 ~0.15–0.17 Sn ~4.5 ~0.21–0.23 Lg ~3.5 ~0.27–0.30 Rg (short-period Rayleigh) ~3 ~0.33

docs.title: Config file (automatic)
docs.text:
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'beam'
    method: 'FK'
    timewindow: 3.0
    overlap: 0.05
    fmin: 0.8
    fmax: 2.2
    smax: 0.3
    slow_grid: 0.05
    output_folder: "./beam_results"

surfquake quick -w "./data/*Z*" -i ./metadata/inventory.xml -c ./configs/beam_config.yaml -a

The beamforming is a stream method that writes its result to disk; the traces passed to the next steps are unchanged. To analyse only a time window, add a cut_stream step before beam (see Processing Stream).

The result is saved in output_folder as <year>.<julday>.beam (year and julian day of the first trace), a compressed file that contains the complete result: power, slowness, back-azimuth, the parameters, the traces and the inventory.

docs.title: Interactive
docs.text:
In the plot of surfquake quick (with -i), select a time window with the keys u (start) and i (end), open the command prompt with v and type:

help beam
beam --fmin 0.8 --fmax 2.2 --smax 0.3 --grid 0.01 --win 3 --overlap 0.05

help smap
smap --method CAPON --fmin 0.8 --fmax 2.2 --smax 0.3 --grid 0.01
  • beam: FK time evolution over the selected window, with the same figure and keys as beamplot.
  • smap: slowness map of the whole selected window. --method: FK, CAPON, MTP.COHERENCE or MUSIC (in capital letters).

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
The result is a TraceBeamResult object with one value per time window:

Attribute Description relpower Relative power (0–1): the coherence of the traces for the best slowness vector. Close to 1 = a coherent plane wave crossing the array; low values = incoherent noise. abspower Absolute power of the beam. It depends on the amplitude of the signal. AZ Back-azimuth (°, 0–360, clockwise from North). Slowness Apparent slowness (s/km). T Start time of each window, as Matplotlib date numbers.

You can load and use a result in Python:

from matplotlib.dates import num2date
from surfquakecore.arrayanalysis.beamrun import TraceBeamResult

beam = TraceBeamResult.from_pickle("./beam_results/2017.246.beam")

best = beam.relpower.argmax()
print(num2date(beam.T[best]), beam.AZ[best], beam.Slowness[best], beam.relpower[best])

docs.title: Plotting and CLI Usage
docs.text: Beamforming results can be visualized and analyzed using the surfquake beamplot command-line utility. It reads a .beam file and provides interactive visualization and automated peak detection.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
surfquake beamplot -h

# Plot a saved FK beamforming result
surfquake beamplot -f ./beam_results/2024.123.beam

# Save the figure instead of showing it
surfquake beamplot -f ./beam_results/2024.123.beam --save_path ./beam_results/2024.123.png

The figure shows three panels sharing the time axis: relative power, slowness and back-azimuth, all coloured by relative power. A wave crossing the array appears as a group of high-power points with stable slowness and back-azimuth; noise appears as scattered, low-power points.

docs.title: Slowness maps
docs.text:
The figure is interactive. Point with the mouse at a time (for example a power peak), press a number to choose the method, and then press e to plot the slowness map of the window starting at that time:

Key Method 1 FK (conventional) 2 Capon 3 Multitaper Coherence 4 MUSIC, 1 signal 5 MUSIC, 2 signals 6 MUSIC, 3 signals e Compute and plot the slowness map

The map shows the power over the \((s_x, s_y)\) plane, with the slowness, back-azimuth and power of the maximum. The distance from the centre to the maximum is the slowness; its direction is the back-azimuth.

docs.title: Peak Detection
docs.text:
--find_solutions searches the time evolution for arrivals of given phases:

  1. For each phase, only the windows whose slowness is inside its slowness range are kept.
  2. The peaks of relative power are found among them.
  3. Peaks below --min_power, or outside --baz_range, are rejected.
  4. Peaks closer than 10 s to an already accepted peak are rejected, so the same arrival is not assigned to two phases.
  5. The strongest remaining peak of each phase is reported.

This is useful for automated or semi-automated phase identification and event location.

# Detect phase peaks with the regional shortcut
surfquake beamplot -f event.beam --find_solutions regional --write_path solutions.txt

# Custom slowness ranges (JSON format)
surfquake beamplot -f event.beam --find_solutions '{"Pn": [0.11, 0.14], "Lg": [0.26, 0.31]}'

# Add back-azimuth filtering
surfquake beamplot -f event.beam --find_solutions regional --baz_range 100 150

# Set the minimum relative power
surfquake beamplot -f event.beam --find_solutions teleseismic --min_power 0.4

The shortcuts use these slowness ranges (s/km):

regional teleseismic Pn 0.11–0.14 P 0.04–0.07 Pg 0.14–0.18 PP 0.06–0.08 Sn 0.20–0.24 PKP 0.05–0.07 Lg 0.26–0.31 PcP 0.05–0.07 Rg 0.31–0.40 S 0.07–0.12 SS 0.09–0.13 SKS 0.07–0.10 ScS 0.09–0.13 Rayleigh 0.20–0.40 Love 0.20–0.35

Tip

The best ranges depend on your array and distance. Compare the shortcut ranges with the typical apparent slowness of the phases, and use your own JSON ranges when needed.

docs.title: CLI Options
docs.text: Option Description --file, -f (required) Path to the .beam file. --save_path File path to save the figure (e.g. beam.png). The figure is then not shown. --find_solutions Phase constraints for peak detection: regional, teleseismic, or a JSON dictionary '{"phase": [smin, smax], ...}'. --baz_range Accept only solutions with back-azimuth between MIN and MAX (degrees). --min_power Minimum relative power to accept a peak (default: 0.6). --write_path Text file where the detected peaks are appended, one line per phase: phase, time, back-azimuth, slowness, power.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Filter and choose the band first by looking at the spectra of your traces: the beamforming only works where the signal is coherent across the array.
  • Check the array response: a slowness map of pure noise, or of a single clear arrival, shows the side lobes of your array; do not interpret them as waves.
  • Relative power is your quality measure: values above ~0.6 indicate a well-defined plane wave.
  • Back-azimuth deviations of a few degrees from the theoretical value are normal (lateral heterogeneity under the array and along the path), and they are systematic for a given direction: they can be calibrated with known events.
  • Small slowness = steep incidence: at very small slowness (core phases, near-vertical P) the back-azimuth becomes poorly constrained.

docs.title: Build MTI config files
docs.text: surfQuake core library incorporates and easy way to generate mti Config Files The only thing you need is a previously crated catalog and a mti.ini files that serves of template (just copy and paste the example in the explanation of config file from MTI). The routine will create the mti.ini files using the information from the event catalogs (date, latitude, lngitude, depth and magnitude) and from the rest of the fields from the template. This action will write a mti.ini file per event and ready to be used by MTI toolbox.

docs.title: Build MTI config files from CLI
Usage
docs.text: >> surfquake buildmticonfig -c [catalog_file_path] -t [mti_config_template] -o [output_folder] -s [if starttime] -e [if endtime] -l [if lat_min] -a [ if lat_max] -d [if lon_min] -k [if lon_max] -w [if depth_min] -f [depth_max] -g [if mag_min] -p [if mag_max]

docs.title: Interactive help
docs.text: >> surfquake buildmticonfig -h

docs.title: Run Build MTI config files from CLI
docs.text: >> surfquake buildmticonfig --catalog_file_path /mti_config_test/catalog_obj.pkl --mti_config_template /mti_confis_test/template.ini --output_folder /mti_confis_test --starttime "30/09/2021, 00:00:00.0" --endtime "30/09/2022, 00:00:00.0" --lat_min 38.0 --lat_max 44.0 --lon_min -2.0 --lon_max 4.0 --depth_min -3.0 --depth_max 50 --mag_min 3.0 --mag_max 4.0

docs.title: Build MTI config files from Library
Classes
docs.text:
BuildMTIConfigs 

class BuildMTIConfigs:
    def __init__(self, catalog_file_path, mti_config: Union[str, MomentTensorInversionConfig], output_path):

        self.catalog_file_path = catalog_file_path
        self.config_mti_template = mti_config
        self.output_path = output_path
        self.catalog = None

        if isinstance(mti_config, str) and os.path.isfile(mti_config):
            self.mti_template_configuration = (load_mti_configuration(mti_config),)

        else:
            raise ValueError(f"mti_config {mti_config} is not valid. It must be a valid .ini file for "
                             f"MomentTensorInversionConfig")

                       mag_min=3.0, mag_max=4.0)

docs.title: Characteristic Functions in SurfQuake
docs.text:
A characteristic function (CF) transforms a seismogram into a curve that rises when a seismic arrival starts. Raw waveforms are difficult to scan automatically: the amplitude of the background noise changes, arrivals can be emergent, and the onset is hidden in the oscillation of the wave. A good CF is flat and low in the noise, and jumps at the onset, so a simple threshold can detect it. CFs are the core of automatic event detection (coincidence triggers), phase picking and array processing.

Each CF responds to a different property of the signal:

CF Reacts to Strengths Weaknesses SNR (STA/LTA) An increase of energy Simple, fast, the classic detector Late or missed for emergent signals; sensitive to noise bursts Envelope Amplitude Simple, robust, smooth Only amplitude: misses arrivals that change the frequency content but not the amplitude Spectral entropy Concentration of energy in few frequencies Detects narrowband signals (tremor, LP events, later phases in a coda) Low time resolution (window based) Kurtosis Impulsiveness (non-Gaussian samples) Sharp, precise onsets in noisy data Does not help emergent signals; sensitive to spikes CWT Energy, spectral contrast, entropy, centroid or kurtosis in many frequency bands at once Combines several CFs from one wavelet transform; robust in low SNR More parameters to choose

All CFs are stream methods: n traces in, n CF traces out, with the same ids and the same time axis as the input. They replace the waveforms, so they are usually the last step of the workflow. Plot them, write them (-o), or use them in your own scripts.

Pre-processing

Every CF works better on clean data. Merge the segments, remove the mean, taper and filter in the band where your events have energy before computing the CF. The template surfquake make_config -c ch_functions contains this pre-processing and a commented block for every CF.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'concat'
  process_2:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_3:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_4:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 8.0
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True
  process_5:
    name: 'snr'          # <- the characteristic function: replace this block
    method: 'classic'
    sign_win: 1
    noise_win: 40

In the examples below only the CF step is shown: add it after the pre-processing steps, with the next free number (process_5 here). Each process_N key must be unique: a repeated key silently replaces the earlier step.

docs.title: 1. Signal-to-Noise Ratio (STA/LTA)
docs.text:
The STA/LTA ratio compares the average energy in a short window (Short-Term Average, the "signal") with the average energy in a long window (Long-Term Average, the "noise"). In the noise both averages are similar and the ratio stays near 1; when an arrival enters the short window, the STA grows much faster than the LTA and the ratio jumps. It is the classic detector of seismology (Allen, 1978).

For a trace \(x_n\) with STA and LTA windows of \(N_s\) and \(N_l\) samples:

\[\mathrm{STA}_n = \frac{1}{N_s}\sum_{k=n-N_s+1}^{n} x_k^2, \qquad \mathrm{LTA}_n = \frac{1}{N_l}\sum_{k=n-N_l+1}^{n} x_k^2, \qquad \mathrm{CF}_n = \frac{\mathrm{STA}_n}{\mathrm{LTA}_n}\]

The recursive version updates both averages with exponential decay, \(\mathrm{STA}_n = \tfrac{1}{N_s}x_n^2 + \left(1-\tfrac{1}{N_s}\right)\mathrm{STA}_{n-1}\) (and likewise the LTA with \(N_l\)).

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: method Description classic Classic STA/LTA: both averages over sliding windows that end at the current sample. recursive Recursive STA/LTA: the averages are updated with exponential decay. Faster and smoother. z_detect Z-detector: the STA expressed in standard deviations from its mean over the trace. Uses only sign_win.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description sign_win STA window, in seconds. About 1–2 periods of the dominant frequency of the arrivals: short windows react faster but are noisier. noise_win LTA window, in seconds. Typically 10–40 times sign_win. Ignored by z_detect.

docs.title: Config Example
docs.text:
process_5:
    name: 'snr'
    method: 'classic'
    sign_win: 1
    noise_win: 40

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Allen, Rex V. "Automatic earthquake recognition and timing from single traces." Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America 68.5 (1978): 1521-1532.
  • Withers, Mitchell, et al. "A comparison of select trigger algorithms for automated global seismic phase and event detection." Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America 88.1 (1998): 95-106.

docs.title: 2. Envelope
docs.text:
The envelope is the instantaneous amplitude of the signal. It is computed from the analytic signal \(x(t) + i\,\mathcal{H}[x(t)]\), where \(\mathcal{H}\) is the Hilbert transform: the envelope is its modulus,

\[E(t) = \sqrt{x(t)^2 + \mathcal{H}[x](t)^2}\]

It follows the amplitude of the wave without its oscillation, so an arrival appears as a smooth bump instead of a wave train. It is simple and robust, but it only reacts to amplitude.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: method Description FULL Raw envelope. SMOOTH Envelope followed by a low-pass filter at corner_freq. Recommended for triggering and for long records.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description method FULL or SMOOTH. corner_freq SMOOTH only: low-pass corner in Hz, written as a float (0.15, not 1). Lower values give smoother envelopes and less time resolution.

docs.title: Config Example
docs.text:
process_5:
    name: 'envelope'
    method: 'SMOOTH'
    corner_freq: 0.15

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: • Kanasewich, Ernest R. Time Sequence Analysis in Geophysics. 3rd ed., University of Alberta Press, 1981.

docs.title: 3. Spectral Entropy
docs.text:
The spectral entropy measures how spread the energy is over frequencies. In each sliding window, the power spectrum is normalised so it sums to 1, like a probability distribution \(p_k\), and its Shannon entropy is computed and divided by its maximum value:

\[H = -\frac{1}{\log_2 N}\sum_{k=1}^{N} p_k \log_2 p_k \qquad (0 \le H \le 1)\]
  • High entropy (close to 1): the energy is spread over all frequencies, as in broadband noise.
  • Low entropy: the energy is concentrated in a few frequencies, as in a seismic arrival, tremor or a long-period event.

So, unlike the other CFs, the entropy drops at an arrival. It is useful for narrowband signals and for arrivals that change the frequency content more than the amplitude.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description win Window length in seconds. It must contain several periods of the lowest frequency of interest. Longer windows give a more stable entropy but less time resolution. overlap Overlap between windows, in percent (default 50).

docs.title: Config Example
docs.text:
process_5:
    name: 'entropy'
    win: 5.0
    overlap: 50

Tip

For a CF that rises at arrivals and is whitened against the background noise, use cwt_cf with cf_type: 'entropy' (section 5).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Shannon, Claude E. "A mathematical theory of communication." The Bell System Technical Journal 27.3 (1948): 379-423.
  • da Silva, Sérgio Luiz E. F., and Gilberto Corso. "Microseismic event detection in noisy environments with instantaneous spectral Shannon entropy." Physical Review E 106.1 (2022): 014133.

docs.title: 4. Kurtosis
docs.text:
The kurtosis is the fourth-order statistical moment of the signal, normalised by the variance. Gaussian noise has a fixed kurtosis, while an impulsive arrival produces a few samples much larger than the rest and the kurtosis rises sharply. It is therefore very sensitive to the onset of impulsive arrivals, even in noisy data, and gives precise onset times.

In a window of samples with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\):

\[K = \frac{\frac{1}{N}\sum_k (x_k-\mu)^4}{\sigma^4}\]

which is 3 for Gaussian noise and grows when a few samples are much larger than the rest.

SurfQuake follows a multi-band approach: the trace is filtered in 20 logarithmically spaced frequency bands between fmin and fmax, a recursive kurtosis CF is computed in each band, and the bands are combined. An arrival that is impulsive in any band raises the CF.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description CF_decay_win Memory of the recursive estimator, in seconds. Shorter windows (e.g. 2 s) give sharper responses but noisier CFs; longer windows give smoother and slower CFs. fmin, fmax Frequency band of the filter bank, in Hz (fmax is capped at 0.98 × Nyquist).

docs.title: Config Example
docs.text:
process_5:
    name: 'kurtosis'
    CF_decay_win: 4.0
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 8.0

Note

Kurtosis does not help emergent signals, and it reacts to spikes: remove them first (remove_spikes). To combine kurtosis with other CFs computed from the same wavelet transform, use cwt_cf with cf_type: 'kurtosis' (section 5).

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: • Poiata, Natalia, et al. "Multi-band array detection and location of seismic sources recorded by dense seismic networks." Geophysical Journal International 205.3 (2016): 1548-1573.

docs.title: 5. CWT Characteristic Functions
docs.text:
The Continuous Wavelet Transform decomposes each trace into many narrow frequency bands, with a time resolution adapted to each frequency (see Time-Frequency Analysis). The result, the scalogram, shows how the energy of the trace is distributed in time and frequency. cwt_cf builds characteristic functions from the scalogram: since every band is analysed at the same time, the CF reacts to arrivals that are clear only in some frequencies, which makes it robust in low signal-to-noise conditions. The original CWT characteristic function was designed to turn the incoherent traces of a large, sparse array into coherent impulse functions suitable for beamforming (Cabieces et al., 2020).

SurfQuake computes the bank of wavelet atoms once and convolves every trace with it, so it is efficient for many traces and long records. From the same scalogram it can compute several CFs in a single pass and combine them.

docs.title: Mathematical description
docs.text:
Scalogram. Each trace \(x(t)\) is convolved with a bank of \(N_f\) wavelet atoms \(\psi_j\) centred at the frequencies \(f_j\) (logarithmically spaced between fmin and fmax, voices_per_octave per octave). The complex coefficients and the power scalogram are

\[W(f_j, t) = (x * \psi_j)(t), \qquad P(f_j, t) = \lvert W(f_j, t)\rvert^2\]

power. The mean over frequencies of the time derivative of the log power (Cabieces et al., 2020):

\[\mathrm{CF}(t) = \frac{1}{N_f}\sum_{j=1}^{N_f}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\log_{10} P(f_j, t)\]

It is large when the power rises suddenly in many frequencies at the same time, which is what an onset does.

Whitening and windows. The other spectral CFs compare a signal window after \(t\) with a background window before \(t\). First, each frequency is divided by its own background level, so all frequencies weigh the same (whitening):

\[\tilde P(f_j, t) = \frac{P(f_j, t)}{\operatorname{median}_t P(f_j, t)}\]

Then, with \(T_a\) = win_after, \(T_b\) = win_before and \(g\) = gap, the mean power in the two windows is

\[A^{+}(f_j, t) = \big\langle \tilde P(f_j, \tau) \big\rangle_{\tau \in [t,\, t+T_a]}, \qquad A^{-}(f_j, t) = \big\langle \tilde P(f_j, \tau) \big\rangle_{\tau \in [t-g-T_b,\, t-g]}\]

and the log ratio of the window amplitudes is

\[D(f_j, t) = \tfrac{1}{2}\log_{10} A^{+}(f_j, t) - \tfrac{1}{2}\log_{10} A^{-}(f_j, t)\]

power_win. The mean spectral ratio, a multi-band STA/LTA in the log domain (Gibbons et al., 2008):

\[\mathrm{CF}(t) = \frac{1}{N_f}\sum_j D(f_j, t)\]

power_mod. The ratio weighted by the energy above the background, so only frequencies with real signal energy contribute; the signed square root brings the result back to log-amplitude units:

\[S(t) = \frac{1}{N_f}\sum_j D(f_j, t)\,\max\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\log_{10} A^{+}(f_j, t),\, 0\right), \qquad \mathrm{CF}(t) = \operatorname{sign}(S)\sqrt{\lvert S\rvert}\]

centroid. The energy centroid in log-frequency (octaves) of each window, and its shift:

\[c^{\pm}(t) = \frac{\sum_j A^{\pm}(f_j, t)\,\log_2 f_j}{\sum_j A^{\pm}(f_j, t)}, \qquad \mathrm{CF}(t) = c^{+}(t) - c^{-}(t)\]

Positive when the energy moves to higher frequencies.

entropy. The normalised spectral entropy of each window, and its drop:

\[p_j^{\pm} = \frac{A^{\pm}(f_j, t)}{\sum_k A^{\pm}(f_k, t)}, \qquad H^{\pm}(t) = -\frac{1}{\ln N_f}\sum_j p_j^{\pm}\ln p_j^{\pm}, \qquad \mathrm{CF}(t) = H^{-}(t) - H^{+}(t)\]

Positive when the energy concentrates in fewer frequencies after \(t\) than before. With direction: 'down' the sign of the centroid and entropy CFs is reversed, and with 'both' their absolute value is taken.

kurtosis. The real part of each row of the scalogram, \(x_j(t) = \operatorname{Re} W(f_j, t)\), is a band-passed version of the trace. In a trailing window of length \(T_k\) = win_kurt, the excess kurtosis of each band is averaged over the bands and compressed:

\[K_j(t) = \frac{m_4\big(x_j;\,[t-T_k,\, t]\big)}{m_2\big(x_j;\,[t-T_k,\, t]\big)^2} - 3, \qquad \bar K(t) = \frac{1}{N_f}\sum_j K_j(t), \qquad \mathrm{CF}(t) = \operatorname{sign}(\bar K)\,\ln\!\big(1 + \lvert\bar K\rvert\big)\]

where \(m_2\) and \(m_4\) are the second and fourth central moments. It is about 0 for Gaussian noise and positive when the signal becomes impulsive.

Finally, every CF is smoothed with a low-pass filter at lowpass_freq.

docs.title: CF types
docs.text:
cf_type Idea Reacts to power Mean over frequencies of the time derivative of the log power. The original CF (Cabieces et al., 2020). A jump in energy: impulsive onsets, typically P. power_win Windowed spectral ratio: mean over frequencies of \(\log(A_{after}/A_{before})\), a multi-band STA/LTA in the log domain (Gibbons et al., 2008). Energy contrast. power_mod As power_win, weighted by the energy above the background (Gibbons et al., 2008). High contrast and high energy: strong, impulsive arrivals. entropy Drop of the spectral entropy of the whitened scalogram. Energy concentrating in a narrow band, even if the total energy barely changes: later phases inside a coda (typically S), narrowband signals (tremor, LP events). centroid Shift of the energy centroid in log-frequency (octaves). A signal spectrally different from the noise, e.g. a local event above the microseism band. kurtosis Multi-band excess kurtosis of the band-passed signals in a trailing window. Impulsive signals: weak sharp onsets, precise timing. Not emergent signals; sensitive to spikes.

Which one?

In our tests power_mod found the P waves (broadband, impulsive) and entropy found the S waves inside the P coda, which the energy CFs missed; kurtosis added weak impulsive onsets and sharper picks. Combining them with combine: 'stouffer' gave the best detections: cf_type: 'power_mod,entropy,kurtosis'.

docs.title: Required parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description fmin, fmax Analysis band in Hz. Keep it inside the band of the pre-processing filter. cycles Number of cycles of the wavelet. Larger = better frequency resolution, worse time resolution. 6 is recommended for cm. voices_per_octave Frequency sampling: 8 = coarse, 16 = standard, 32 = fine. wavelet_type cm = Complex Morlet (recommended), mh = Mexican Hat (real wavelet, power CF only), pa = Paul.

docs.title: Optional parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Description cf_type power One type, or several separated by commas. With several types they are combined into one CF per trace. lowpass_freq 0.15 Low-pass corner applied to the CF (Hz). Lower = smoother CF, less time resolution. The window-based CFs are already smoothed by their windows: use 0.5–1.0 for them. win_before 10.0 power_win, power_mod, entropy, centroid: background window before each sample (s). win_after 2.0 Same CFs: signal window after each sample (s). Use at least ~2 periods of fmin (fmin = 0.5 Hz → ≥ 4 s); win_before ~5–10 × win_after. gap 0.5 The background window ends gap s before each sample, so the start of an emergent arrival does not enter the background (Gibbons et al., 2008). 0 = no gap. direction up entropy and centroid: up = increase, down = opposite sign, both = absolute value. win_kurt 3.0 kurtosis: trailing window (s), 1–5 s, at least a few periods of fmin. Shorter = sharper and noisier.

docs.title: Combining several CFs
docs.text:
When cf_type has several types, each CF is standardised and they are merged into one CF per trace:

Parameter Default Description combine max max: fires if any CF fires (more detections, more false alarms). mean: fires only if the CFs agree (conservative). stouffer: sum divided by the square root of the sum of their correlations: rewards agreement and does not count correlated CFs twice (recommended). gmean: between mean and max, controlled by p. p 3.0 gmean power: 1 = mean, large = max. tolerance 0.0 Running maximum of each CF over ± tolerance s before combining, so peaks slightly offset in time add up. 0.3–0.5 s recommended; the trigger can move up to this amount earlier. norm mad Standardisation of each CF. mad: \((x - \text{median}) / (1.4826 \cdot \text{MAD})\). tail: the tail_quantile is mapped to its Gaussian value (0.99 → 2.33 σ), so the same threshold gives a similar false-alarm rate for every CF (recommended). tail_quantile 0.99 Quantile used by norm: 'tail'. It must be above the fraction of time occupied by events: 0.95 for ~1 h windows containing an event, 0.99–0.999 for full days. final_norm False Standardise the combined CF again, so thresholds mean the same for every combine rule.

In formulas, each CF \(x_i(t)\) is first standardised:

\[z_i(t) = \frac{x_i(t) - \operatorname{median}(x_i)}{s_i}, \qquad s_i = \begin{cases} 1.4826\,\operatorname{median}\lvert x_i - \operatorname{median}(x_i)\rvert & \texttt{norm: 'mad'} \\[4pt] \dfrac{Q_q(x_i) - \operatorname{median}(x_i)}{\Phi^{-1}(q)} & \texttt{norm: 'tail'} \end{cases}\]

where \(Q_q\) is the tail_quantile \(q\) of the CF and \(\Phi^{-1}\) the inverse of the standard normal distribution. Then, for \(M\) CFs:

combine Combined CF max \(\max_i z_i(t)\) mean \(\frac{1}{M}\sum_i z_i(t)\) stouffer \(\dfrac{\sum_i z_i(t)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i,k} R_{ik}}}\), with \(R\) the correlation matrix of the \(z_i\). For independent CFs the denominator is \(\sqrt{M}\) (Stouffer's method); for correlated CFs it is larger, so they are not counted twice. gmean \(\left(\frac{1}{M}\sum_i \max(z_i(t), 0)^p\right)^{1/p}\)

Output units: a single cf_type gives the raw CF (not normalised). Several types give a CF in σ units, so thresholds like 4–5 σ apply. Calibrate them on a quiet day: with combine: 'max' the background is higher than for a single CF.

    win_kurt: 4.0
    combine: 'stouffer'
    tolerance: 0.5

  process_5:
    name: 'cwt_cf'
    cycles: 6
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 8.0
    voices_per_octave: 16
    wavelet_type: 'cm'

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Cabieces, Roberto, et al. "Slowness vector estimation over large-aperture sparse arrays with the Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT): application to Ocean Bottom Seismometers." Geophysical Journal International 223.3 (2020): 1919-1934.
  • Gibbons, Steven J., Frode Ringdal, and Tormod Kværna. "Detection and characterization of seismic phases using continuous spectral estimation on incoherent and partially coherent arrays." Geophysical Journal International 172.1 (2008): 405-421.

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
CF Typical use SNR Event detection, coincidence triggers, first-arrival picking. Envelope Energy bursts, surface waves, coda analysis, tremor. Spectral Entropy Narrowband signals, tremor and LP events, discrimination of signal vs noise. Kurtosis Precise onsets of impulsive phases in noisy signals. CWT Robust detection in low SNR, P and S in the same CF, array processing with sparse arrays.

The CF traces can be plotted, written to disk (-o), used by the coincidence trigger, or analysed in your own scripts.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Each CF replaces the trace data with the calculated function, keeping the trace ids and the time axis. In the following example, all CFs were computed on the same filtered seismograms.

  1. Filtered seismograms: bandpass 0.5–8.0 Hz.

  1. SNR: classic STA/LTA, 1 s / 40 s.

  1. Envelope: smoothed with a 0.15 Hz low-pass filter.

  1. Kurtosis: 0.5–8.0 Hz, CF_decay_win 4.0 s.

  1. CWT: power_mod, entropy and kurtosis between 0.5 and 8.0 Hz, combined with stouffer.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Coincidence Trigger proceess input wavefroms to surrogate it as Charachteristic Functions. Then, associate CFs threshold in time spans to events. It is very useful to roughtly detect event time and separate picks for those events. surfQuake offer a coincidence trigger tool that uses signal-to-noise ratio and kurtosis CFs. The core of the coincidence trigger can be also found here ObsPy

References: 

        Allen, R. (1982). Automatic phase pickers: Their present use and future prospects. Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America, 72(6B), S225-S242.

        Poiata, N., C. Satriano, J.-P. Vilotte, P. Bernard, and K. Obara (2016). Multi-band array detection and 
        location of seismic sources recorded by dense seismic networks, Geophys. J. Int.,
        205(3), 1548-1573, doi:10.1093/gji/ggw071.

docs.title: Coincidence Trigger from CLI
docs.text: The command trigg runs the coincidence trigger. It is important to set the config.ini file to determine the methodoly and the parametrization. Let's see it.

docs.title: Config file
docs.text:
This config.ini is used for setting the coincidence trigger for a regional event scenario. Be in mind that is split in specific algorythms parametrization (SNR or Kurtosis), and the clustering, where user configurate the frquency bandwidth for processing waveforms and the association thresholds.

[Kurtosis]
CF_decay_win = 4.0

[STA_LTA]
method = classicstalta
sta_win = 1
lta_win = 40

[Cluster]
method_preferred = Kurtosis
centroid_radio = 60
coincidence = 4
threshold_off = 5
threshold_on = 35
fmin = 0.5
fmax = 8.0

Details:

CF_decay_win: The constant CF_decay_win (in seconds) determines the memory of the recursive envelope/kurtosis.

sta_win: signal window in seconds.

lta_win: noise window in seconds.

method_preferred: SNR or Kurtosis.

coincidence: Number of traces satisfying the threshold_on to declare an event.

threshold_on / threshold_ff: Threshold to determine when it is trigger the coincidences in the charachteristic functions.

fmin / fmax: Frequency range where is be applied the nawworband filter bank (kurtosis) or the bandpass filter for SNR.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
surfquake trigg

Key Arguments:
            -p, --project_file        [REQUIRED] Path to a saved project files
            -o, --output_folder       [REQUIRED] Directory for processed output
            -c, --config_file         [REQUIRED] Processing configuration (YAML)
            -n, --net                 [OPTIONAL] Network code filter
            -s, --station             [OPTIONAL] Station code filter
            -ch, --channel            [OPTIONAL] Channel filter
            --min_date                [OPTIONAL] Filter Start date (format: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), DEFAULT min date of the project
            --max_date                [OPTIONAL] Filter End date   (format: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), DEFAULT max date of the project
            --span_seconds            [OPTIONAL] Select and merge files in sets of time spans, DEFAULT 86400
            --plot                    [OPTIONAL] Plot events and Characteristic Functions
            --picking_file            [OPTIONAL] If set a picking file, this will be separated accoring to found events inside cluster

Usage Example:
            > surfquake trigg -p ./project.pkl  -c config.yaml -o ./output_folder -ch "HHZ" --min_date "2024-01-01 00:00:00" 
            --max_date "2024-01-04 00:00:00" --span_seconds  86400 --picking_file ./pick.txt --plot

            > surfquake trigg -h # request help

If user set for example --picking_file ./pick_file.txt, the picking file will be separated according to cluster parametrization. Be in mind that might be you have pick all seismograms inside your project and generate the picking file, but before locate, you need to associate this picks to events. The output of the coincidence trigger is as follows coincidence_sum.txt

date;hour;num_traces;coincidence_sum;duration
2015-09-17;15:12:08.4;17;17.0;56.1

In the figure it is shown a very simple example of the plotting output from trigg tool. The plot shows a vertical red line with the event and the CFs in orange together with the raw seismograms.

  1. SNR Coincidence Trigger

  2. Kurtosis Coincidence Trigger

    def __init__(self, projects: list, coincidence_config: Union[str, CoincidenceConfig], picking_file=None,
                 output_folder=None, plot=None)

        """


        Attributes:
        - projects (list): a list of projects surfproject objects
        - coincidence_config (str, CoincidenceConfig): path to config.ini or directly a Dataclass CoincidenceConfig
        - picking_file (str): path to the picking file

docs.title: Examples Scripts
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime
from surfquakecore.project.surf_project import SurfProject



def parse_datetime(dt_str: str) -> datetime:
    # try with microseconds, fall back if not present
    for fmt in ("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%f", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"):
        try:
            return datetime.strptime(dt_str, fmt)
        except ValueError:
            continue
    raise ValueError(f"Date string not in expected format: {dt_str}")

def make_abs(path: Optional[str]) -> Optional[str]:
    return os.path.abspath(path) if path else None


if __name__ == '__main__':

    project_file = "./project.pkl"
    config_file = "./config.ini"
    picking_file = "./nll_picks.txt" # output of surfquake pick or surfquake polarity
    output_folder = "./"

    net = None
    channel = "HHZ|BHZ"
    station = None
    span_seconds = 86400 # 1 day in seconds
    min_date = None # example 2024-01-01 00:00:00
    max_date = None # example 2024-01-06 00:00:00

    # --- Load project --
    sp = SurfProject.load_project(make_abs(project_file))

    # --- Apply key filters ---
    filters = {}
    if net:
        filters["net"] = net
    if station:
        filters["station"] = station
    if channel:
        filters["channel"] = channel
    if filters:
        print(f"[INFO] Filtering project by: {filters}")
        sp.filter_project_keys(**filters)


    # --- Decide between time segment or split ---
    info = sp.get_project_basic_info()
    min_date_info = info["Start"]
    max_date_info = info["End"]
    dt1 = parse_datetime(min_date_info)
    dt2 = parse_datetime(max_date_info)

    diff = abs(dt2 - dt1)
    if diff < timedelta(days=1):
        sp.get_data_files()
        subprojects = [sp]

    else:
        print(f"[INFO] Splitting into subprojects every {parsed_args.span_seconds} seconds")
        subprojects = sp.split_by_time_spans(
            span_seconds=span_seconds,
            min_date=min_date,
            max_date=max_date,
            file_selection_mode="overlap_threshold",
            verbose=True)

    config_file = make_abs(config_file)
    picking_file = make_abs(picking_file)
    output_folder = make_abs(output_folder)


    ct = CoincidenceTrigger(subprojects, config_file, picking_file, output_folder, plot=True)
    ct.optimized_project_processing()

docs.title: Create Metadata from CLI
docs.text:
The csv2xml tool allows users to generate StationXML metadata required by SurfQuake modules.

It supports two common scenarios:

  1. Only station coordinate file available → A valid StationXML is generated with default channel information.
  2. Station file + RESP/Inventory files available → Full response information is incorporated automatically.

docs.title: Run Create Metadatafrom CLI
docs.text:
# Ask for interactive help
surfquake csv2xml -h

# Command description
>> surfquake csv2xml -c [csv_file_path] -r [resp_files_path] -o [output_path] -n [stations_xml_name]

# Example
>> surfquake csv2xml -c ./stations_file.txt -r ./resp_files_folder -o ./output_path -n metadata.xml

Arguments

  • -c [Required], --csv_file_path → Path to station table
  • -o [Required], --output_path → Directory for output StationXML
  • -n [Required], --stations_xml_name → Output filename

Optional Argument

  • -r [Optional], --resp_files_path → Directory containing RESP/Inventory files

docs.title: Station File
docs.text:
The station table must contain at least the following columns:

Net Station Lat Lon elevation start_date starttime end_date endtime

Example (space-separated or CSV format supported):

WM ARNO 37.0988 -6.7322 117.0 2007-01-01 00:00:00 2050-12-31 23:59:59
WM AVE 33.2981 -7.4133 230.0 2007-01-01 00:00:00 2050-12-31 23:59:59
WM CART 37.5868 -1.0012 65.0 2007-01-01 00:00:00 2050-12-31 23:59:59
  • Columns are case-insensitive.
  • The tool automatically detects whitespace or comma-separated files.
  • Date format must follow:
    YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS

Start/end times can be wide ranges (e.g., 2007 → 2050).

If no channel information is provided, a default channel is created: - Channel code: HHZ - Sample rate: 100.0 Hz

  • Optional Columns (Advanced Metadata)

The tool automatically uses additional columns if present.

site_name Human-readable station name

clock_drift Clock drift rate (seconds/second). Applied to all channels unless overridden

  • Channel-Level Optional Columns

location_code SEED location code

If multiple rows exist for the same station with different channels, all channels will be included in the StationXML.

docs.title: Using RESP / Inventory Files
docs.text:
If a RESP (or StationXML inventory) directory is provided:

  • The tool scans recursively.
  • All channels found in RESP files are indexed by: (Network, Station, Location, Channel)
  • If the CSV does not specify channels, RESP channels are used automatically.
  • If the CSV specifies channels, matching RESP responses are attached when available.

RESP files must correspond to the correct Network and Station codes.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The updated csv2xml tool now:

  • Accepts whitespace or comma-separated files
  • Validates numeric and date fields
  • Supports multi-channel stations
  • Integrates RESP metadata robustly
  • Supports OBS clock drift metadata
  • Applies intelligent defaults when optional columns are missing

This makes metadata creation flexible, robust, and suitable for both simple deployments and advanced OBS workflows.
