docs.title: Dispersion Curves Processing
docs.text:
Dispersion Curves Processing in SurfQuake estimates surface-wave group and phase velocity dispersion curves mainly from Empirical Green's Functions (EGFs) produced by the Ambient Noise Tomography workflow, or from earthquake seismograms in SAC/H5 format. Moreover, can manually create an origin-station event record, but it have to be symethic from the central sample.

The module is exposed through the cwt_aftan command and implements an automatic Frequency-Time Analysis workflow. It can use a Complex Morlet Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) or the original AFTAN-style filter bank to extract group velocity ridges, estimate phase velocity branches, optionally apply a phase-match filter, and export dispersion tables and diagnostic plots.

The general workflow is:

  1. Select the EGF branch: fold, causal, or acausal
  2. Optionally apply a phase-match filter using a reference model
  3. Compute the time-frequency representation with Morlet CWT or AFTAN filters
  4. Extract group-velocity ridges
  5. Apply AFTAN-style jump correction
  6. Estimate phase velocity branches
  7. Save .grp.disp, .phv.disp, and optional PDF plots

The command is especially useful after running ant_cross_stack, because the stacked EGFs stored in HDF5 format can be processed directly.

References

Herrmann, R. B. Computer programs in seismology: An evolving tool for instruction and research. Seismological Research Letters, 2013, vol. 84, no. 6, p. 1081-1088.

Thanks bob!

docs.title: CWT-AFTAN CLI
docs.text:
This command measures surface-wave dispersion from EGFs or earthquake seismograms.

The default method uses Complex Morlet wavelets to build a frequency-time map and extract group velocity from the maximum energy ridge. The command can also run the AFTAN filter-bank approach with --wavelet aftan.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: >> surfquake cwt_aftan -i [input_path] -o [output_path]

docs.title: Interactive help
docs.text: >> surfquake cwt_aftan -h

docs.title: Key Arguments
docs.text:
-i,  --input              [REQUIRED] Input folder with H5 EGFs or a single H5/SAC file
-o,  --output             [REQUIRED] Output folder for dispersion tables and plots
--pattern                 [OPTIONAL] Glob pattern for folder mode (default: *.H5)

--tmin                    [OPTIONAL] Minimum period in seconds (default: 5.0)
--tmax                    [OPTIONAL] Maximum period in seconds (default: 150.0)
--vmin                    [OPTIONAL] Minimum group velocity in km/s (default: 2.0)
--vmax                    [OPTIONAL] Maximum group velocity in km/s (default: 5.0)

--wavelet                 [OPTIONAL] Filter bank: morlet or aftan (default: morlet)
--nf                      [OPTIONAL] Number of log-spaced frequencies (default: 100)
--w                       [OPTIONAL] Morlet wavelet cycles (default: 6.0)
--ffact                   [OPTIONAL] AFTAN filter width factor (default: 0.2)

--branch                  [OPTIONAL] EGF branch: fold, causal, or acausal (default: fold)
--source_type             [OPTIONAL] Source type: egf or earthquake (default: egf)

--min_db                  [OPTIONAL] dB floor used for display and ridge picking (default: -25.0)
--min_dist_kms            [OPTIONAL] Minimum separation between ridge peaks in km/s (default: 0.5)
--num_ridges              [OPTIONAL] Number of ridges to extract (default: 3)
--ref_tolerance_kms       [OPTIONAL] Maximum distance from reference velocity for ridge acceptance (default: 0.5)

--ref                     [OPTIONAL] Reference model name or CSV file (see section reference models for more details)
--wave                    [OPTIONAL] Surface wave type: rayleigh or love
--use_pmf                 [OPTIONAL] Apply phase-match filtering; requires --ref
--filter_param            [OPTIONAL] Phase-match Gaussian window width in seconds (default: 15.0)

--tresh                   [OPTIONAL] Jump detection threshold for group velocity cleaning (default: 3.0)
--npoints                 [OPTIONAL] Maximum correctable jump length in periods (default: 5)

--n_branches              [OPTIONAL] Number of 2π phase-velocity branches (default: 10)
--force_dist_km           [OPTIONAL] Override distance from waveform headers
--plot                    [OPTIONAL] Save a PDF frequency-time map and dispersion plot

docs.title: Output files
docs.text:
For each input file, SurfQuake writes:

*.grp.disp     Group velocity dispersion table
*.phv.disp     Phase velocity branches table
*.pdf          Diagnostic plot, only when --plot is used

The group velocity file contains period, group velocity and ridge power:

# Period_s    GroupVel_kms    Power_dB

The phase velocity file contains all valid phase branches:

# Period_s        k       PhaseVel_kms

docs.title: Reference Curves
docs.text:
Surface-wave dispersion images may contain:

  • multiple modes
  • interfering arrivals
  • noise-generated ridges
  • branch ambiguities
  • weak signal energy at long periods

A reference dispersion curve provides an expected phase velocity trend as a function of period. SurfQuake uses this information to:

  1. Select physically realistic ridges
  2. Reject spurious energy maxima
  3. Stabilize phase velocity branch selection
  4. Build phase-match filters
  5. Improve automatic processing in noisy datasets

Without a reference model, automatic ridge extraction can become unstable, especially for long-period or low-SNR measurements.

Built-in models are loaded with --ref. Available shorthand names include:

    ak135_earth
    ak135_earth_first
    ak135_ocean_deep
    ak135_ocean_deep_first
    ak135_ocean_intermediate
    ak135_ocean_intermediate_first
    ak135_ocean_shallow
    ak135_ocean_shallow_first

Users may also pass a full path to a custom CSV/TXT file, with columns comma separated: 

    period,phase_velocity_rayleigh,phase_velocity_love,group_velocity_rayleigh,group_velocity_love
    1.0,3.1425,3.2721,1.6231,3.0846
    1.1,3.3333,3.2941,2.6703,3.0435
    1.2,3.3896,3.3214,2.8773,2.9913

docs.title: Process all stacked EGFs in a folder
docs.text: >> surfquake cwt_aftan -i ./output/stacks/ -o ./output/dispersion/ --pattern "*.H5" --plot

docs.title: Process a period and velocity window
docs.text:
>> surfquake cwt_aftan -i ./output/stacks/ -o ./output/dispersion/ \
--tmin 5 --tmax 80 --vmin 2.0 --vmax 5.0 --plot

docs.title: Use a reference model
docs.text:
A reference model helps guide ridge picking and enables more stable phase velocity estimation.

>> surfquake cwt_aftan -i ./output/stacks/ -o ./output/dispersion/ \
--tmin 5 --tmax 80 --vmin 2.0 --vmax 5.0 \
--ref ak135_earth --wave rayleigh --plot

docs.title: Apply phase-match filtering
docs.text:
The phase-match filter is useful for isolating the fundamental mode before extracting the dispersion curve. It requires a reference model.

>> surfquake cwt_aftan -i ./output/stacks/ -o ./output/dispersion/ \
--tmin 5 --tmax 80 --vmin 2.0 --vmax 5.0 \
--ref ak135_earth --wave rayleigh \
--use_pmf --filter_param 15.0 --plot

docs.title: Process only the causal branch
docs.text:
>> surfquake cwt_aftan -i ./output/stacks/ -o ./output/dispersion/ \
--branch causal --tmin 10 --tmax 40 --plot

docs.title: Process a single file
docs.text:
>> surfquake cwt_aftan -i ./event.SAC -o ./output/dispersion/ \
--source_type earthquake --plot

docs.title: Use the original AFTAN filter bank
docs.text:
>> surfquake cwt_aftan -i ./output/stacks/ -o ./output/dispersion/ \
--wavelet aftan --ffact 0.20 --ref ak135_earth --plot

docs.title: Compare Morlet CWT and AFTAN
docs.text:
>> surfquake cwt_aftan -i ./data/ -o ./output/morlet/ \
--tmin 6 --tmax 28 --vmin 2.0 --vmax 5.0 \
--ref_tolerance_kms 1.0 --min_db -10.0 \
--wavelet morlet --num_ridges 1 --ref ak135_earth --plot

docs.title: Dispersion Curves Processing
docs.text:
>> surfquake cwt_aftan -i ./data/ -o ./output/aftan/ \
--tmin 6 --tmax 28 --vmin 2.0 --vmax 5.0 \
--ref_tolerance_kms 1.0 --min_db -10.0 \
--wavelet aftan --ffact 0.20 --num_ridges 1 --ref ak135_earth --plot

docs.title: Recommended workflow after Ambient Noise Processing
docs.text:
After creating cross-correlations and stacks:

>> surfquake ant_create_dict -d ./mseed -i ./meta/inventory.xml -s ./output/data_dict.pkl
>> surfquake ant_process_matrix -c config_process_matrix.json
>> surfquake ant_cross_stack -c config_cross_stack.json

run dispersion processing on the resulting stacks:

>> surfquake cwt_aftan -i ./output/stacks/ -o ./output/dispersion/ \
--pattern "*.H5" --tmin 5 --tmax 80 --vmin 2.0 --vmax 5.0 \
--ref ak135_earth --use_pmf --plot

The resulting .grp.disp files can be used as group velocity measurements, while .phv.disp contains the possible phase velocity branches for each period.

docs.title: Practical notes
docs.text:
1. Use --branch fold for standard EGFs when causal and acausal branches are both reliable.
  2. Use --branch causal or --branch acausal when one side of the EGF is cleaner.
  3. Use --ref when the ridge is weak, multimodal, or noisy.
  4. Use --use_pmf only with a suitable phase velocity reference model.
  5. Decrease --min_db to include weaker arrivals; increase it to make ridge picking stricter.
  6. Tune --tresh if jump correction is too aggressive or too permissive.
  7. Use --force_dist_km when the waveform header does not contain a valid inter-station distance.

docs.title: Example 1: Using quick
docs.text: This example shows how to basically use surfquake quick for waveform processing and visualization.

docs.title: Bash Command Example
docs.text:
# File paths can be absolute or relative

# reading a simple file
surfquake quick -w "/Users/admin/surf_test/carf220201000000.hhz"

# reading more than one file. It is a list of comma seprataed paths
surfquake quick -w "/Users/admin/surf_test/carf220201000000.hhz,/Users/admin/surf_test/arbs220201000000.hhz"

# Using wildcards. In the example will read all files inside the folder
surfquake quick -w "/Users/admin/surf_test/data/*"

Let's work with two seismograms.

After running the command surfquake quick -w ... both seismograms are plot on screen. I zoomed in the main event and then I clicked with right button over the first seismogram to select the starttime and I draged to the right to select the endtime. After this operation, I pressed the keyboard v to activate the prompt in the terminal. Over the terminal, I proceed first to cut the seismograms and plotting the spectrum of the first seismogram. Then, I pressed esc to re-activate the prompt. Then, I plot both spectrums and finally I plot the spectrogram. Finally I returned to picking mode. This are the actions I took in the terminal propt:

>> cut
>> sp 0
>> spec all
>> spec 0
>> help spectrogram
>> spec 0 3.0 95
>> p

If users want processing with no vilualization use the -a option and set and -o to set an output folder. This idea was designed to automatically process data. Be in mind that you can proceed using commands inside a bash script. Moreover might be useful to set your plotting configuration first --plot_config.

docs.title: Example 2: Using a Post-Script with SurfQuake
docs.text: This example demonstrates how to use a custom Python post-processing script with surfquake quick for waveform processing and visualization.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: You can enhance your SurfQuake processing by injecting a custom Python script into the workflow using the --post_script option. This allows advanced users to modify waveform data, inject metadata, or apply event-specific logic dynamically.

docs.title: Bash Command Example
docs.text:
surfquake quick \
    -w "/Users/admin/Desktop/surf_test/nuclear/cut_event/*" \
    --post_script /Users/admin/surf_test/my_script.py \
    -c /Users/admin/surf_test/config.yaml \
    -i /Users/admin/surf_test/metadata/metadata.xml

docs.title: Example Output
docs.text:
You can visualize the waveform data as output from this processing command. An example of what the output looks like is shown below:

Ensure you have your plotting configuration (--plot_config) properly set to produce visual output. In this example is shown the default plotting config. Drag with the right mouse from left to right to set the starttime and endtime. Thsi enable cut wavefrom or plot spectrogram from plotting commands, pressing v.

docs.title: The Post-Processing Script
docs.text:
This is the contents of the user-defined my_script.py:

import numpy as np

def run(stream, inventory, **kwargs):
    """
    User-defined post-processing hook for each event.
    :param stream: obspy Stream
    :param inventory: obspy Inventory (passed via kwargs)
    :param event: dict with keys like origin_time, latitude, longitude, depth (passed via kwargs)
    """

    inventory = kwargs.pop('inventory', None)
    event = kwargs.pop('event', None)

    if event is not None:
        print(f"Post-processing {len(stream)} traces from event at {event['origin_time']}")
    else:
        print(f"Post-processing {len(stream)} traces (no event info provided)")

    # Example: print mean of all traces
    all_data = np.hstack([tr.data for tr in stream])
    print("Mean amplitude:", np.mean(all_data))

    for tr in stream:
        tr.data = np.diff(tr.data)

    return stream

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
This script will:

  1. Print metadata about the event (if available).
  2. Concatenate all trace data and print the mean amplitude.
  3. Apply a numerical difference (np.diff) to each trace in the stream.

Such post-scripts are ideal for user-specific filtering, header modification, or transforming waveform data before further analysis or plotting.

You can insert this script into any SurfQuake mode that accepts --post_script, including quick, processing, or daily batch modes.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Always return the modified stream.
  • You can access additional metadata via kwargs (like event, inventory, etc.).
  • You can also modify trace headers using tr.stats.<attribute> if needed.

SurfQuake’s post-script interface allows flexible and programmable interaction with seismic datasets. Great for prototyping, automation, or embedding research logic!

docs.title: Example 3: Standard Events Processing
docs.text:
This example demonstrates how to use surfquake processing to perform batch waveform analysis and visualization using event metadata, inventory files, and configuration settings.

surfquake processing \
    -p /Users/admin/surf_test/project.pkl \
    -i /Users/admin/surf_test/metadata/inv_all.xml \
    -e /Users/admin/surf_test/events/events.csv \
    --plot_config /Users/admin/surf_test/config/plotting_config.yaml \
    -ch HHZ \
    -c /Users/admin/surf_test/config/config.yaml

Also, we can cut waveforms around the origin time of the events set in picks.csv, usinf -r ref. This is nice if we want to chop waveforms around specific time windows. Remember picks.csv have the same structure as events.csv and there is no need to set the columns lat, long...

surfquake processing \
    -p /Users/admin/surf_test/project.pkl \
    -c /Users/admin/surf_test/config.yaml \
    -e /Users/admin/surf_test/events/events.csv \
    -s CARF -ch HHZ -t 60 -r ref

Alternatively, we can cut waveforms according a specific wave speed. For example, very useful for cutting surface waves.

surfquake processing \
    -p /Users/admin/surf_test/project.pkl \
    -e /Users/admin/surf_test/events/picks.csv \
    --vel 4.5 \
    --cut_start_time 5 \
    --cut_end_time 25

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
• -p: Path to a previously saved project file (used for loading existing data).
  • -i: Inventory metadata file (StationXML or RESP).
  • -e: CSV file with event origin time and focal parameters, if -r ref option is inlcuded, only set otigin time is required.
  • --plot_config: YAML file defining how traces are plotted.
  • -s: Select only specific station (e.g., -ch HHN,HHZ). Comma separated list. Valid if a project loaded
  • -ch: Select only specific channels (e.g., -s ARNO). Comma separated list. Valid if a project loaded
  • -c: YAML config file specifying processing pipeline (filtering, tapering, etc.).

This method cuts traces based on a specified group velocity (useful for surface wave analysis).

  • --vel: Surface wave velocity (km/s) used to calculate expected arrival time.
  • --cut_start_time: Seconds before the expected arrival.
  • --cut_end_time: Seconds after the expected arrival.

docs.title: Sample Plot Configuration (plotting_config.yaml)
docs.text:
plotting:
  traces_per_fig: 3 # default 6
  sort_by: distance            # options: 'distance', 'backazimuth', or null
  vspace: 0.05                 # vertical space between subplots
  show_legend: true
  title_fontsize: 9
  plot_type: record         # 'standard', 'record' for record section and overlay for all traces at the same plot 
  sharey: False
  show_arrivals: False
  pick_output_file: ./picks.csv # picks will be written here
  auto_load_pick_file: False   # if user wants that picking file is automatically loaded and plot
  show_info_picks: False # show pick info on screen interactively
  backend: TkAgg # TkAgg (maximum robustness, default), MacOSX (only for mac), Qt5Agg (fast, picking  & interactive commands raise problems)

docs.title: Sample Processing Configuration (config.yaml)
docs.text:
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 5.5
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True

This processing pipeline: 1. Removes the mean. 2. Applies a cosine taper. 3. Applies a zero-phase bandpass filter (0.5–5.5 Hz).

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
• Figures are plotted interactively unless automatic is enabled: surfquake processing -a and it is set and -o to set an output folder.
  • Processed traces can be exported in .h5 format.
  • Cuts are based on the first teoretical arrival time metadata (events.csv) or selected method (--vel, -r, etc.).

plot_type: standard

plot_type: record

docs.title: Explore Data Availability
docs.text:
Before any analysis, it is really worth exploring the availability of your data: which stations and channels you have, which time span they cover, and where the gaps are. A few minutes here can save hours later: a missing component makes a rotation fail, a gap creates artefacts after filtering, and a station with a different time span can silently drop out of a stack or a beamforming.

surfquake explore scans your files and draws one horizontal line per file over a time axis:

  • Black line: the time span with data.
  • Red line: a gap inside the file (missing samples).
  • No line: no file covers that time (for example, a missing day).

Only the headers of the files are read, not the samples, and several files are read in parallel, so it is fast even for large archives. For big datasets the progress is shown on screen.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
surfquake explore -h

You can explore a set of files, or a project:

surfquake explore -w [path to your files, e.g. './data/*']
surfquake explore -p [path to your project file, e.g. './project.pkl']
Argument Description -w, --wave_files Glob pattern or path to the waveform files. -p, --project_file_path A saved surfquake project. -n, --net Network filter (with -p), e.g. ES,IU. -s, --station Station filter (with -p), e.g. EALB,EMAZ. -ch, --channel Channel filter (with -p), e.g. HHZ. --min_date, --max_date Time window (with -p), format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.

Either -w or -p must be set.

Wildcards

Wildcards select files by their file name, not by their header. With the usual naming NET.STA.LOC.CHA.D.YEAR.DAY:

  • './data/*': all files (non-seismic files are skipped).
  • './data/*Z*': all vertical components.
  • './data/*EALB*': only station EALB.
  • './data/*.2022.03*': days 030 to 039 of 2022.

Quote the pattern ('./data/*'), so that surfquake, and not your terminal, expands it.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
In this example, I simply navigate to the folder where I have placed three stations with three channels each, so nine files, and run the command:

surfquake explore -w "./*"

docs.title: What to look for
docs.text:
What you see What it means What to do Red segments Gaps inside the files. Short gaps: fill_gaps or concat before processing. Long gaps: avoid analysing those windows. One component shorter than the others The three components of a station do not cover the same time. rotate cuts them to the common window automatically; for other analyses, cut them with cut_stream. A station starting later or ending earlier Different time span. For stream methods (stacking, beamforming), cut all traces to a common window. A missing line A channel or a day is missing. Check your download, or exclude that station.

ℹ️ All the files of the same channel are drawn on the same row (NET.STA.CHANNEL), so consecutive daily files appear as one continuous line, and the location code is not shown.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
Once you know what you have, look at the details of each file with surfquake info: sampling rate, number of samples, picks... See Trace Header.

surfquake info -w './data/*' -c 3

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
FocMec is a core library that includes several tools. Each of this tools can be run from the CLI or yo can call them from your python script.

  • Automatic first motion polarity determination
  • Focal mecanism estimation
  • Plotting tools

References: 

    Chakraborty, M., Cartaya, C. Q., Li, W., Faber, J., Rümpker, G., Stoecker, H., & Srivastava, N. (2022). 
    PolarCAP–A deep learning approach for first motion polarity classification of earthquake waveforms. 
    Artificial Intelligence in Geosciences, 3, 46-52.

    Snoke, J. A. (2003). “FOCMEC: Focal Mechanism Determinations.” 
    International Handbook of Earthquake and Engineering Seismology, Part B, Academic Press, pp. 1629–1630.
    https://seiscode.iris.washington.edu/projects/focmec

docs.title: FOCMEC from CLI
docs.text:
1. Automatic P-wave first motion polarity determination. The inputs are the project and the picking file in nonlinloc pick format (i.e., might be generated using command pick). Output is an edited pick file with polarities.
  2. FOCal MEChanism determinations (FOCMEC) software for determining and displaying double-couple earthquake focal mechanisms using the polarity and amplitude ratios of P and S waves.
  3. Plot fault planes, T & P axis, and P-wave polarities.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
surfquake polarity
# Determines Polarities from P-wave first motion

Key Arguments:
        -p, --project_file_path     [REQUIRED] Path to a surfquake project
        -f, --picking_file_path     [REQUIRED] Path to a picking files
        -o, --output_file_path      [REQUIRED] Path to the new picking file edited with polarities
        -t, --thresh                [OPTIONAL] Threshold for Polarity declaration

Example usage:
        > surfquake polarity -f ./nll_picks.txt -p ./project_file.pkl -o ./nll_picks_polarities.txt -t 0.95

output file "nll_picks_polarities.txt"

Station_name    Instrument  Component   P_phase_onset   P_phase_descriptor  First_Motion    Date    Hour_min    Seconds Err ErrMag  Coda_duration   Amplitude   Period
EADA   ?    HHZ  ? P      U 20150917 1512 31.9770 GAU 7.00e-02 -1.0 6.23e+07 -1.0
ETOB   ?    HHZ  ? P      U 20150917 1513 00.3900 GAU 2.00e-02 -1.0 1.64e+08 -1.0
ETOB   ?    HHZ  ? S      ? 20150917 1513 56.3200 GAU 5.00e-01 -1.0 8.22e+07 -1.0
CEU    ?    HHZ  ? P      U 20150917 1512 08.3600 GAU 2.00e-02 -1.0 1.82e+08 -1.0

surfquake focmec
# Focal Mechanism from P-Wave first motion polarity

Key Arguments:
        -d, --hyp_folder        [REQUIRED] Path to folder containing hyp files
        -o, --output_folder     [REQUIRED] Path to the output folder
        -a, --accepted          [OPTIONAL] Number of accepted wrong polarities (float, default 1.0)

Example usage:
        > surfquake focmec -h # Interactive help
        > surfquake focmec -d ./folder_hyp_path -a 1.0 -o ./output_folder

surfquake plotmec
# Plot fault planes, T & P axis, and P-wave polarities

Key Arguments:
        -f, --focmec_file           [OPTIONAL] Path to a specific *.lst file
        -d, --focmec_folder_path    [OPTIONAL] Path to folder with all *.lst files (focmec output)
        -o, --output_folder         [REQUIRED] Path to the output folder
        -a, --all_solutions         [OPTIONAL] If set, all searching fault planes will be plot
        -p, --plot_polarities       [OPTIONAL] If plot P-Wave polarities on the beachball
        -m, --format                [OPTIONAL] Format output plot (defaults pdf)

Example usage:
        > surfquake plotmec -h # Interactive help
        > surfquake plotmec -d ./focmec_folder_path -o ./output_folder
        > surfquake plotmec -f ./focmec_file_path.lst -o ./output_folder -p -a -m pdf

Output plot example

docs.title: Classes & Methods
docs.text:
In this section, we will explain the class RunPolarity and we will explain how to manage your project from a simple example:

RunPolarity

class RunPolarity:

    def __init__(self, project, pick_file:str, output_path:str, threshold=0.9):
        """
        Attributes:
        - project (SurfProject): SurfProject object
        - pick_file (str): path to picking file
        - output_path (str): path to output_path
        Methods
        - send_polarities(self): Run automatic determination
        """

class FirstPolarity:

    def __init__(self):
        """
        Manage FOCMEC files for run nll program.

        Important: The  obs_file_path is provide by the class :class:`PickerManager`.

        Methods:

        find_hyp_files: 
        return list of hyp_files

        set_head(hyp_file_path): staticmethod, helps to set a string in comments of focmec input, check that input file is valid. 
        return header

        create_input(self, hyp_file_path, header): creates the focmec input from a hyp_file. return path to the input file

        check_no_empty(input_file): staticmethod, check that the input file has been created correctly.

        run_focmec(self, input_focmec_path, num_wrong_polatities, new_output_path=None): Run focal mechanism estimation and write the 

        output in folder new_output_path
        """

class FirstPolarity:

    def __init__(self):
        """
        Manage FOCMEC files for run nll program.

        Important: The  obs_file_path is provide by the class :class:`PickerManager`.

        Methods:

        return list of hyp_files

        return header

        output in folder new_output_path

docs.title: Examples Scripts
docs.text: Next, the example of using this class and its methods.

docs.title: Script for automatic polarities determination
docs.text:
from multiprocessing import freeze_support
from surfquakecore.project.surf_project import SurfProject
from surfquakecore.first_polarity.get_pol import RunPolarity

project_file = "/Volumes/LaCie/test_surfquake_core/testing_data/projects/surfquake_project_new.pkl"
picking_file = "/Volumes/LaCie/test_surfquake_core/testing_data/picking_file.txt"
output_file = "/Volumes/LaCie/test_surfquake_core/testing_data/picking_file_polarities.txt"
threshold = 1.0

if __name__ == '__main__':

    project = SurfProject.load_project(project_file)
    RunPolarity(project, picking_file, output_file, threshold).send_polarities()

docs.title: Script for running focmec

docs.title: Earth Model Settings
docs.text:
We have created a repository with an example of 1D and 3D model that describes the SW Iberian Peninsula using a Grandin et ., 2007 to rapidly visualize the model Cabieces et al 2020

The model 1D: In the root path to your model, in this case at /Volumes/LaCie/surfquake_test/test_nll_final/model1D create two files called modelP and modelS. The files will be exactly the same but called differnlt. The are easily described as follows:

LAYER depth VpTop VpGrad VsTop VsGrad rhoTop rhoGrad

  • depth (float) depth to top of layer (use negative values for layers above z=0)
  • VpTop VsTop rhoTop P velocity, and S velocity in km/s and density in kg/m**3 at the top of the layer.
  • VpGrad VsGrad rhoGrad Linear P velocity and S velocity gradients in km/s/km and density gradient in kg/m**3/km increasing directly downwards from the top of the layer.

Summarizing for the hungry users. Copy and paste this lines into your files called modelP and modelS and place it into the root folder previouly set as PATH_TO_1D_MODEL in the config file or for GUI users in the root folder you select as earth model.

LAYER   0.0  6.1 0.0    3.49  0.0  2.7 0.0
LAYER  11.0  6.4 0.0    3.66  0.0  2.7 0.0
LAYER  24.0  6.9 0.0    3.94  0.0  2.7 0.0
LAYER  31.0  8.0 0.0    4.57  0.0  2.7 0.0
LAYER    45.63   8.0412  0.000118   4.4737  0.000353
LAYER    56.25   8.0425  0.000118   4.4775  0.000353
LAYER    66.88   8.0437  0.000118   4.4813  0.000353
LAYER    77.50   8.0450  0.000118   4.4850  0.000353
LAYER    88.13   8.0463  0.000118   4.4887  0.000353
LAYER    98.75   8.0475  0.000118   4.4925  0.000353
LAYER   109.38   8.0488  0.000120   4.4962  0.000353
LAYER   120.00   8.0500  0.002775   4.5000  0.000200

The model 3D:

Every depth layer must be placed in files called, for example

    
For the P wave --> layer.P.mod5.mod
For the S wave --> layer.S.mod5.mod

Which means that inside this file there is the grid with the value of the Vp or Vs, for the layer at depth 5km.

The layer must be a matrix with the values in the rows from top to bottom S -> N, and from left to right E -> W. That's mean following the next example that the file corresponding to a depth layer 5km "layer.P.mod5.mod" could be like this:

    
4.5759 4.5735 ...... 4.5707 4.5677
4.5760 4.5755 ...... 4.5766 4.5670
...... ...... ...... ...... ......
4.6800 4.6500 ...... 4.6730 4.5678

This matrix means that, for example corresponds to geographic points long,lat (separated in cells of, dx dy of 0.5 x 0.5 degrees.

    
(-10.0,34.0) (-9.5,34.0) ...... (-9.0,34.0) (-8.5,34.0)
(-10.0,34.5) (-9.5,34.5) ...... (-9.0,34.5) (-8.5,34.5)
....... ..... ..... .... ...... .... ...... ...........
(-10.0,40.0) (-9.5,40.0) ...... (-9.0,40.0) (-8.5,40.0)

Warning grid cells must be [dx = dy = dz] for a correct interpretation.

docs.title: Grid Definition
docs.text: One the most important parts is the geographic framework settings. In the figure is displayed an example of stations distrubition (orange triangles and blue squares) inside the region of study(shaded square) with probable epicenters (red circle). Simply, the user must set the grid coordinates origin, the resolution dx, dy and dz, plus the number of points in the grid X, Y, Z. Remind that the configuration follow the left hand rule so positive W->E, S->N, Top -> Bottom in depth.

docs.title: Config file description
docs.text:
[GRID_CONFIGURATION]
LATITUDE = 41.0000
LONGITUDE = 0.0000
DEPTH_KM = -3.0
X = 400
Y = 400
Z = 50
DX = 1
DY = 1
DZ = 1
GEO_TRANSFORMATION = SIMPLE
GRID_TYPE = SLOW_LEN
PATH_TO_PICKS = /Volumes/LaCie/surfquake_test/test_real_final/nll_input.txt
PATH_TO_1D_MODEL = /Volumes/LaCie/surfquake_test/test_nll_final/model1D
PATH_TO_3D_MODEL = NONE
MODEL = 1D
P_WAVE_TYPE = TRUE
S_WAVE_TYPE = TRUE
#
[TRAVEL_TIMES_CONFIGURATION]
DISTANCE_LIMIT = 500
GRID = 1D

#
[LOCATION_PARAMETERS]
SEARCH = OCT-TREE
METHOD = GAU_ANALYTIC
  • GRID_CONFIGURATION:
    • LATITUDE: Latitude reference of the grid (not used in GLOBAL grids)
    • LONGITUDE: Longitude reference of the grid (not used in GLOBAL grids)
    • DEPTH_KM: Depth reference of the grid. Please use egative values to use stations with altitude above 0 m.
    • Grid Dimension in the X, Y and Z number of points and DX,DY,DZ the size in each dimension. For example the size in the X/East axis, X = DX*(X-1)
    • GEO_TRANSFORMATION: SIMPLE or GLOBAL.
    • GRID_TYPE: SLOW_LEN (Default)
    • P_WAVE_TYPE & S_WAVE_TYPE (bool): To create the velocity grid create.
    • MODEL: 1D or 3D
    • PATH_TO_1D_MODEL & PATH_TO_3D_MODEL: Set the path to your 1D or 3D model folder.
    • PATH_TO_PICKS: Set the path to the pick file. Picking file nll_input.txt output from associator toolbox contains all phase info o run the event locations. This picks can also be generated from pick the seismogram (i.e surfquake quick -w "./my_trace.mseed")
  • TRAVEL_TIMES_CONFIGURATION:
    • Select type of grid GRID1D or GRID3D and the corresponding wave P & S or S
    • Distance Limit: The maximum distance from the center of the grid - station, to compute the travel-time
  • LOCATION_PARAMETERS:
    • SEARCH: Algorythm to be used in the search of the location solution. Just available OCT-TREE that corresponds to the Octree algorythm.

    • METHOD:

      • GAU_ANALYTIC the inversion approach of Tarantola and Valette (1982) with L2-RMS likelihood function.
      • EDT Equal Differential Time likelihood function cast into the inversion approach of Tarantola and Valette (1982)
      • EDT_OT_WT Weights EDT-sum probabilities by the variance of origin-time estimates over all pairs of readings. This reduces the probability (PDF values) at points with inconsistent OT estimates, and leads to more compact location PDF's.
      • EDT_OT_WT_ML version of EDT_OT_WT with EDT origin-time weighting applied using a grid-search, maximum-likelihood estimate of the origin time. Less efficient than EDT_OT_WT which uses simple statistical estimate of the origin time.

NllManager

class NllManager:

    def __init__(self, nll_config: Union[str, NLLConfig], metadata_path, working_directory):
        """
        Manage NonLinLoc program to locate seismic events.
        :param nll_config: Path to nll_config.ini file or to NLLConfig object.
        :param metadata_path: Path to metadata file.
        :param working_dirctory: Root path to folder to establish the working and output structure.
        """
        self.__get_nll_config(nll_config)
        self.__location_output = working_directory
        self.__create_dirs()
        self.__dataless_dir = metadata_path
        self.__metadata_manager = None

docs.text:
import os
from surfquakecore.earthquake_location.run_nll import Nllcatalog, NllManager

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cwd = os.path.dirname(__file__)
    # Basic input: working_directory, inventory file path and config_file input
    working_directory = os.path.join(cwd, "earthquake_locate")
    inventory_path = os.path.join(working_directory, "inventories", "inv_surfquakecore.xml")
    path_to_configfiles = os.path.join(working_directory, "config/nll_config.ini")
    nll_manager = NllManager(path_to_configfiles, inventory_path, working_directory)
    nll_manager.vel_to_grid()
    nll_manager.grid_to_time()
    for iter in range(0, 10):
        print('Locating ', iter)
        nll_manager.run_nlloc()
    nll_catalog = Nllcatalog(working_directory)
    nll_catalog.run_catalog(working_directory)

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Seismic recordings become scientifically useful only when we know where, when, and how they were recorded. This contextual information is called seismic metadata. Whereas waveform files contain the recorded time series, metadata describe the seismic network, the stations, the sensors and acquisition channels, and (when provided) their instrument responses.

In SurfQuake / Integrated Seismic Program (ISP), metadata allow the software to associate seismic traces with their acquisition configuration and station information. They are essential for tasks such as mapping stations, identifying the channels available at a given time, determining source–receiver geometry, and converting raw recordings into physical ground-motion units.

Waveforms and metadata are complementary

A MiniSEED file typically stores samples and basic trace identifiers (network, station, location, channel, and start time), along with sampling information. It does not normally contain the complete station coordinates or the sensor's response. These details are provided separately by metadata files.

docs.title: Metadata formats supported in the workflow
docs.text:
SurfQuake / ISP uses station metadata provided as FDSN StationXML (.xml) or SEED dataless files. Both can describe station and channel attributes and instrument responses, although their structure and tooling differ.

SurfQuake has a specific tool to create metadata. You can also find example of STATIONXML file here and RESP files

StationXML is a good default for new projects, because it is widely supported in ObsPy and other modern seismic tools. Dataless SEED remains useful when working with older networks and archives.

For additional background, see the ObsPy tutorial on creating StationXML.

docs.title: How seismic metadata are organized
docs.text:
The commonly used FDSN StationXML format organizes information hierarchically:

Figure: An ObsPy Inventory contains networks, each network contains stations, and each station contains channels. Each level has its own attributes.

Level Description Examples of information Inventory A collection of network metadata. Networks, provenance, creation date. Network A group of seismic stations identified by a network code. Network code, description, active time span. Station A seismic site within a network. Station code, latitude, longitude, elevation, operational dates. Channel A particular data stream produced by a sensor/acquisition system. Channel and location codes, position, depth, azimuth, dip, sampling rate, operating dates, response.

A station may contain several channels, including different components (for example, vertical and two horizontal components), different sensors, or different acquisition epochs. The metadata can also contain multiple epochs for the same channel if its installation, calibration, or other properties changed over time.

docs.title: Identifying a channel: NET.STA.LOC.CHA
docs.text:
A seismic channel is commonly identified by four codes:

Network.Station.Location.Channel
   XX  .  ABC .   00   . BHZ
  • Network (XX): the seismic network identifier.
  • Station (ABC): the station identifier within that network.
  • Location (00): distinguishes separate sensors or data streams at the same station; it can also be empty.
  • Channel (BHZ): describes the recorded stream using the FDSN channel naming convention. For example, BHZ commonly denotes a broadband-class, high-gain seismometer vertical component, but the exact instrument and sample rate must be checked in the metadata.

The combination NET.STA.LOC.CHA plus the recording time is important: identifiers alone may not uniquely identify a historical instrument configuration.

docs.title: Station position and channel orientation
docs.text:
A station's latitude, longitude, and elevation locate the observation site. A channel can additionally specify its own coordinates, depth relative to the station reference, and orientation:

  • Azimuth: horizontal direction of the positive sensitivity axis, measured clockwise from north.
  • Dip: inclination of that axis from horizontal; in StationXML, a vertical channel pointing upward commonly has a dip of −90°.

These properties are important for station maps, source–receiver distances, rotating horizontal components into radial and transverse directions, and comparing observations at different sites.

docs.title: Sampling rate and operating period
docs.text:
The sampling rate (samples per second, Hz) controls temporal resolution. For a sampling rate \(f_s\), the sample interval is

\[ \Delta t = \frac{1}{f_s}. \]

The theoretical Nyquist frequency is \(f_N=f_s/2\). However, the usable frequency band also depends on the sensor response and acquisition filters.

The channel's start date and end date specify when a particular metadata configuration was valid. When processing historical waveforms, use the metadata epoch corresponding to the trace time. An absent end date can indicate an open-ended epoch; it does not by itself guarantee that the station is currently operating.

docs.title: Instrument response and physical units
docs.text:
A sensor and digitizer modify the input ground motion before it is stored as digital samples. Their frequency-dependent behavior is represented by an instrument response. In simplified form,

\[ D(f) = H(f)\,U(f), \]

where \(U(f)\) is the Fourier transform of the physical input (for example, ground velocity), \(H(f)\) is the instrument transfer function, and \(D(f)\) is the measured output (commonly in digital counts). The input/output units and the response stages must be read from the actual metadata.

To estimate ground motion, software removes (deconvolves) the instrument response, using suitable stabilization and frequency limits. Depending on the requested output and the sensor, the result may be expressed as displacement (m), velocity (m/s), or acceleration (m/s²).

Do not equate counts with ground motion

Digital counts are not automatically physical ground-motion units. A complete and correct instrument response is normally required for reliable amplitude calibration. Response removal can amplify noise outside the instrument's useful passband, so pre-filtering or water-level regularization may be necessary.

A complete response may comprise several stages, such as sensor poles and zeros, analog or digital filters, gains, and digitizer sensitivity. Overall sensitivity alone is generally insufficient to reproduce the full frequency-dependent response.

docs.title: How SurfQuake / ISP associates waveforms and metadata
docs.text:
A useful design principle in ISP is to maintain one metadata collection covering all stations and channels used in a processing project, rather than embedding station information in each MiniSEED waveform file. This can be represented by a single comprehensive metadata file where supported by the workflow.

When waveform files are read, the software can use their trace header identifiers and acquisition times to find the corresponding network, station, channel, and valid metadata epoch.

MiniSEED trace
  ├─ network = XX
  ├─ station = ABC
  ├─ location = 00
  ├─ channel = BHZ
  └─ recording time = ...
                 │
                 ▼
Metadata inventory (StationXML / dataless)
  └─ network XX → station ABC → channel 00.BHZ
                                    └─ matching time epoch
                 │
                 ▼
Station coordinates, orientation, sampling rate,
and instrument response (when available)

This separation makes the processing workflow easier to maintain, reuse, and validate. It is especially valuable when organizing waveforms by earthquake, calculating event–station distances, or performing calibrated waveform analysis.

Recommended preparation before processing

Ensure that the metadata collection contains the correct network, station, location, and channel codes, covers the dates of your recordings, and includes the instrument response for analyses requiring physical units. Check consistency between the sampling rate in the waveform header and the channel metadata.

docs.title: Practical examples with ObsPy
docs.text: ObsPy represents seismic metadata with the Inventory class.

docs.title: Read and inspect a StationXML file
docs.text:
from obspy import read_inventory

inv = read_inventory("metadata.xml")
print(inv)

for network in inv:
    for station in network:
        print(network.code, station.code,
              station.latitude, station.longitude)
        for channel in station:
            print("  ", channel.location_code, channel.code,
                  channel.sample_rate, channel.start_date,
                  channel.end_date)

To load a dataless SEED file, read_inventory() can also be used for compatible files and installed ObsPy support:

inv = read_inventory("metadata.dataless", format="SEED")

docs.title: Verify whether metadata match a MiniSEED trace
docs.text:
from obspy import read, read_inventory

st = read("waveforms.mseed")
inv = read_inventory("metadata.xml")

for tr in st:
    matched = inv.select(
        network=tr.stats.network,
        station=tr.stats.station,
        location=tr.stats.location,
        channel=tr.stats.channel,
        time=tr.stats.starttime,
    )

    channels = sum(
        len(station.channels)
        for network in matched
        for station in network
    )
    print(tr.id, "MATCH" if channels else "NO MATCH")

This is a basic start-time check, not a full validation. For a trace spanning a change of equipment or metadata epoch, check the entire time interval and whether the correct response applies to every sample.

docs.title: Remove the instrument response
docs.text:
from obspy import read, read_inventory

st = read("waveforms.mseed")
inv = read_inventory("metadata.xml")

st.detrend("linear")
st.taper(max_percentage=0.05)

# Example only: adjust the frequencies to your sensor,
# sampling rate, signal band, and scientific objective.
st.remove_response(
    inventory=inv,
    output="VEL",
    pre_filt=(0.01, 0.02, 20.0, 25.0),
    water_level=60,
)

Choose your response-removal frequencies carefully

The four pre_filt frequencies are illustrative, not universal defaults. They must be strictly increasing and should be compatible with the trace's Nyquist frequency and the instrument's usable passband. Inappropriate settings can severely distort amplitudes. Some sensors and target units also require special attention to the response-removal regularization.

docs.title: Where to obtain or create metadata
docs.text:
Metadata can be obtained from a network operator or an FDSN station service, or built from verified instrument and installation information. Useful tools include:

  • PDCC (Portable Data Collection Center) — a tool historically used to manage seismic station metadata.
  • Station Management Portal — a platform for station metadata management.
  • ObsPy StationXML tools — for creating and editing metadata programmatically.

For publicly available network metadata, ObsPy can query an FDSN station service. Requesting level="response" is important when the complete instrument response is needed:

from obspy.clients.fdsn import Client

client = Client("IRIS")  # Use an available FDSN provider
inv = client.get_stations(
    network="IU",
    station="ANMO",
    location="*",
    channel="BH?",
    level="response",
)
inv.write("station_metadata.xml", format="STATIONXML")

The example requires network access, and availability depends on the provider and selected station epochs.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Metadata tell us how to interpret seismic waveforms. Their hierarchical structure links networks, stations, and channels to geographical, temporal, acquisition, and instrument-response information. Within SurfQuake / ISP, keeping a coherent metadata collection alongside MiniSEED files supports reliable matching, station geometry calculations, and physically meaningful signal processing.

Before starting an analysis, verify not only that the station and channel codes match, but also that the metadata describe the instrument installed at the time of recording.

docs.title: Automatic Moment Tensor Inversion
docs.text:
Info

The focal mechanism of the pre-located events is automatically estimated using a optimized version of Bayesian Isola (Vackâr et al., 2017).

Warning

Please do not mix in your project seismic files with same net, station, channel but with different location.

docs.title: Run MTI from CLI
docs.text:
• Create quickly a template for a single event.

  • The MTI is run over a set of events. The Core library and CLI users, it can be automatically generated the MTI config files from a catalog object, see Build MTI config files in Utilities section.

surfquake make_config -c mti_config -o ./configs
  • Normally, you would like to review the solution so make a first run using --save_green. Once the solucion is generated review the fit of stations and proceed to depurate it., and run the command with option --use_pre_green. Do not touch the frequency range, only the stations/channels combination!.

docs.title: MTI Config File
docs.text:
In the following sections CLI and Core library the user can use mti_config.ini files to define each event where surfquake will carry out the MTIs. You can storage a single event per file. So, place all files inside the same folder. Please find here an example of mti_config.ini file (the name of the .ini file doen't matter just extension .ini). Additionally, be in mind that users can create automatically mti config files. Go to section Build MTI config files using the Library inside Utils. You can use the following mti config file information to make your own template.

[ORIGIN]
ORIGIN_DATE = 21/08/2018 00:28:57.000
LATITUDE = 42.7059
LONGITUDE= -7.6974
DEPTH_KM = 11.0
MAGNITUDE = 3.5

[STATIONS_AND_CHANNELS]
# add the station name follow by channels split by a comma , and use .+ for all channels
ELOB = HHZ, HHN, HHE 
EPON = .+
EMAZ = .+

[MTI_PARAMETERS]
EARTH_MODEL_FILE = /earth_models/Iberia.dat
LOCATION_UNC = 3000
TIME_UNC = 0.5
DEVIATORIC = True
DEPTH_UNC = 3000
COVARIANCE = True
RUPTURE_VELOCITY = 2500
SOURCE_TYPE = Triangle
MIN_DIST = 50
MAX_DIST = 500
MAX_NUMBER_STATIONS = 15
SOURCE_DURATION = 2

[SIGNAL_PROCESSING]
REMOVE_RESPONSE = True
MAX_FREQ = 0.08
MIN_FREQ = 0.04
RMS_THRESH = 5.0

Units: LOCATION_UNC [m], TIME_UNC [s], DEPTH_UNC[m], RUPTURE_VELOCITY [m/s], MIN_DIST [km], MAX_DIST [km], SOURCE_DURATION [s], RMS_THRESH [avarage ratio signal / noise]. If MIN_DIST and MAX_DIST automatically will be used MIN_DIST = 2 * rupture_length, MAX_DIST = 2 ** (mti_config.magnitude) * 2

  • Grid search: Defines a geographic grid centered in the estimated hypocenter where surfquake will proceed with the search of the best MTI.

    • Horizontal Location Uncertainity: Maximum horizontal range of the search.

    • Horizontal search step: Horizontal resolution of the grid search.

    • Depth Uncertainty: Maximum vertical range of the search.

    • Depth Search step: Vertical resolution of the grid search.

    • Time Uncertainity: Time shift around the event origin time.

  • Inversion Parameters: Defines parameters realtd to the source and the inversion process.

  • Traces Selection Criteria: Defin the criteria to include or not seismograms to your inversion

Now, that you have parametrized your inversion follow the steps:

  1. Inside Project: Load your project and load your Metadata.
  2. Inside The DataBase dedicated GUI.
    • Fill your DataBase loading that files from the folder where you have the location files.
    • Not required but very recommended populate your DataBase with the information from the output of Source. This will give the database information about Magnitudes and will facilitate the MTI.
  3. Make a Query to filter your Database
  4. Without closing DataBase GUI, press Run Inversion.
  5. Track the evolution of your inversions in the output dirctory, finally press print Results.
  6. Populate your dataBase with the information from the output of MTIs.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
As a seismic wave passes, each particle of the ground moves along a path in three dimensions. A three-component station (Z, N, E) records this path, and its shape tells us what kind of wave is passing and where it comes from:

  • P waves push and pull the ground along the direction of propagation: the motion is linear, pointing towards (or away from) the source and tilted by the incidence angle.
  • S waves move the ground perpendicular to the propagation: also linear, but perpendicular to the P direction.
  • Rayleigh waves move the ground along an ellipse in the vertical plane that contains the source and the station.
  • Love waves move the ground horizontally, perpendicular to the propagation.
  • Noise usually has no preferred direction: a cloud of points.

Particle motion (or polarisation) analysis quantifies this shape. With a single station you can estimate the direction of a wave, its incidence angle and its type, which helps to identify phases, check the orientation of the sensors, and separate body waves from surface waves.

SurfQuake plots the particle motion in three planes (Z–N, Z–E and N–E) and computes the polarisation parameters of Flinn (1965): azimuth, incidence, rectilinearity and planarity.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The three components in a time window form a cloud of points in 3D. SurfQuake computes the covariance matrix of the three components (after removing the mean) and its eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \lambda_3\) and eigenvectors. The eigenvectors are the axes of the ellipsoid that best fits the cloud, and the eigenvalues their squared lengths:

  • The first eigenvector (largest eigenvalue) is the main direction of the motion.
  • The ratio between the eigenvalues describes the shape: a needle (linear), a disc (planar, elliptical) or a sphere (no polarisation).
Parameter Definition Meaning Azimuth (°) Horizontal direction of the first eigenvector, clockwise from North. Direction of the main horizontal motion. Reported between 0° and 180° (see note below). Incidence (°) Angle between the first eigenvector and the vertical, 0°–90°. 0° = vertical motion, 90° = horizontal motion. For a P wave it is the apparent incidence angle at the surface. Rectilinearity \(1 - \sqrt{\lambda_2 / \lambda_1}\) 1 = perfectly linear motion (body waves); 0 = no dominant direction. Planarity \(1 - \dfrac{2\lambda_3}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}\) 1 = the motion lies in a plane (e.g. elliptical Rayleigh motion, or linear motion); 0 = 3D cloud.

The 180° ambiguity

A linear motion back and forth along a line has no sign: the polarisation tells the direction of the line, not which way the wave is going. For this reason the azimuth is given between 0° and 180°, and the back-azimuth of the source is either the azimuth or the azimuth + 180°. For a P wave, the first-motion polarity solves it: a compressional first motion (Z up) moves the ground away from the source.

docs.title: Interpreting the results
docs.text: Wave Rectilinearity Planarity Incidence Azimuth P high (> 0.8) high small to moderate along the source direction S (SV, SH) high high large (mostly horizontal) perpendicular to the source direction (SH) Rayleigh low to moderate high — elliptical motion in the vertical plane towards the source Love high high ~90° (horizontal) perpendicular to the source direction Noise low low — not meaningful

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Three components per station, recognised automatically by the last letter of the channel: Z-N-E, Z-1-2 or Z-Y-X. They are mapped to Z, N, E. Note that 1 and 2 are taken as North and East: if your sensor is not oriented to North, the azimuth is relative to its own axes.
  • The traces are cut to a common time window before the analysis.
  • Stations without a complete three-component set are skipped.

Getting good results

  • Filter the traces in a narrow band where the phase is clear (e.g. 1–5 Hz for local P waves): noise at other frequencies spreads the cloud and lowers the rectilinearity.
  • Use a short window around the phase: a few periods of the dominant frequency, starting at the onset. A long window mixes P, coda and S, and the result describes none of them.
  • If the instrument response is different between components, remove it first (remove_response).

docs.title: Interactive
docs.text:
In the plot of surfquake quick (or processing), select a short window around the phase with the keys u (start) and i (end), open the command prompt with v and type:

help pm
pm

The particle motion of each station shown in the plot is computed in the selected window and displayed.

docs.title: Config file (automatic)
docs.text:
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 1.0
    fmax: 5.0
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True
  process_4:
    name: 'cut_stream'
    method: 'reference'
    t_before: 0.5
    t_after: 2.0
  process_5:
    name: 'particle_motion'
    output_path: './pm_results'

In this example, the traces are filtered and cut around the last reference time before the analysis. A reference time (key w on the plot) is added to all the traces, so the three components are cut to the same window. In automatic mode, read files that keep the reference in their header, i.e. HDF5 files saved after marking it (see Trace Header).

ℹ️ With method: 'phase', each trace is cut around its own pick, and traces without that pick are skipped. Use it only if the three components of each station are picked; otherwise the horizontal components are dropped.

The particle motion is a stream method that writes its results to disk: the traces passed to the next steps are unchanged.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: • output_path: folder where the plots and the results are saved. Set it always.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
For each valid three-component station:

  • Figure <trace_id>.D.<year>.<julday>.png in output_path, with four panels:
    1. Z vs. N plane, with the incidence angle.
    2. Z vs. E plane, with the incidence angle.
    3. N vs. E plane (map view), with an arrow along the azimuth.
    4. A summary with azimuth, incidence, rectilinearity and planarity.
  • Text file pm.txt in output_path. One line per station is appended:
NET.STA.LOC.CHAN, YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Azimuth°, Incidence°, Rectilinearity, Planarity

The time is the start of the analysed window.

docs.title: Scientific Background
docs.text:
Particle motion analysis is widely used in seismology for polarisation studies, phase identification, wavefield separation, sensor orientation and source characterization. For more details, see:

  • Flinn, E. A. (1965). Signal analysis using rectilinearity and direction of particle motion. Proceedings of the IEEE, 53(12), 1874–1876.
  • Montalbetti, J. F., & Kanasewich, E. R. (1970). Enhancement of teleseismic body phases with a polarization filter. Geophysical Journal International, 21(2), 119–129.
  • Vidale, J. E. (1986). Complex polarization analysis of particle motion. Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America, 76(5), 1393–1405.
  • Jurkevics, A. (1988). Polarization analysis of three-component array data. Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America, 78(5), 1725–1743.

docs.title: Phase Picker
docs.text:
The phase picker of surfQuake uses the deep neural network PhaseNet (Zhu and Beroza, 2019) to estimate the arrival times of the P and S waves of local and regional earthquakes in continuous data. The picks are saved in three formats, ready to be used by the associator (surfquake associate), the location (surfquake locate), the first-motion polarities (surfquake polarity) or the interactive plot.

For a complete example with real data, see the Phase Picking Tutorial.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
PhaseNet was trained with a large set of P and S arrivals picked by analysts. For every sample of a seismogram it returns three probabilities that add up to 1: P, S and noise. A pick is a peak of the P (or S) probability curve higher than a threshold, and its height is the probability of the pick, between 0 and 1.

surfQuake runs PhaseNet on every file of a project:

  1. Reading and preprocessing. Every file is read, detrended (spline), merged (gaps filled with zeros), resampled to 100 Hz if it has another sampling rate, and high-pass filtered at 0.5 Hz. The trace is trimmed to the UTC day that contains most of its samples.
  2. Prediction. The network computes the P, S and noise probabilities along the whole trace. Files are processed in batches (3 files at a time by default), on the GPU if available.
  3. Peak detection. The peaks of the P and S curves above the thresholds become picks. Two picks of the same phase must be at least 50 samples apart (0.5 s at 100 Hz).
  4. Amplitude. For every pick, the maximum absolute amplitude of the trace in a window after it (10 s for P, 5 s for S, or until the next pick) is measured.
  5. Output. The picks are written in three formats (see Output files).

Things to know before picking

  • Each file is picked alone, one component at a time. The same arrival is usually picked on Z, N and E, giving up to three picks per arrival. The associator handles these duplicates.
  • PhaseNet works at 100 Hz, the sampling rate used to train it. Files with another sampling rate are resampled automatically; the pick times are not affected.
  • All the files should cover the same time span. The input length of the network is taken from the first file, so longer files are cut. Daily files are the ideal input.
  • Components named 1 and 2 are treated as E and N.

docs.title: Phase picker from CLI
docs.text:
Key Arguments:
        -f, --project_file        [REQUIRED]    Path to your seismic project file
        -o, --output_dir          [REQUIRED]    Directory to save pick results (created if it does not exist)
        -pt, --p_thresh           [OPTIONAL]    Threshold for P-wave probability (0–1) (default: 0.3)
        -st, --s_thresh           [OPTIONAL]    Threshold for S-wave probability (0–1) (default: 0.3)
        -n, --net                 [OPTIONAL]    Network code filter (default: *)
        -s, --station             [OPTIONAL]    Station code filter (default: *, e.g. "SFS|ARNO")
        -ch, --channel            [OPTIONAL]    Channel filter (default: *, e.g. "BH?")
        --min_date                [OPTIONAL]    Filter Start date (format: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), DEFAULT min date of the project
        --max_date                [OPTIONAL]    Filter End date   (format: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), DEFAULT max date of the project
        --device                  [OPTIONAL]    auto | cpu | gpu (default: auto, the GPU if available)
        -v, --verbose             [OPTIONAL]    Print the number of P and S picks of every file

The filters -n, -s and -ch accept a pattern with * and ? ("HH?", "E*") or a list of names separated by | ("ARNO|UCM|EMAL"). Write them between quotes. --min_date and --max_date select the files of the project that cover the interval; they do not cut the files.

docs.title: Interactive help
docs.text: >> surfquake pick -h

docs.title: Run Phase Picker from CLI
docs.text:
>> surfquake pick -f ./project/surfquake_project.pkl -o ./picks -pt 0.3 -st 0.3 --verbose

Only the vertical components of some stations, on the CPU:

>> surfquake pick -f ./project/surfquake_project.pkl -o ./picks -s "ARNO|UCM" -ch "HHZ" --device cpu

At the end, a summary is printed with the number of files, stations with picks, P and S picks, and the total time.

docs.title: Choosing the thresholds
docs.text: A low threshold finds the arrivals of small events but also picks noise; a high threshold keeps only clear arrivals but misses small events and many S waves, whose probabilities are usually lower than those of the P waves. The usual strategy is to keep the default (0.3) and let the association and the location reject the false picks, which do not fit with the other stations.

docs.text:
--output_dir
    --original_picks.csv
    --nll_picks.txt
    --20220131
        --CA.ARBS.P.txt
        --CA.ARBS.S.txt
        ......

docs.title: original_picks.csv
docs.text:
The complete table, one line per pick:

date,fname,year,month,day,net,station,flag,tt,date_time,weight,amplitude,phase,channel
20220131,CA.ARBS.P,2022,1,31,CA,ARBS,1,39383.88,2022-01-31T10:56:23.880000,0.5383206605911255,8557892.700195312,P,HHZ
20220131,CA.ARBS.S,2022,1,31,CA,ARBS,1,85480.59,2022-01-31T23:44:40.590000,0.30124416947364807,8481788.269042969,S,HHZ
Column Meaning date Day of the file (YYYYMMDD) fname NET.STATION.PHASE year, month, day Day of the file net, station, channel Where the pick was made flag Always 1 tt Arrival time in seconds from 00:00:00 of the day date_time Arrival time (UTC) weight Probability of the pick given by PhaseNet (0–1) amplitude Maximum amplitude after the pick, in counts multiplied by a fixed factor (2080 × 25). It is not a calibrated amplitude: use it only to compare picks of the same channel phase P or S

docs.title: Daily folders (REAL format)
docs.text:
One folder per day (YYYYMMDD) and one file per station and phase (NET.STATION.P.txt, NET.STATION.S.txt), with three columns: tt, probability and amplitude, sorted by time. This is the input of the associator REAL (surfquake associate -p output_dir).

39383.88 0.538321 8.557893e+06

docs.title: nll_picks.txt (NonLinLoc format)
docs.text:
All the picks in the NonLinLoc phase format:

Station_name    Instrument  Component   P_phase_onset   P_phase_descriptor  First_Motion    Date    Hour_min    Seconds Err ErrMag  Coda_duration   Amplitude   Period
ARBS   ?    HHZ  ? P      ? 20220131 1056 23.8800 GAU 5.00e-01 -1.00e+00 8.56e+06 -1.00e+00

The uncertainty ErrMag (in seconds) is obtained from the probability of the pick:

Probability ErrMag (s) > 0.95 0.02 0.90 – 0.95 0.04 0.80 – 0.90 0.07 0.70 – 0.80 0.10 0.60 – 0.70 0.15 ≤ 0.60 0.50

This file can be loaded in the interactive plot with load_picks --file nll_picks.txt (see Plotting Interaction), and is the input of surfquake polarity.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
PhasenetISP

class PhasenetISP:
    def __init__(files, batch_size=3, highpass_filter=0.5, min_p_prob=0.3, min_s_prob=0.3, min_peak_distance=50,
                 amplitude=False, output=None, device="auto", verbose=False):

    """
    Main class to initialize the picker

    :param files: the project dictionary (SurfProject.project), with the paths of the seismograms and their stats
    :type dict: required (see Project section)

    :param batch_size: number of files processed at once (larger batch size uses more memory)
    :type int:

    :param highpass_filter: corner frequency (Hz) of the high-pass filter applied to the raw seismogram.
                            Set to 0 to not apply any pre-filter
    :type float:

    :param min_p_prob: probability threshold for P picks
    :type float:

    :param min_s_prob: probability threshold for S picks
    :type float:

    :param min_peak_distance: minimum distance in samples between two picks of the same phase
    :type int:

    :param amplitude: if True, the amplitude after every pick is measured
    :type bool:

    :param output: output directory, created if it does not exist (optional)
    :type str:

    :param device: "auto" (GPU if available, otherwise CPU), "cpu" or "gpu"
    :type str:

    :param verbose: print the number of P and S picks of every file
    :type bool:

    :returns:
    :rtype: :class:`surfquakecore.phasenet.phasenet_handler.PhasenetISP`
    """

PhasenetUtils: static methods to convert and write the picks.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
PhasenetISP.phasenet

# instance method
def phasenet(self):
    """
    Runs PhaseNet on all the files of the project.

    :return: a pandas DataFrame with the raw predictions (one row per file)
    """

PhasenetUtils.split_picks

@staticmethod
def split_picks(picks):
    """
    Converts the output of phasenet() into a table with one row per pick
    (the columns of original_picks.csv).

    :param picks: output of PhasenetISP.phasenet()
    :type picks: pandas DataFrame
    :return: pandas DataFrame
    """

PhasenetUtils.convert2real

@staticmethod
def convert2real(picks, pick_dir: str, clean_output_folder=False):
    """
    Writes the picks in daily folders, in the input format of the associator REAL.

    :param picks: output of split_picks
    :param pick_dir: output directory
    :param clean_output_folder: if True, the content of pick_dir is deleted first
    """

PhasenetUtils.save_original_picks

@staticmethod
def save_original_picks(original_picks, original_p_dir):
    """
    Writes original_picks.csv.

    :param original_picks: output of split_picks
    :param original_p_dir: output directory
    """

PhasenetUtils.write_nlloc_format

@staticmethod
def write_nlloc_format(dataframe, output, starttime=None, endtime=None):
    """
    Writes nll_picks.txt in NonLinLoc phase format.

    :param dataframe: output of split_picks
    :param output: output directory
    :param starttime: only picks after this time (optional, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S" or UTCDateTime)
    :param endtime: only picks before this time (optional)
    """

docs.title: Example using library
docs.text:
from multiprocessing import freeze_support
from surfquakecore.phasenet.phasenet_handler import PhasenetUtils
from surfquakecore.phasenet.phasenet_handler import PhasenetISP
from surfquakecore.project.surf_project import SurfProject

### Set Paths to project file and output folder ###
path_to_project = "./project/surfquake_project.pkl"
output_picks = "./picks"

if __name__ == '__main__':
    freeze_support()

    # Load project
    sp_loaded = SurfProject.load_project(path_to_project_file=path_to_project)

    # Instantiate the class PhasenetISP
    phISP = PhasenetISP(sp_loaded.project, amplitude=True, min_p_prob=0.30, min_s_prob=0.30, output=output_picks)

    # Running Stage
    picks = phISP.phasenet()

    # From PhaseNet output to the three output formats
    picks_results = PhasenetUtils.split_picks(picks)
    PhasenetUtils.convert2real(picks_results, output_picks)
    PhasenetUtils.save_original_picks(picks_results, output_picks)
    PhasenetUtils.write_nlloc_format(picks_results, output_picks)

if __name__ == '__main__': and freeze_support() are needed because the files are read in parallel.
