docs.title: Processing Individual Traces Options
docs.text:
Trace methods are applied to each trace independently: the result of one trace never depends on the others. They are the building blocks of any processing workflow: preparing the waveforms (gaps, trends, edges), changing their physical meaning (instrument response, derivative, integral), selecting the frequency content (filters, resampling) and cleaning them (denoising, spikes, normalisation).

Each method is a step under the Analysis section of your config file. Steps run in order: process_1, process_2, ...

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05

General rules

  • Each process_N key must be unique. A repeated key silently replaces the earlier step.
  • Times are in seconds, frequencies in Hz.
  • Write decimals with a dot (0.5, 2.0). Some options require a float: fmin: 1 fails, fmin: 1.0 works.
  • A full reference with every method is available with surfquake make_config -c config_all.

A typical workflow follows this order:

  1. Prepare the data: fill_gaps, cut, rmean, taper.
  2. Physical units: remove_response, differentiate / integrate.
  3. Frequency content: filter, resample.
  4. Clean: remove_spikes, wavelet_denoise, wiener_smoothing, wiener_filter, smoothing.
  5. Normalise: normalize, time_normalization, whitening.

docs.title: Fill Gaps
docs.text:
Real data often contain gaps (missing samples due to telemetry problems, instrument restarts...) or are split into several segments. Most signal processing operations (FFT, filters, correlations) need a continuous, evenly sampled series. fill_gaps merges the segments of the same channel and fills the missing samples.

Parameter Values Description method latest Repeat the last valid value across the gap (a flat line). interpolate Linear interpolation between the samples on both sides of the gap. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'fill_gaps'
    method: 'latest'

Warning

Filling a gap invents data. For short gaps (a few samples) it is harmless; for long gaps the filled segment can create artefacts after filtering (steps at the edges of the gap ring like an impulse). Avoid interpreting signals inside long filled gaps.

docs.title: Cut
docs.text:
Keep only a time window of the trace. Cutting reduces the computation time and focuses the analysis on the signal of interest (an event, a phase, a noise window).

Parameter Description method absolute: between two dates. phase: around a pick of the trace. reference: around the last reference time saved in the trace header. start, end (absolute) UTC date-times, e.g. 2018-10-26T05:20:03. phase_name (phase) name of the picked phase, e.g. 'P'. t_before, t_after (phase, reference) seconds before and after the pick or reference (floats). pad (optional, default False) if True, the window can go beyond the data; the extra samples are filled with fill_value. fill_value (optional, default None) value for the padded samples. With None, traces with gaps become NumPy masked arrays. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'cut'
    method: 'absolute'
    start: 2018-10-26T05:20:03
    end: 2018-10-26T06:25:03

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'cut'
    method: 'phase'
    phase_name: 'P'
    t_before: 10.5
    t_after: 120.0

Tip

Picks and references are stored in the trace header, see Trace Header. To cut all traces of a stream to a common window, use cut_stream in Processing Stream.

docs.title: Detrending (rmean)
docs.text:
Seismic records usually carry an offset (DC level) and slow trends (sensor drift, temperature, tilt). They are not part of the seismic signal, and they are harmful for later steps: an offset becomes a huge peak at 0 Hz in the spectrum, and a trend behaves like a very long-period signal that leaks energy into the band of interest after filtering.

method What it removes simple A straight line joining the first and the last sample. linear The best-fit (least-squares) straight line. The usual choice. constant / demean The mean value only. polynomial A best-fit polynomial of degree order (int). For curved drifts. spline A smoothing spline of degree order (1–5) with nodes every dspline samples (int). For complex, slow drifts. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'polynomial'
    order: 3

docs.title: Tapering
docs.text:
The FFT assumes that the signal repeats periodically. If the trace does not start and end at zero, this repetition creates a sudden jump at the edges, which spreads energy over all frequencies (spectral leakage) and makes filters ring at the beginning and end of the trace. A taper is a window that smoothly brings the trace ends to zero.

Parameter Description method Window shape: cosine, hann, hamming, blackman, kaiser, flattop, slepian, bartlett, triang, ... (ObsPy window types). max_percentage Fraction of the trace tapered at each end, 0.0–0.5 (float). 0.05 = 5 %. max_length (optional) maximum taper length at each end, in seconds. side (optional, default both) both, left or right. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05

Tip

Always detrend before tapering, and taper before filtering, resampling or any FFT-based method. A 5 % cosine taper is a good default. Keep in mind that the tapered ends are attenuated: do not place your signal of interest there.

docs.title: Remove Instrument Response
docs.text:
A seismometer does not record ground motion directly: it records counts, the output of the sensor and the digitizer. Their response depends on frequency (a broadband sensor, for example, is flat in velocity only between its corner periods). Removing the response deconvolves the instrument and converts the counts into ground displacement, velocity or acceleration, so that records of different stations can be compared.

Deconvolution means dividing by the instrument spectrum. Where the instrument is not sensitive (very low and very high frequencies) this division amplifies noise enormously, so two stabilisation tools are used:

Parameter Description units Output: DISP (m), VEL (m/s), ACC (m/s²) or Wood Anderson (simulates a Wood-Anderson seismograph, used for local magnitudes). pre_filt Four frequencies [f1, f2, f3, f4] (Hz) of a cosine band-pass applied in the frequency domain: flat between f2 and f3, tapered to zero below f1 and above f4. Choose f4 below the Nyquist frequency. water_level Water level in dB below the maximum of the response. It sets a floor to the instrument spectrum, so the division never explodes where the response is very small. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'remove_response'
    water_level: 90
    units: 'VEL'
    pre_filt: [0.005, 0.008, 45, 48]

⚠️ WARNING: Remember to include your inventory: e.g., surfquake quick -w "waveform_file" -i "inventory_file.xml". If the response of a trace is not found, its data are removed and a message is printed.

docs.title: Differentiate
docs.text:
Computes the time derivative of the trace, for example to convert displacement into velocity, or velocity into acceleration. In the frequency domain, differentiation multiplies the spectrum by \(i\omega\): it amplifies high frequencies.

method Description spectral Multiplies the spectrum by \(i 2\pi f\) (after demean, taper and zero-padding). Exact for band-limited signals. gradient Finite differences in the time domain (NumPy gradient). Simple and robust. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'differentiate'
    method: 'spectral'

Tip

Since high-frequency noise is amplified, apply a low-pass or band-pass filter before or after differentiating.

docs.title: Integrate
docs.text:
Computes the time integral of the trace, for example to convert acceleration into velocity, or velocity into displacement. In the frequency domain, integration divides the spectrum by \(i\omega\): it amplifies low frequencies, so any small offset or long-period noise grows into a drift.

method Description spectral Divides the spectrum by \(i 2\pi f\) and removes the 0 Hz component (after demean, taper and zero-padding). cumtrapz Cumulative trapezoidal rule in the time domain. spline Integral of a spline interpolation of the data. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'integrate'
    method: 'spectral'

Tip

Detrend and high-pass filter before integrating, otherwise the result drifts.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
A filter keeps the frequencies where your signal lives and attenuates the others: microseismic noise (0.1–0.5 Hz), cultural noise (> 1 Hz), long-period drifts... It is the most used tool in seismology.

Parameter Description type bandpass, bandstop, lowpass, highpass (Butterworth), or the band filters cheby1, cheby2, elliptic, bessel. fmin, fmax Corner frequencies in Hz (floats). highpass uses fmin, lowpass uses fmax. corners Filter order (number of poles). Higher = sharper cut, but more ringing. 2–4 is usual. zerophase True: the filter is applied forwards and backwards, so there is no phase shift and the onsets do not move (recommended for picking). The effective order is doubled. False: causal filter, the waveform is delayed and distorted, but nothing appears before the onset.

About the filter families:

  • Butterworth (bandpass, lowpass, ...): maximally flat pass-band, smooth roll-off. The standard choice.
  • Chebyshev I (cheby1): sharper roll-off at the cost of ripple in the pass-band.
  • Chebyshev II (cheby2): flat pass-band, ripple in the stop-band, sharp roll-off.
  • Elliptic (elliptic): the sharpest roll-off, ripple in both bands.
  • Bessel (bessel): the smoothest roll-off, but it preserves the waveform shape best (almost linear phase).

ℹ️ Ensure fmin < fmax for band filters, and fmax below the Nyquist frequency (half the sampling rate). The traces are detrended and tapered (5 %) internally before filtering.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 8.5
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True

docs.title: Resampling
docs.text:
Changes the sampling rate of the trace, for example to bring all stations to the same rate, or to reduce the size of long datasets.

When downsampling, frequencies above the new Nyquist frequency (half the new sampling rate) fold back into the band and contaminate the signal: this is aliasing. To avoid it, the trace must be low-pass filtered before reducing the rate.

Parameter Description sampling_rate New sampling rate in Hz. pre_filter True (recommended): anti-alias low-pass filter at 90 % of the new Nyquist before each downsampling step. Large factors are done in several steps (at most ×10 each). 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'resample'
    sampling_rate: 20
    pre_filter: True

docs.title: Quick Resampling (raw)
docs.text:
A very fast decimation: it keeps one sample out of every factor. It is designed to speed up the plot of long seismograms, not for analysis.

⚠️ No anti-alias filter is applied: high frequencies fold into the new band. Do not use the output for spectral analysis or picking.

Parameter Description factor Decimation factor (int). integers True: scale the data and convert them to int32, which reduces memory. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'raw'
    factor: 20
    integers: True

docs.title: Spike Removal
docs.text:
Spikes are isolated samples with huge amplitude (digitizer glitches, telemetry errors). They are very harmful: a single spike is broadband, so after filtering it becomes a wavelet that looks like a real arrival.

remove_spikes uses the Hampel filter: for each sample, it computes the median and the MAD (median absolute deviation) of a window centred on it. Since median and MAD are robust statistics, they are not affected by the spike itself. If the sample is further than sigma robust standard deviations (1.4826 × MAD) from the median, it is replaced by the median.

Parameter Description window_size Total length of the moving window, in seconds. It must be clearly longer than the spikes, but short compared to the signals you want to keep. sigma Threshold in robust standard deviations. 3–4 is usual; lower values remove more samples (and may clip real signals). 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'remove_spikes'
    window_size: 10
    sigma: 4

docs.title: Wavelet Denoise
docs.text:
Decomposes the trace with the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) into an approximation (the smooth trend) and several levels of details (one per octave of frequency). A coherent signal is concentrated in a few large coefficients, while random noise is spread over many small ones. Shrinking the small coefficients (soft thresholding) and reconstructing the trace removes much of the noise while keeping the sharp features of the signal (onsets), which a simple low-pass filter would smooth.

Parameter Description dwt Wavelet family: db2–db20 (Daubechies), sym2–sym20 (Symlets), coif2–coif16 (Coiflets), bior... (biorthogonal). sym8 is a good default. threshold Fraction (0–1) of the largest coefficient of each level below which the coefficients are shrunk. Larger = stronger denoising, but also more signal removed. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 8.5
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True
  process_4:
    name: 'wavelet_denoise'
    dwt: 'sym8'
    threshold: 0.1

docs.title: Wiener Smoothing
docs.text:
An adaptive (local) Wiener filter in the time domain (SciPy). For each sample, it estimates the local mean and variance in a short window. Where the local variance is much larger than the noise (a signal is present), the sample is kept almost unchanged; where the variance is close to the noise level, the sample is replaced by the local mean. The result is a smoothing that adapts to the signal: strong in quiet parts, weak during arrivals.

Parameter Description time_window Local window, in seconds. 0 = SciPy default (3 samples). noise_power Noise level as a multiple of the trace standard deviation. 0 = estimated from the data (mean of the local variances). 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'wiener_smoothing'
    time_window: 1.0
    noise_power: 0

docs.title: Wiener Filter (SAC WIENER)
docs.text:
The equivalent of the SAC WIENER command: an adaptive prediction-error filter. A linear predictor with ncoeff coefficients is designed on a window of the trace (normally pre-event noise). The filter predicts what the trace "should" be from its past samples and outputs the prediction error. Everything that is predictable (stationary noise, narrow-band hum, microseisms) is removed, while the new, unpredictable information (an arrival) remains. This is also called prewhitening, because the output noise has a flat spectrum. It is very effective to sharpen onsets before picking.

Parameter Description window_start, window_end Design window: seconds from the trace start, or UTC date-times. Choose a window of noise before the event. ncoeff (optional, default 30, range 2–100) filter length including the leading 1 (prediction order = ncoeff − 1). More coefficients describe more complex noise spectra. mu (optional, float) adaptation step. If not given, the filter is fixed (designed once on the window). If given, the coefficients keep adapting along the trace, as in SAC. epsilon (optional, float) relative ridge added to the zero-lag autocorrelation to stabilise the design. If not given, the values 0, 1e-5, ..., 1e-2 are tried until the filter is stable (SAC default). 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'wiener_filter'
    window_start: 0
    window_end: 20

docs.title: Smoothing
docs.text:
Reduces high-frequency jitter by averaging neighbouring samples. Smoothing is a low-pass filter in disguise, useful for envelopes and characteristic functions rather than for raw waveforms.

method Description mean Moving average over time_window seconds. Simple, but its spectrum has side lobes. gaussian Convolution with a Gaussian of full width at half maximum FWHM seconds. Smooth response, no side lobes. adaptive Savitzky–Golay filter (polynomial of order 3) over time_window seconds: smooths while preserving peak heights and widths. tkeo Teager–Kaiser Energy Operator \(x_n^2 - x_{n-1}x_{n+1}\): not a smoother but an instantaneous energy estimator, sensitive to both amplitude and frequency. It highlights sudden onsets.

Both time_window and FWHM must be given, even if the selected method uses only one of them.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'smoothing'
    method: 'gaussian'
    time_window: 5
    FWHM: 0.05

docs.title: Normalize
docs.text:
Rescales the amplitude of the traces. It is useful to compare waveform shapes of stations with different gains or distances, for plotting record sections, and before machine learning.

Parameter Description norm True: divide by the absolute maximum (the trace peaks at ±1). A number (float): divide by that value. global_max (optional, default False) True: divide every trace by the absolute maximum of the whole stream, which keeps the relative amplitudes between traces. Use it with norm: True. Since it needs all traces, it runs together with the stream methods. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'normalize'
    norm: True

docs.title: Time Normalization
docs.text:
Used mainly in ambient noise processing. Earthquakes and other large transients dominate a cross-correlation of continuous data, while we want the contribution of the diffuse noise. Time normalisation reduces the weight of those high-amplitude windows.

method Description 1bit Keep only the sign of each sample (+1 / −1). The most aggressive: all amplitude information is lost, but it is very robust. clipping Clip the samples above 6 × the standard deviation. clipping iteration Repeatedly divide the samples above 6 × the standard deviation by 10, until none remains above it. time normalization Running-absolute-mean normalisation (Bensen et al., 2007): each sample is divided by the mean absolute amplitude in a window of norm_win seconds centred on it. Parameter Description norm_win Window of the running mean, in seconds (time normalization only). About half the longest period of interest. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'time_normalization'
    method: 'time normalization'
    norm_win: 10

Scientific Reference:

Bensen, G. D., et al. (2007). Processing seismic ambient noise data to obtain reliable broad-band surface wave dispersion measurements. Geophysical Journal International, 169(3), 1239–1260.

docs.title: Spectral Whitening
docs.text:
Flattens the amplitude spectrum inside a frequency band while keeping the phase. The spectrum is divided by a smoothed version of its own amplitude, so all frequencies of the band get the same weight. Outside the band the spectrum is strongly attenuated.

In ambient noise processing it broadens the band of the cross-correlations (otherwise dominated by the microseism peak) and removes monochromatic sources. Before cross-correlation or array analysis it also sharpens the correlation peaks.

Parameter Description fmin, fmax Whitening band, in Hz. freq_width Width (Hz) of the running average used to smooth the amplitude spectrum. Too small = noisy whitening; too large = incomplete whitening. taper_edge True: taper the band edges to reduce ringing in the time domain. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'whitening'
    fmin: 0.05
    fmax: 24.5
    freq_width: 0.02
    taper_edge: True

docs.title: Reverse
docs.text:
Reverses the order of the samples (time reversal): the last sample becomes the first. Useful to build anticausal operations, to check the symmetry of correlation functions, or to apply a causal filter backwards.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'reverse'

docs.title: Flip
docs.text:
Multiplies the samples by −1, which inverts the polarity of the trace. Use it to correct sensors installed with reversed polarity, or to compare first-motion polarities.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'flip'

docs.title: Add Noise
docs.text:
Adds synthetic random noise to the trace. It is used to test the robustness of a method (picking, location, magnitudes) at decreasing signal-to-noise ratios. The noise level is set relative to the trace (an SNR). To add noise with the level and spectrum of real seismic noise, use Add Seismic Noise.

The noise is generated in the frequency domain with a power spectral density proportional to \(1/f^{\alpha}\):

noise_type \(\alpha\) Character white 0 Flat spectrum, all frequencies equal. pink 1 More energy at low frequencies. brown 2 Dominated by low frequencies (random walk). blue −1 More energy at high frequencies. violet −2 Dominated by high frequencies. Parameter Description SNR_dB Signal-to-noise ratio of the result, in dB, as the ratio of the mean power of the trace to the mean power of the noise. 0 dB = same power; 20 dB = noise power 100 times smaller. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'add_noise'
    noise_type: 'white'
    SNR_dB: 1

docs.title: Add Seismic Noise
docs.text:
Adds realistic seismic background noise, with the spectrum and the absolute level of the noise recorded by real stations. While add_noise uses a mathematical spectrum and a level relative to the trace (an SNR), add_seismic_noise uses the Peterson (1993) noise models: the New Low Noise Model (NLNM), the quietest noise observed at the stations of a global network, and the New High Noise Model (NHNM), the noisiest. The real noise of almost every station lies between the two. They include the main features of the seismic noise: the microseism peaks between about 3 and 20 s and the increase of noise at long periods.

It is useful to test a method with the noise that a quiet or a noisy station would really record, for example to see down to which magnitude an event is still detected or picked, or to add noise to synthetic seismograms that have none.

How the noise is built (a Python port of R. Herrmann's sacnoise):

  1. Gaussian white noise is generated, with the same length and sampling rate as the trace.
  2. Its spectrum is shaped so that its power spectral density \(P(f)\), in acceleration, follows the noise model: \(|X(f)| = |W(f)|\sqrt{P(f)/(2\,\Delta t)}\), where \(W(f)\) is the spectrum of the white noise and \(\Delta t\) the sampling interval.
  3. The noise, in acceleration, is converted to the units of the trace (see units).
  4. The noise is added to the trace.

The level between the two models is set with noise_level. It is interpolated in decibels: \(P_{dB}(f) = (1 - \text{noise\_level})\, \text{NLNM}(f) + \text{noise\_level}\, \text{NHNM}(f)\).

Parameter Description noise_level (optional, default 0.5) 0 = NLNM (very quiet station), 0.5 = intermediate noise, 1 = NHNM (very noisy station). Values above 1 give noise above the NHNM, and below 0 noise under the NLNM. units (optional, default counts) units of the trace data. counts: raw data; the noise goes through the instrument response, as if recorded by the real sensor and digitizer. ACC (m/s²), VEL (m/s) or DISP (m): data already corrected for the instrument; the noise is converted by integration in the frequency domain, and no metadata is needed. seed (optional, default None) integer seed of the random generator. The same seed gives the same noise, so the test can be repeated. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'add_seismic_noise'
    noise_level: 0.5
    units: 'counts'
    seed: 12345

Example with data already in velocity: the response is removed first, then a quiet-station noise is added:

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'remove_response'
    water_level: 90
    units: 'VEL'
    pre_filt: [0.005, 0.008, 45, 48]
  process_4:
    name: 'add_seismic_noise'
    noise_level: 0.2
    units: 'VEL'

⚠️ WARNING: With units: 'counts' the metadata is required: include your inventory, e.g. surfquake quick -w "waveform_file" -i "inventory_file.xml". If there is no inventory, or the response of a trace is not found, a warning is printed and the noise is not added to that trace (the trace is kept unchanged).

Tip

  • Choose units according to the current state of the trace: counts before remove_response, and the output units of remove_response after it.
  • The models are defined for periods between 0.1 and 100000 s. At higher frequencies (above 10 Hz, when the sampling rate is above 20 Hz), the value of the model at 0.1 s is used.
  • The noise is added to the whole trace, also to the signal: compare the result with the original trace to see how the noise affects your method.

Scientific Reference:

Peterson, Jon R. "Observations and modeling of seismic background noise." U.S. Geological Survey Open-File Report 93-322 (1993): 1-95.

docs.title: Rename
docs.text:
Changes the network, station, location or channel codes of the traces. It is useful to harmonise data from different sources, or to change 1/2 components into N/E.

All maps are optional; write them as old: new.

Parameter Description networks, stations, locations Maps of whole codes. channels Map of whole channel codes (e.g. HHZ → BHZ). components Map of the last channel letter (e.g. 1 → N). Used only when the channel is not matched in channels.

Special keys: '*' = any code not matched explicitly; '' = empty code.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rename'
    networks:
      'XX': 'ES'
    locations:
      '': '00'
    components:
      '1': 'N'
      '2': 'E'

⚠️ Always quote the codes: unquoted 00 becomes 0, and NO (Norway) becomes False.

docs.title: Time-frequency products
docs.text: The methods spectrum, spectrogram, cwt, cepstrum and cepstrogram are also trace methods: they compute a time-frequency object of each trace and save it to disk, without modifying the trace. Please review Time-Frequency Analysis.

docs.title: Time Shifting
docs.text: Shifting traces in time is a stream method, see Processing Stream.

docs.title: Data Processing with SurfQuake
docs.text:
Welcome to the Signal Processing Module of SurfQuake — a scalable command-line tool for applying signal processing pipelines to large collections of seismic waveform data.

Whether you're analyzing earthquake catalogs, preparing continuous data for ambient noise or array analysis, or building datasets for machine learning models, this module lets you define, control, and automate your signal processing workflow with precision: the same config file processes one trace or ten years of data.

📘 Learn more in our Signal Processing Tutorial and in the Tutorial Book.

Remember that you can use real data files and metadata to learn how to use surfquake processing commands with Case of study.

In the following link, you will find config file templates. You can also generate them in your working folder:

surfquake make_config -h
surfquake make_config -c config_all -o ./configs      # every trace method, as a reference
surfquake make_config -c stream_config -o ./configs   # stream methods
surfquake make_config -c ch_functions -o ./configs    # characteristic functions

docs.title: How the processing works
docs.text:
A processing workflow is a list of steps written in a YAML config file. Each step names a method and its parameters:

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 8.0
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True

The steps run in the order of their number: process_1, process_2, ... Before anything is computed, the config is validated: a misspelled method or a missing parameter stops the run with a message, so a long job does not fail halfway through.

There are two kinds of methods:

Kind Works on Examples Documentation Trace methods each trace independently rmean, taper, filter, remove_response, resample, whitening Processing Traces Stream methods several traces together rotate, cross_correlate, stack, shift, beam, algebra Processing Stream

Order of execution

Trace methods and stream methods run as two blocks. By default (-op trace_first) all trace methods are applied first, and then all stream methods, each block in its own order. With -op stream_first, the stream methods run first. This is the natural order for most workflows: first clean each trace, then combine them.

General rules for config files

  • Each process_N key must be unique. A repeated key silently replaces the earlier step.
  • Times in seconds, frequencies in Hz.
  • Write decimals with a dot (0.5, 2.0): some options require a float, and fmin: 1 fails while fmin: 1.0 works.
  • Quote text values ('linear') and station codes ('00').

docs.title: Why this order? A basic signal processing recipe
docs.text:
Most workflows start with the same preparation, and the order matters:

  1. Merge and fill gaps (concat, fill_gaps): FFTs and filters need continuous, evenly sampled data.
  2. Remove the mean and trend (rmean): an offset or a drift would leak into the band of interest.
  3. Taper (taper): brings the trace ends smoothly to zero, avoiding spectral leakage and filter ringing at the edges.
  4. Remove the instrument response (remove_response): converts counts to ground motion, so that stations can be compared.
  5. Filter (filter): keeps the band of your signal.
  6. Resample (resample), if needed, after the anti-alias filter.
  7. Analysis: rotation, correlation, stacking, beamforming, spectral analysis...

Some example pipelines:

Goal Typical steps Local earthquakes, picking rmean → taper → filter (bandpass 1–20 Hz, zerophase: True) Magnitudes / ground motion rmean → taper → remove_response (VEL, DISP or Wood Anderson) → filter Teleseismic body waves rmean → taper → remove_response → filter (0.02–2 Hz) → rotate (NE->RT, GAC) → shift (phase_theo) → stack Ambient noise rmean → taper → remove_response → filter → resample → time_normalization → whitening → cross_correlate Receiver functions rmean → taper → filter → rotate (ZNE->LQT) → deconv (reference: L component) Array analysis rmean → taper → cut_stream → beam

docs.title: Running the Process
docs.text:
This tool runs via the terminal. There are three processing commands: quick, processing and processing_daily. They share the same config files and differ in how they read the data:

Command Input Use it when quick waveform files (-w) You want to process files directly, without a project. Fast workflows and exploration. processing a project (-p) or files (-w) and an event file (-e) You want to cut and process the waveforms of a list of events. processing_daily a project (-p) You work with continuous data: merging daily files, or processing long time spans.

First, in the terminal you can ask for help:

surfquake quick -h

All of them have two modes:

  • Interactive (default): the waveforms are plotted and you can pick, inspect and process them with the interactive command prompt (see Plotting).
  • Automatic (-a): no plots and no questions, the output is written to disk. Use it for big datasets and bash scripts.

And all of them accept a post-script: your own Python script applied to each stream (see Scripts and surfquake make_config -c script_template). With --post_script_stage you choose when it runs: before plotting (good for filtering or editing headers) or after plotting (good to act on the picks or metadata you added).

docs.title: surfquake quick
docs.text:
Overview:
    Process seismic traces.
    You can:
        - Apply processing steps (filtering, normalization, etc.)
        - Optionally visualize the waveforms (interactive mode)
        - Apply a user-defined post-processing script before or after plotting

Modes:
    Default  : Interactive mode (plotting + user prompts)
    --auto   : Non-interactive mode (no plots, no prompts, outputs written automatically)

Post-Script Logic:
    Use `--post_script` to apply a custom script to each event stream.
    Use `--post_script_stage` to control **when** it runs:
        • before : script runs before plotting (good for filtering, editing headers)
        • after  : script runs after plotting (good if picks or metadata are added)

Examples:
    Process waveform files with a config and plot interactively:
        surfquake quick -w "./data/*.mseed" -c ./config.yaml -i ./inventory.xml -o ./out --plot_config plot.yaml

Key Arguments:
    -w, --wave_files         [REQUIRED | OPTIONAL] Glob pattern or path to waveform files, (not needed if the config has a 'Source' section)
    -f, --fast               [OPTIONAL] Quick-and-Dirty plotting
    -c, --config_file        [OPTIONAL] YAML config defining processing steps
    -i, --inventory_file     [OPTIONAL] Station metadata (StationXML or RESP)
    -o, --output_folder      [OPTIONAL] Directory to save processed traces
    -a, --auto               [OPTIONAL] Run in automatic (non-interactive) mode
    -m, --merge              [OPTIONAL] If merge traces as first action
    -op, --order_preference  [OPTIONAL] 'trace_first' (default) or 'stream_first' — controls
                              whether trace-level steps (rmean, filter, taper...) run before
                              or after stream-level steps (cross_correlate, rotate, stack...)
        --min_date           [OPTIONAL] Filter Start date (format: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), DEFAULT None
        --max_date           [OPTIONAL] Filter End date   (format: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), DEFAULT None
        --plot_config        [OPTIONAL] Plotting settings YAML
        --post_script        [OPTIONAL] Python script to apply to each stream
        --post_script_stage  [OPTIONAL] When to run post-script: 'before' or 'after' (default: before)

With quick all the selected files are read and processed together as one stream, which is what stream methods (rotation, correlation, beamforming...) need.

Synthetic test signals

A config file with a Source section instead of -w generates synthetic signals (impulses, sines, chirps...). They are very useful to understand what a method does before applying it to real data: for example, filter an impulse to see the impulse response of the filter. See surfquake make_config -c test_sign_config.

docs.title: surfquake processing
docs.text:
Overview:
    Process or cut waveforms associated with seismic events.
    You can:
        - Cut traces using event times and headers
        - Apply processing steps (filtering, normalization, etc.)
        - Optionally visualize the waveforms (interactive mode)
        - Apply a user-defined post-processing script before or after plotting

Modes:
    Default  : Interactive mode (plotting + user prompts)
    --auto   : Non-interactive mode (no plots, no prompts, outputs written automatically)

Post-Script Logic:
    Use `--post_script` to apply a custom script to each event stream.
    Use `--post_script_stage` to control **when** it runs:
        • before : script runs before plotting (good for filtering, editing headers)
        • after  : script runs after plotting (good if picks or metadata are added)

Usage Example:
    surfquake processing -p "./project.pkl" -i inventory.xml -e events.txt -c config.yaml -o ./output_folder --phases P,S --plot_config plot_settings.yaml --post_script custom_postproc.py

Key Arguments:
    -p, --project_file         [OPTIONAL] Path to an existing project file
    -w, --wave_files           [OPTIONAL] Path or glob pattern to waveform files
    -f, --fast                 [OPTIONAL] Quick-and-Dirty plotting
    -i, --inventory_file       [OPTIONAL] Station metadata file (XML, RESP)
    -e, --event_file           [OPTIONAL] Event catalog in txt format (columns: date;hour;latitude;longitude;depth;magnitude)
    -c, --config_file          [OPTIONAL] Processing configuration file (YAML)
    -a, --auto                 [OPTIONAL] Run in automatic mode
    -o, --output_folder        [OPTIONAL] Folder where processed files are saved
    -n, --net                  [OPTIONAL] Project net filter Example: NET1,NET2,NET3
    -s, --station              [OPTIONAL] Project station filter Example: STA1,STA2,STA3
    -ch, --channel             [OPTIONAL] Project channel filter Example: HHZ,BHN
    -t, --cut_time             [OPTIONAL] pre & post first arrival in seconds (symmetric)
    -cs, --cut_start_time      [OPTIONAL] Cut pre-first arrival in seconds
    -ce, --cut_end_time        [OPTIONAL] Cut post-first arrival in seconds
    -r, --reference            [OPTIONAL] The pick time for cutting the waveforms is the origin time of the event
    -op, --order_preference    [OPTIONAL] trace_first (default) | stream_first. Controls whether trace-level
                               steps (rmean, filter, taper...) run before or after stream-level steps
                               (cross_correlate, rotate, stack...)
    --phases                   [OPTIONAL] Comma-separated list of phases for arrival estimation (e.g., P,S)
    --vel                      [OPTIONAL] Phase speed to estimate the first arrival time (reference for cutting waveform)
    --plot_config              [OPTIONAL] Optional plot configuration file (YAML)
    --post_script              [OPTIONAL] Python script to apply per event stream
    --post_script_stage        [OPTIONAL] When to apply the post-script: before | after (default: before)

Notes:
You might need to set -w for individual files or -p for loading your project file

For each event of the event file, surfquake estimates the arrival times of the --phases at every station (or uses the origin time with -r), cuts the waveforms around them (-t, -cs, -ce) and processes one stream per event. The event and arrival information is stored in the trace headers, so methods like rotate (GAC) and shift (phase_theo) can use it.

docs.title: surfquake processing_daily
docs.text:
This command is different from surfquake processing because it is intended to merge daily seismograms and to work with big continuous datasets. For example, imagine that you need three days of seismograms for the normal-mode analysis of a large event, or that you would like to process all your daily MiniSEED files for ambient noise.

Overview:
    Cut seismograms and apply processing to continuous waveforms.
    You can perform either or both of these operations.

Modes:
    Default : Interactive mode (with plotting and prompts)
    --auto  : Non-interactive mode (no plots, no prompts, automatic output)

Post-Script Logic:
    Use --post_script to apply a custom script per station/day stream.
    Use --post_script_stage to control when the script is applied:
        • before : apply script before plotting (e.g., for filtering or cleanup)
        • after  : apply script after plotting (e.g., to act on manual picks)

Usage Example:
    surfquake processing_daily \
        -p ./project.pkl \
        -i inventory.xml \
        -c config.yaml \
        -o ./output_folder \
        --min_date "2024-01-01 00:00:00" \
        --max_date "2024-01-02 00:00:00" \
        --span_seconds 86400 \
        --plot_config plot_settings.yaml \
        --post_script my_custom.py \
        --post_script_stage after

Key Arguments:
    -p, --project_file        [REQUIRED] Path to a saved project file
    -f, --fast                [OPTIONAL] Quick-and-Dirty plotting
    -o, --output_folder       [OPTIONAL] Directory for processed output
    -i, --inventory_file      [OPTIONAL] Station metadata (XML/RESP)
    -c, --config_file         [OPTIONAL] Processing configuration (YAML)
    -a, --auto                [OPTIONAL] Run in automatic mode
    -n, --net                 [OPTIONAL] Network code filter
    -s, --station             [OPTIONAL] Station code filter
    -ch, --channel            [OPTIONAL] Channel filter
    -op, --order_preference   [OPTIONAL] trace_first (default) | stream_first. Controls whether trace-level
                              steps (rmean, filter, taper...) run before or after stream-level steps
                              (cross_correlate, rotate, stack...)
    --min_date                [OPTIONAL] Filter Start date (format: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), DEFAULT min date of the project
    --max_date                [OPTIONAL] Filter End date   (format: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), DEFAULT max date of the project
    --time_tolerance          [OPTIONAL] Tolerance in seconds for time filtering, excluded files with smaller time span
    --span_seconds            [OPTIONAL] Select and merge files in sets of time spans, DEFAULT 86400
    --time_segment            [OPTIONAL] If set, process entire time window as a single merged stream of traces
    --plot_config             [OPTIONAL] Optional plotting configuration (YAML)
    --post_script             [OPTIONAL] Path to Python script for custom post-processing
    --post_script_stage       [OPTIONAL] When to apply the post-script: before | after (default: before)

The project is divided into time spans of --span_seconds (one day by default); the files of each span are merged and processed as one stream. With --time_segment, the whole window between --min_date and --max_date is merged and processed as a single stream.

docs.title: Event File Format (events.txt)
docs.text:
This is the input of surfquake processing -e ./events.txt. One event per line, columns separated by ;:

date;hour;latitude;longitude;depth;magnitude
2022-02-02;23:35:29.7;42.5089;1.4293;20.7;1.71
2022-02-03;12:01:21.6;42.3047;2.2741;0.0;1.65

Depth in km. A template is available with surfquake make_config -c events.

docs.title: Sample Processing Configuration (config.yaml)
docs.text:
The config file defines your signal processing pipeline step by step. You can process files directly, full daily waveform files, or segments extracted around events, and the interactive plotting tool helps you to visually inspect and validate every step.

surfquake quick -w ./mseed_file -c ./config.yaml                         # reading directly mseed files
surfquake processing -p ./project.pkl -c ./config.yaml -e ./events.txt    # loading a project and using event files

Detailed information on every method is in Processing Traces and Processing Stream.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 8.0
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True

docs.title: Processing Stream Options
docs.text:
Stream methods use several traces together: the three components of a station, a reference trace and the others, the stations of an array, or the whole stream. Typical examples are rotating components, cross-correlating, stacking or beamforming.

They are written in the same Analysis section as the trace methods:

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 8.0
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True
  process_4:
    name: 'stack'
    method: 'pw'
    order: 2

Order of execution

Trace methods and stream methods run as two blocks. By default (-op trace_first) all trace methods are applied first, in their order, and then all stream methods, in their order. With -op stream_first the stream methods run first. The position of a stream step among the trace steps in the config file does not change this.

General rules

  • Each process_N key must be unique. A repeated key silently replaces the earlier step.
  • Times in seconds, frequencies in Hz. Write decimals with a dot (0.5, 2.0).
  • Most stream methods need traces with the same sampling rate. Use resample first if needed.
  • Some methods only write results to disk and pass the same traces to the next step: this is noted as stream unchanged.
  • A template with every stream method is available with surfquake make_config -c stream_config.

docs.title: Concatenate
docs.text:
Joins the time-continuous segments of the same channel into a single trace. Data are often split into several segments (daily files, instrument restarts, transmission delays). Internally it uses ObsPy Stream.merge() with linear interpolation:

  • Overlapping segments are merged into one continuous trace.
  • Gaps are filled by linear interpolation between the adjacent samples.
  • Traces with different ids or sampling rates are left unmerged.
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'concat'

Note: concatenation is done automatically by surfquake processing and surfquake processing_daily, but not by surfquake quick, which gives you full control.

docs.title: Synchronization
docs.text:
Puts all traces on a common time reference, which is needed before stacking or comparing waveforms.

  • starttime: gives all traces the same (dummy) start time. Use it to overlay or stack records that start at a meaningful point but belong to different events or dates, for example traces already cut around the P arrival.
  • MCCC (Multi-Channel Cross-Correlation): measures the relative delays between all pairs of traces by cross-correlation, and solves for the set of delays that best fits all pairs in a least-squares sense. Using all pairs together makes the alignment much more robust than correlating each trace with a single reference, which is very effective with noisy data, or when arrivals differ due to path effects or clock drifts.
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'synch'
    method: 'MCCC'

Scientific Reference:

VanDecar, J. C., & Crosson, R. S. (1990). Determination of teleseismic relative phase arrival times using multi-channel cross-correlation and least squares. Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America, 80(1), 150–169.

docs.title: Shift
docs.text:
Moves the traces in time. It is used to align waveforms on a phase before stacking, comparing or plotting them. Please review Trace Header to fully understand this method. Use one of the options:

Option Description phase_theo Align on a theoretical arrival time, stored in trace.stats.geodetic['arrivals'] (computed when the traces are processed with an event file). Use it when model-based timing is reliable, e.g. teleseismic body waves. phase Align on an observed pick, stored in trace.stats.picks. Use it when you trust your picks more than the theoretical times. time_shifts Add a fixed offset (seconds) to the start time of each trace, one value per trace, in stream order. For full manual control.

With phase_theo or phase, the samples before the phase are removed and every trace starts at the same time (1970-01-01, i.e. t = 0 at the phase). Traces without that phase are skipped with a warning.

If several options are given, the order of priority is phase_theo, then phase, then time_shifts. If none is valid, the stream is returned unchanged.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'shift'
    time_shifts: [-5.0, 2.0]

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'shift'
    phase_theo: 'P'
    time_shifts: []

ℹ️ The key time_shifts must always be present, even when you align by phase. In that case write an empty list.

docs.title: Cut Stream
docs.text:
Cuts all traces of the stream to the same window. Unlike the trace method cut, the traces are padded with zeros where they have no data, so all of them end with the same length, which is required by array methods.

Parameter Description method absolute (start, end), phase (phase_name, t_before, t_after around each trace's pick) or reference (t_before, t_after around the reference time). 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'cut_stream'
    method: 'absolute'
    start: 2018-08-21T00:27:15
    end: 2018-08-21T00:31:45

docs.title: Stack
docs.text:
Combines all traces into one trace (id NET.STA..STK). Summing aligned traces reinforces the coherent signal, while the incoherent noise partially cancels: with N traces and random noise, the signal-to-noise ratio improves by about \(\sqrt{N}\). The traces must be aligned first (see shift and synch); they are cut to the shortest length before stacking.

method Description linear Arithmetic mean of the traces. Preserves amplitudes; the reference method. pw Phase-weighted stack (Schimmel & Paulssen, 1997). The linear stack is multiplied by the phase coherence of the traces (computed from their instantaneous phase), raised to the power order. Samples where the phases agree are kept; incoherent samples are suppressed. Excellent noise reduction for weak coherent signals, but amplitudes are no longer reliable. root N-th root stack: the N-th root of each sample is stacked (keeping its sign) and the result is raised back to the power N. It enhances coherent signals and suppresses incoherent noise, but distorts the waveform. Parameter Description order (pw, root) integer exponent. Higher values give stronger weighting to coherent signals. pw: 1–2 are usual. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'stack'
    method: 'pw'
    order: 2

Scientific Reference:

Schimmel, M., & Paulssen, H. (1997). Noise reduction and detection of weak, coherent signals through phase-weighted stacks. Geophysical Journal International, 130(2), 497–505.

docs.title: Rotate Seismograms
docs.text:
The horizontal sensors record in the North and East directions, which are not related to the earthquake. Rotating to the ray coordinates separates the wave types: on the Radial (R) component, along the great circle from the source, you find P and SV energy and Rayleigh waves; on the Transverse (T) component, perpendicular to it, SH energy and Love waves. The 3D rotation LQT goes one step further and uses the ray direction itself: L along the P ray, Q (SV) and T (SH) perpendicular to it.

Before rotating, the components of each station are standardised to Z/N/E and cut to their common time window.

  • type: the rotation.

    • NE->RT: North and East to Radial and Transverse.
    • RT->NE: Radial and Transverse back to North and East.
    • ZNE->LQT: Z, North, East to the ray-based L, Q, T system.
    • LQT->ZNE: L, Q, T back to Z, North, East.

  • method: how the angles are obtained.

    • GAC: Great Arc Circle. The back-azimuth (and the inclination) come from the trace headers, so the event information must be available (e.g. processing with an event file).
    • FREE: the angles given by the user.

  • angle (float): back-azimuth from the station to the source, in degrees (FREE).

  • inclination (float): inclination of the ray at the station, in degrees (FREE). Only used by the LQT rotations; write 0.0 for NE->RT.
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rotate'
    type: 'NE->RT'
    method: 'FREE'
    angle: 30.0
    inclination: 0.0

docs.title: Particle Motion
docs.text:
Analyses the polarisation of the ground motion at each station: the 3D path followed by a particle of the ground during the arrival. P waves are linearly polarised along the propagation direction, S waves perpendicular to it, and Rayleigh waves elliptical in the vertical-radial plane. The polarisation gives the back-azimuth and incidence angle of a wave from a single station, and helps to identify phases. Stream unchanged.

It needs complete Z-N-E (or Z-1-2, Z-Y-X) sets; the traces are cut to their common window. Please review Particle Motion.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'particle_motion'
    output_path: './particle_motion'

docs.title: C. Operations against a reference trace
docs.text: These methods take the trace at position reference_idx as a reference and process every trace of the stream against it: n traces in, n traces out. The reference trace is processed with itself (autocorrelation, autodeconvolution).

docs.title: Cross Correlation & Convolution
docs.text:
Cross-correlation measures the similarity of two signals as a function of the time lag between them. The lag of its maximum is the delay between the signals, which is the basis of relative arrival times, template matching, repeating events and ambient noise interferometry (the correlation of the noise at two stations approximates the Green's function between them).

Convolution is the same operation with one of the signals reversed in time. It is the response of a linear system: for example, convolving a source time function with a Green's function gives a synthetic seismogram.

  • name: cross_correlate or convolve.

  • mode: which lags are returned, following the NumPy correlate method:

    • full: all lags, including partial overlaps. Best if you want to scan the entire signal.
    • valid: only the lags where the signals fully overlap. Safer when you want to avoid edge effects.
    • same: output of the same length as the input, centred around zero lag.

  • normalize: how the correlation is normalised (not applied in convolution).

    • full: zero-normalised cross-correlation (ZNCC), normalised by the local energy of the signals. The result is a correlation coefficient between −1 and 1, the most statistically meaningful.
    • naive: normalised by the global energy of both signals. Faster, but it may be biased if the amplitude changes along the traces.

  • reference_idx: index of the reference trace (int).

  • trim: if True, all traces are first cut to the common time window (latest start, earliest end). Recommended, because then the zero lag means the same time for every pair.

The output traces are named <ref_station>_<station> with an X in the channel (e.g. HXZ).

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'cross_correlate'
    mode: 'full'
    normalize: 'full'
    reference_idx: 0
    trim: True

docs.title: Deconvolution
docs.text:
Deconvolution is the inverse of convolution: it removes the reference signal from the other traces. Dividing the spectrum of each trace by the spectrum of the reference cancels everything they share (source time function, instrument, common path) and leaves what is specific to each trace.

Typical uses are receiver functions (the radial component deconvolved by the vertical, leaving the P-to-S conversions under the station) and empirical Green's functions (a large event deconvolved by a small co-located one, leaving the source time function of the large event).

The spectral division is unstable where the reference spectrum is close to zero, so it is stabilised with a water level (Clayton & Wiggins, 1976): the reference power spectrum is never allowed below a fraction of its maximum.

Parameter Description reference_idx Index of the reference trace (int). water_level Fraction of the maximum reference power used as floor (float, default 0.001). Typical 0.001–0.1: larger = more stable, but lower resolution. normalize True: scale so that the reference deconvolved by itself peaks at 1. trim True: cut all traces to the common time window first. gaussian_filter (optional) width a of a Gaussian low-pass \(G(f) = e^{-(2\pi f)^2 / 4a^2}\) applied to the result, which removes the high-frequency noise amplified by the division. a = 2.5 keeps up to about 1 Hz, as in receiver functions. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'deconv'
    reference_idx: 0
    water_level: 0.0001
    normalize: True
    trim: True
    gaussian_filter: 2.5

docs.title: Cross Spectrum
docs.text:
Compares every trace with the reference trace in the frequency domain. Stream unchanged: the results are saved in output_path.

  • Cross-spectral density: the spectrum of the cross-correlation. Its phase gives the delay between the traces at each frequency.
  • Coherence: between 0 and 1, how linearly related the two traces are at each frequency. It shows in which band two stations record the same signal.
  • Transfer function: the frequency response that turns the reference into the other trace (e.g. site amplification relative to a rock station).
Parameter Description method welch (average of overlapping windows) or multitaper (several orthogonal tapers, lower variance). win Window length in seconds (welch). overlap_percent Overlap between windows, in percent. reference_idx Index of the reference trace (int). output_path Folder for the results. optional nw (multitaper time-bandwidth, default 4.0), linf / lsup (band limits in Hz), trim (default True), compress (default True). 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'cross_spectrum'
    method: 'welch'
    win: 20.0
    overlap_percent: 50.0
    reference_idx: 0
    output_path: './cross_spectrum'

docs.title: Beamforming
docs.text:
Estimates the back-azimuth and apparent slowness of the waves crossing an array, by testing a grid of slowness vectors, shifting and stacking the traces for each one, and keeping the one with the maximum coherent energy. Stream unchanged: the results are saved in output_folder. It needs an inventory with the coordinates of every station (-i).

Please review Beamforming for the description of every parameter.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'beam'
    method: 'FK'
    timewindow: 3.0
    overlap: 0.05
    fmin: 1.0
    fmax: 8.0
    smax: 0.3
    slow_grid: 0.05
    output_folder: './beamforming'

docs.title: E. Arithmetic Operation (algebra)
docs.text:
Computes a new trace from a mathematical expression of the traces of the stream. Some examples of its use in signal processing:

  • Horizontal amplitude: sqrt(tr1**2 + tr2**2) combines N and E into the total horizontal motion.
  • H/V ratios, differences between co-located sensors (to check their response), sums and differences of components.
  • Energy and power: tr1**2.
  • Instantaneous phase of an analytic signal: arctan2(tr2, tr1).
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'algebra'
    expression: "tr1 + tr2 - tr3"
    trim: True
    fill_gaps: True
Option Type Description expression str The expression. tr1 is the first trace of the stream, tr2 the second, ... trim bool Cut all traces to the common time window [max(starttimes), min(endtimes)] before evaluating the expression. Raises an exception if there is no overlap. fill_gaps bool Merge the stream and fill internal gaps or overlaps using linear interpolation.

All traces are resampled to the highest sampling rate of the stream before evaluating the expression. The output channels are named ALG, ALG1, ...

  • Basic Functions
Category Operators Example Arithmetic +, -, *, /, % tr1 + tr2 * 2 Power ** tr1 ** 2 Floor Division // tr1 // 2 Unary +, - -tr1 Function Description abs(x) Absolute value sqrt(x) Square root exp(x) Exponential log(x) Natural logarithm log2(x) Base-2 logarithm log10(x) Base-10 logarithm power(x, n) x to the power n mod(x, n) Remainder of x / n
  • Trigonometric Functions
Function sin, cos, tan, arcsin, arccos, arctan, arctan2 sinh, cosh, tanh
  • Rounding Functions
Function Description ceil(x) Round up floor(x) Round down round(x) Round to nearest value
  • Signal Processing Helpers
Function Description sign(x) Sign of the signal diff(x) First difference (the output is one sample shorter) cumsum(x) Cumulative sum gradient(x) Numerical gradient
  • Complex Number Helpers
Function Description real(x) Real component imag(x) Imaginary component
  • Constants
Constant Value pi π e Euler's number
  • Usage examples
Goal Expression Simple sum of two traces tr1 + tr2 * 1e-3 Horizontal amplitude sqrt(tr1**2 + tr2**2) Complex math pipeline exp(tr1) + sin(tr2) * sqrt(abs(tr3)) Multi-output (sum and difference) tr1 + tr2, tr1 - tr2 Negate a trace -tr1 Cumulative integral proxy cumsum(tr1) Numerical derivative gradient(tr1) Signal power tr1 ** 2 Normalized ratio tr1 / (abs(tr2) + 1e-12) Phase extraction arctan2(tr2, tr1)

docs.title: F. Characteristic functions
docs.text:
A characteristic function (CF) transforms a waveform into a curve that rises when a seismic arrival starts. It is the core of automatic detection and picking. They are stream methods: n traces in, n CF traces out, with the same ids.

Name Idea snr STA/LTA: ratio of short-term to long-term average energy. The classic detector. envelope Instantaneous amplitude from the Hilbert transform. kurtosis Fourth-order statistics: high when the signal becomes impulsive. Sharp onsets. entropy Spectral entropy: drops when energy concentrates in a few frequencies. cwt_cf Wavelet-based CFs (energy, spectral ratio, entropy, centroid, kurtosis), optionally combined.

Please review Characteristic Functions and the template surfquake make_config -c ch_functions.

docs.title: Chop continuous data
docs.text:
Cuts continuous data into clock-aligned files of fixed length (e.g. one MiniSEED file per hour starting at hh:00:00). It is the usual way to prepare continuous archives for ambient noise, PPSD or detection workflows. Stream unchanged.

Parameter Description chunk_length Length of each output file, in seconds (e.g. 3600 = 1 h). min_length Minimum amount of real recorded data a file must contain, in seconds. Files with less data are not written. overlap Overlap between consecutive files, in seconds (0 = contiguous). output_dir Folder for the MiniSEED files. max_interpolation_gap (optional, default 2) largest gap that is interpolated, in seconds. 
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'chop'
    chunk_length: 1800.0
    min_length: 1760.0
    overlap: 0.0
    output_dir: './chop_data'

docs.title: Create your project
docs.text:
In surfQuake a project is simply a python object that can store the path to valid seismogram files plus the associated metadata in its attributes . This strategy allows to proceed with fast filters or join different projects. Project is the necessary input for the toolboxes Picker, Associator, Event Locator, Seismic Source and MTI.

Here we will explain how the user can manage a project and be ready to proceed with the rest of toolboxes.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This command allows you to create a seismic project, which is essentially a dictionary storing the paths to seismogram files along with their corresponding metadata.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Key Arguments:
    -d, --data           [REQUIRED]         Path to waveform data directory (or file pattern)
    -s, --save_path      [REQUIRED]         Directory to save the project file
    -n, --name           [REQUIRED]         Name of the project (e.g., "my_experiment")
    -v, --verbose        [OPTIONAL]         Print detailed file discovery and indexing logs

# Interactive help
>> surfquake project -h

>> surfquake project -d "./testing_data" -s "./Volumes/LaCie/test_surfquake_core/testing_data/projects" -n "/surfquake_project_new.pkl" --verbose

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
In this section, we will explain the class SurfProject and we will explain how to manage your project from a simple example:

SurfProject

class SurfProject:

    def __init__(self, root_path: Union[str, List[str]]):

        """

        SurfProject class is designed to be able to storage the path to seismograms
        files plus the file metadata information (i.e. sampling_rate, starttime...)

        Attributes:
        - root_path (str): The root path to the folder where the user have the data files.

        Methods:
        - __init__(root_path): Initialize a new instance of MyClass.
        - load_project(path_to_project_file: str): Load a project from a file storage in hard-drive
        - save_project(path_file_to_storage: str): Saves a project as a pickle file in hard-drive
        - search_files(verbose=True, **kwargs): Create a project. It can be used filters by nets,
        stations, channels selection and/or filter by timestamp
        - filter_project_keys(**kwargs): Filter a project (once is crated) using regular expressions.
        """

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
search_files

    def search_files(self, format="NONE", verbose=True, **kwargs):

        Args:

        - verbose (bool): Description of arg1.
        - nets (str): String with the name of selected nets to be filtered (i.e., "WM,ES")
        - stations (str): String with the name of selected stations to be filtered (i.e., "ARNO,UCM,EMAL")
        - channels (str): String with the name of selected channels to be filtered (i.e., "HHN,HHZ,HHE")
        - starttime (str "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S" ): String with the reference starttime, upper time spam threshold
        (i.e.,"2023-12-10 00:00:00")
        - endtime (str "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S" ): String with the reference endtime, lower time spam threshold
        (i.e.,"2023-12-23 00:00:00")

        """

        - station (str): String with the name of selected stations to be filtered (i.e., "ARNO|UCM|EMAL")
        - channel (str): String with the name of selected channels to be filtered (i.e., "HH.")
        """

filter_project_time

        (i.e., "2023-12-10 00:00:00")

# Saves the project object as a pickle file.
