docs.title: Attibutes
docs.text:
project :Dict
data_files :List

Next, the example of using this class and its methods. This example script is available in SurfQuakeCore/examples/manage_project_new.py

from multiprocessing import freeze_support
from surfquakecore.project.surf_project import SurfProject
import time

path_to_data = "/Volumes/LaCie/test_surfquake_core/testing_data"
path_to_project = "/Volumes/LaCie/test_surfquake_core/testing_data/projects/surfquake_project_new.pkl"

if __name__ == '__main__':

    freeze_support()
    sp = SurfProject(path_to_data)
    #sp.search_files(starttime="2022-01-30 23:55:00", endtime="2022-02-01 00:30:00", stations="SALF,VALC", channels="HHZ")
    sp.search_files(verbose=False)
    #sp_original_project = copy.copy()
    sp.filter_project_keys(station="SALF|VALC|CEST")
    sp_original1 = sp.copy()
    sp_original1.filter_project_keys(station="SALF")
    sp_original2 = sp.copy()
    sp_original2.filter_project_keys(station="VALC")

    sp_join = sp_original1 + sp_original2
    print("With no filter")
    print(sp_join)
    sp_join.filter_project_time(starttime="2022-01-30 23:55:00", endtime="2022-02-01 00:30:00")
    print("With filter")
    print(sp_join)
    sp_join.save_project(path_file_to_storage=path_to_project)
    time.sleep(5)
    sp_loaded = SurfProject.load_project(path_to_project_file=path_to_project)
    print(sp_loaded)

The first step is create the object from the class SurfProject 

sp = SurfProject

The necessary input to create the sp object is the root path where you have storage the seismogram files. Then, you can proceed to apply the method "search_files". This method includes the possibility of filter the inclusion of files inside the project.

sp.search_files(starttime="2022-01-30 23:55:00", endtime="2022-02-01 00:30:00", stations="SALF,VALC", channels="HHZ")
print(sp) # To see the contain of the project

Additionally, once the project has been created, you can also filter it by using ´regular expressions´ net, station, channel using:

Note: some util Regex info at Wiki Regex and Python keywords 

sp.filter_project_keys(station="SALF|VALC|CEST")

or filterintg the time spam using:

sp_join.ilter_project_time(starttime="2022-01-30 23:55:00", endtime="2022-02-01 00:30:00")

Adding projects using "+" symbol

sp_original1 = sp.copy()
sp_original1.filter_project_keys(station="SALF")
sp_original2 = sp.copy()
sp_original2.filter_project_keys(station="VALC")

sp_join = sp_original1 + sp_original2

Finally, you can save the project by, 

sp_join.save_project(path_file_to_storage=path_to_project)
and loading it

sp_loaded = SurfProject.load_project(path_to_project_file=path_to_project)

docs.title: Custom User Scripts in SurfQuake
docs.text:
The config files cover the standard processing methods. But research is rarely standard: you may want to test a new algorithm, apply a correction only you know about, reject bad traces with your own criteria, or export a table of measurements. User scripts let you plug your own Python code into any SurfQuake workflow, with full access to the waveforms, their headers, the station metadata and the event.

You write a small Python file with one function. SurfQuake does the rest: reading the files, cutting around events, processing, plotting and writing the output. Your function receives the stream of traces in the middle of the workflow and returns it, possibly modified.

There are two ways to use a script:

Pipeline post-script Interactive script Where quick, processing, processing_daily the interactive command prompt of the plot How --post_script myscript.py runpy myscript.py Function run(stream, **kwargs) process(stream) Runs automatically, for every stream (each event, each day...) once, when you type the command Receives stream + inventory (+ event with processing) stream of the plotted traces

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Some examples of what you can do with a script:

  • Your own algorithms: a new picker, a polarisation analysis, a machine learning model, a custom filter or correction.
  • Quality control: remove dead, flat, clipped or noisy traces with your own criteria.
  • Read and write the header: use picks, theoretical arrivals and event information, and store your own results (tr.stats.snr = ...). See Trace Header.
  • Add picks automatically, which are then shown on the plot and saved in the HDF5 output.
  • Export measurements: amplitudes, SNR, peak values, spectral parameters... to a CSV table.

docs.title: Where the script runs
docs.text:
For each stream, quick, processing and processing_daily follow these steps:

  1. Read the files (and, with processing, cut them around each event and fill the header with the event information).
  2. Apply the trace methods and the stream methods of your config file.
  3. Your script, if --post_script_stage before (default).
  4. Plot (interactive mode).
  5. Your script, if --post_script_stage after.
  6. Write the output files (-o, with -a).

So your script always receives the processed traces, and what it returns is what is plotted and written.

  • before: the script runs before plotting. Good for data transformations, quality control, automatic picks or header editing: you will see the result on the plot.
  • after: the script runs after plotting. Good to act on what you did on the plot: the manual picks and references are already in the header.

docs.title: Pipeline post-script: run(stream, **kwargs)
docs.text:
Each script must define a function run(stream, **kwargs):

  • stream: an ObsPy Stream with the current group of traces (one event with processing, one time span with processing_daily, all the files with quick).
  • kwargs["inventory"]: the ObsPy Inventory given with -i, or None.
  • kwargs["event"]: only with processing, a dict with the event of the current stream: origin_time (UTCDateTime), and latitude, longitude, depth (km) and magnitude when they are in the event file.

The function must return the stream.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
You can generate this template in your working folder with surfquake make_config -c script_template -o ./scripts.

import numpy as np

def run(stream, **kwargs):
    '''
    User-defined post-processing hook for each stream.

    :param stream: obspy Stream
    :param inventory: obspy Inventory (passed via kwargs)
    :param event: dict with origin_time, latitude, longitude, depth, magnitude
                  (passed via kwargs, only with surfquake processing)
    '''
    inventory = kwargs.pop('inventory', None)
    event = kwargs.pop('event', None)

    if event is not None:
        print(f"Post-processing {len(stream)} traces from event at {event['origin_time']}")
    else:
        print(f"Post-processing {len(stream)} traces (no event info provided)")

    # Example: calculate global mean amplitude
    all_data = np.hstack([tr.data for tr in stream])
    print("Mean amplitude:", np.mean(all_data))

    # Example: apply a simple differencing operator to each trace
    for tr in stream:
        tr.data = np.diff(tr.data)

    return stream

docs.title: Usage in CLI
docs.text:
surfquake quick -w "./data/*" -c config.yaml -i inventory.xml \
    --post_script myscript.py --post_script_stage before

surfquake processing -p project.pkl -i inventory.xml -e events.txt -c config.yaml \
    -o ./output -a --post_script myscript.py

surfquake processing_daily -p project.pkl -c config.yaml \
    --post_script myscript.py --post_script_stage after
Argument Description --post_script Path to your Python script. --post_script_stage before (default) or after plotting.

docs.title: Quality control: remove dead and flat traces
docs.text:
# qc_traces.py
import numpy as np
from obspy import Stream

def run(stream, **kwargs):
    kept = Stream()
    for tr in stream:
        data = tr.data
        flat = np.ptp(data) == 0                      # constant signal
        zeros = np.mean(data == 0) > 0.2              # more than 20 % of zeros
        if flat or zeros:
            print(f"[qc] {tr.id} removed")
            continue
        kept.append(tr)
    return kept

docs.title: A custom automatic picker
docs.text:
This script runs a recursive STA/LTA on each trace and writes the onsets into the header as picks. With --post_script_stage before, the picks are drawn on the plot, where you can review, delete or add picks before saving.

# stalta_picker.py
from obspy.signal.trigger import recursive_sta_lta, trigger_onset

STA, LTA = 1.0, 20.0        # seconds
ON, OFF = 3.5, 1.0          # trigger thresholds

def run(stream, **kwargs):
    for tr in stream:
        fs = tr.stats.sampling_rate
        cf = recursive_sta_lta(tr.data, int(STA * fs), int(LTA * fs))
        onsets = trigger_onset(cf, ON, OFF)

        if "picks" not in tr.stats:
            tr.stats.picks = []
        for on, _ in onsets:
            t = tr.stats.starttime + on / fs
            tr.stats.picks.append({"time": t.timestamp, "phase": "P",
                                   "amplitude": float(tr.data[on]), "polarity": "?"})
        print(f"[picker] {tr.id}: {len(onsets)} pick(s)")
    return stream

docs.title: Signal-to-noise ratio around the theoretical P (with processing)
docs.text:
With surfquake processing and an event file, every trace knows its theoretical arrivals. This script measures the SNR around P, stores it in the header and removes the traces below a threshold.

# snr_filter.py
import numpy as np
from obspy import Stream, UTCDateTime

NOISE, SIGNAL = 5.0, 5.0     # seconds before / after P
MIN_SNR = 3.0

def rms(x):
    return np.sqrt(np.mean(x ** 2)) if len(x) else np.nan

def run(stream, **kwargs):
    kept = Stream()
    for tr in stream:
        arrivals = tr.stats.get("geodetic", {}).get("arrivals", [])
        p = next((UTCDateTime(a["time"]) for a in arrivals if a["phase"] == "P"), None)
        if p is None:
            kept.append(tr)              # no theoretical P: keep the trace untouched
            continue

        noise = tr.slice(p - NOISE, p).data
        signal = tr.slice(p, p + SIGNAL).data
        snr = rms(signal) / rms(noise)
        tr.stats.snr = float(snr)        # your own header field, saved in HDF5

        if snr >= MIN_SNR:
            kept.append(tr)
        else:
            print(f"[snr] {tr.id}: SNR = {snr:.1f}, removed")
    return kept

docs.title: Export a table of measurements
docs.text:
A script is imported once, so variables at the top of the file keep their value from one stream to the next. This is useful to build a table over all your events. This example writes the peak amplitude of each trace, for each event; with remove_response (units: 'VEL') in the config, it is the peak ground velocity.

# peak_table.py
import csv
import os

OUTPUT = "./peak_values.csv"

def run(stream, **kwargs):
    event = kwargs.get("event") or {}
    inventory = kwargs.get("inventory")
    new_file = not os.path.exists(OUTPUT)

    with open(OUTPUT, "a", newline="") as f:
        writer = csv.writer(f)
        if new_file:
            writer.writerow(["origin_time", "magnitude", "trace_id", "lat", "lon",
                             "distance_km", "peak"])
        for tr in stream:
            lat = lon = None
            if inventory is not None:
                try:
                    coords = inventory.get_coordinates(tr.id, tr.stats.starttime)
                    lat, lon = coords["latitude"], coords["longitude"]
                except Exception:
                    pass
            distance = tr.stats.get("geodetic", {}).get("geodetic", [None])[0]
            writer.writerow([event.get("origin_time"), event.get("magnitude"), tr.id,
                             lat, lon, distance, float(abs(tr.data).max())])
    return stream

docs.title: Interactive scripts: runpy
docs.text:
Scripts can also be run from the interactive command prompt of the plot (press v). This is useful to try an idea on the traces you are looking at, without leaving the plot. Here the script must define a function process(stream):

  • stream: an ObsPy Stream with the traces currently loaded in the plot, including your picks and references.
  • What you return replaces the plotted traces, and the plot is redrawn. If you return None, the traces are left unchanged.
help runpy
runpy ./scripts/drop_flat_traces.py

Three examples are available with surfquake make_config:

Template What it does script_air_1 Removes the mean of each trace and prints a summary. script_air_2 Drops flat or empty traces. script_air_3 Reads the reference times and the theoretical P arrival from the header, computes an SNR around P and tags the low-SNR traces in tr.stats. 
surfquake make_config -c script_air_3 -o ./scripts

# drop_flat_traces.py
from obspy import Stream

def process(stream):
    threshold = 1e-6
    kept = [tr for tr in stream if tr.data.max() - tr.data.min() > threshold]
    removed = len(stream) - len(kept)
    if removed:
        print(f"[post_script] Dropped {removed} flat/empty trace(s).")
    return Stream(traces=kept)

Tip

You can write a single file valid for both uses, with a process(stream) that simply calls run(stream).

docs.title: Combining scripts and config files
docs.text:
Config files and scripts work together: let the config do the standard processing, and your script the part that is specific to your research. For example, filter and normalise the traces with a config, then detect and annotate phase arrivals with your own picker:

# config.yaml
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 1.0
    fmax: 10.0
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True

surfquake quick -w "./data/*" -c config.yaml --post_script stalta_picker.py --post_script_stage before

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Always return the stream from run(). If the script returns nothing, there is nothing to plot or to write.
  • Errors do not stop the workflow: if your script raises an exception, a warning is printed and the stream continues unchanged. Watch the terminal for [WARNING] Post-script ... failed.
  • Test your script on a few files first, with quick in interactive mode, before running it on a big dataset with -a.
  • Read optional header fields with a default (getattr(tr.stats, "picks", []), tr.stats.get("geodetic", {})): traces without picks or events do not have them.
  • Store your results in the header (tr.stats.my_value = ...) to use them in later steps; they are kept in the HDF5 output.
  • Print useful information: it is your log.
  • Performance: when a post-script is given, the stations are processed one after the other instead of in parallel, so large runs take longer.

This feature makes SurfQuake highly adaptable for both research and operational seismic processing pipelines: everything SurfQuake does is the frame, and your science goes inside.

docs.title: Seismic Data Files
docs.text:
Seismic instruments record ground motion as a sequence of measurements through time. These measurements are stored in waveform files, which contain the digital samples of a seismic signal together with basic information needed to interpret their timing and acquisition. Depending on the sensor, the recordings may represent earthquakes, ambient seismic noise, controlled seismic sources, or other vibrations.

In SurfQuake / Integrated Seismic Program (ISP), waveform handling is based on ObsPy, a Python framework widely used in seismology. Consequently, SurfQuake can work with the seismic waveform formats supported by ObsPy, subject to the requirements of each particular SurfQuake workflow.

Waveforms and metadata are complementary

A waveform file contains the recorded samples and essential trace information, such as the channel identifier, start time, and sampling rate. Station metadata, often stored separately in StationXML, describe the station location, sensor orientation, and instrument response. Both are needed for many quantitative analyses. See the Metadata section for further information.

docs.title: Common seismic waveform formats
docs.text:
Several file formats are used in observational and exploration seismology. They differ in their structure, metadata fields, compression, and typical applications.

Format Common extension Description and typical use MiniSEED .mseed, .msd, .seed Compact, widely used waveform format for continuous monitoring and data exchange between seismic networks. A .seed extension alone does not establish the file type. SAC .sac Seismic Analysis Code format, commonly used for individual traces and earthquake or signal-processing studies. Includes an extensive waveform header. GSE2 .gse, .gse2 Exchange format for seismic waveform data, encountered in network archives and legacy datasets. SEGY .sgy, .segy Multi-trace format widely used for active-source seismic surveys and exploration. SEG2 .seg2, .dat Format often found in near-surface and engineering seismology, especially acquisition-system exports. Seismic Unix (SU) .su Trace-oriented format used in seismic exploration and processing workflows. Other supported formats Varies ObsPy also provides readers for formats such as SEISAN, AH, CSS, K-NET, and several instrument-specific formats.

MiniSEED is a good default for continuous seismic recordings, while SAC is particularly convenient when working with individual traces and their analysis headers. The appropriate choice depends on the dataset and processing objective.

File extensions do not guarantee the format

Filename extensions are conventions, not definitive identifiers. ObsPy usually detects the format from the file contents. Support for a format in ObsPy does not necessarily mean every SurfQuake feature accepts every possible file variant or acquisition-specific header.

For an authoritative list, consult the ObsPy waveform reading documentation.

docs.title: How waveform data are organized
docs.text:
ObsPy uses two principal objects to represent waveform recordings:

Object Description Main contents Stream Collection of one or more seismic traces. A set of Trace objects, possibly from different stations, components, or time intervals. Trace One regularly sampled time-series segment. Sample array (data) and a header (stats) with identifiers, timing, and sampling information.

A Stream may contain several traces, for example the vertical, north–south, and east–west components from one seismic station. The same channel may appear in multiple traces when a recording is divided into separate time segments.

ObsPy Stream
  ├── Trace: XX.ABC.00.BHZ
  │     ├── data  → waveform samples
  │     └── stats → identifiers, timing, sampling rate
  ├── Trace: XX.ABC.00.BHN
  │     ├── data
  │     └── stats
  └── Trace: XX.ABC.00.BHE
        ├── data
        └── stats
  • Identifying a seismic trace: NET.STA.LOC.CHA

Waveforms are commonly identified by four codes:

Network.Station.Location.Channel
   XX  .  ABC .   00   . BHZ
  • Network (XX): the seismic network.
  • Station (ABC): the recording station.
  • Location (00): identifies a particular sensor or data stream at the station; it may be empty.
  • Channel (BHZ): identifies the acquisition channel, including its component designation under the relevant naming convention.

These codes connect a waveform to the corresponding station and channel metadata. They do not, by themselves, specify the recording interval or guarantee that the instrument configuration remained unchanged.

docs.title: What information matters most?
docs.text:
• Sampling rate and recording time

Each regularly sampled trace has a sampling rate \(f_s\), measured in samples per second (Hz). The time interval between consecutive samples is

\[ \Delta t = \frac{1}{f_s}. \]

For example, at 100 Hz the interval between samples is 0.01 s. The theoretical Nyquist frequency is \(f_N=f_s/2\), although the frequency band that can be interpreted reliably also depends on the recording instrument and its acquisition filters.

A trace header normally includes its start time, sampling rate, and number of samples (npts). ObsPy uses these quantities to determine the time associated with each sample. Times are normally handled in UTC through UTCDateTime.

  • Data gaps, overlaps, and continuity

Continuous archives may contain gaps (missing time intervals), overlaps (repeated or conflicting samples), or segments with different sampling rates. These issues can affect filters, spectral analyses, event detection, and other processing methods.

Check continuity before signal processing

Do not assume that all files from one station form an uninterrupted record. Inspect missing intervals and overlaps before merging data. Filling gaps with zeros or interpolated samples changes the time series and can introduce artificial signal content.

  • Sample amplitudes and physical units

Seismic waveforms are often stored as digital counts. Counts are not necessarily displacement, velocity, or acceleration. Obtaining calibrated physical measurements generally requires the corresponding instrument response and an appropriate response-removal procedure.

For more details, see the Metadata section.

docs.title: Preparing waveform files for SurfQuake / ISP
docs.text:
Before importing data into a processing project, it is good practice to:

  • Confirm that the files can be read and contain the expected channels and time intervals.
  • Check the sampling rates and identify any gaps or overlaps.
  • Ensure that network, station, location, and channel identifiers are consistent.
  • Prepare matching StationXML or other compatible station metadata when station positions, orientation, or response corrections are required.
  • Preserve the original recordings and perform processing on separate copies when practical.

These checks are especially useful for continuous monitoring, earthquake waveform analysis, ocean-bottom seismometer recordings, and ambient-noise processing.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
Seismic waveform files contain the recorded time series and their basic acquisition information. Different formats serve different applications, but SurfQuake / ISP benefits from ObsPy's common Stream and Trace interface for working with them.

MiniSEED and SAC are particularly common in observational seismology. Regardless of the format, reliable processing begins by checking trace identifiers, timing, sampling rates, continuity, and the availability of corresponding station metadata.

docs.title: Source Parameters
docs.text:
The tool Source Parameters is designed to estimate events source parameters (i.e., Mw, ML, seismic moment, corner frequency, radiated energy, source size and stress drop`) and the attenuation parameters (t-star, quality factor).

Info

It is based in the implementation of Satrinano et al., 2023. A detailed theoretical background can be found here
