docs.title: Time-Frequency Analysis
docs.text:
A seismogram is a function of time, but much of what it tells us is hidden in its frequency content: the corner frequency of an earthquake, the resonance of a site, the microseism peak, the tones of a ship's engine, the dispersion of surface waves. Spectral analysis moves the trace to the frequency domain to look at these properties.

SurfQuake offers six tools, each answering a different question:

Tool Question it answers Output file Spectrum Which frequencies are in the whole trace, and how strong are they? .sp Spectrogram How does the frequency content change with time? .spec CWT (Continuous Wavelet Transform) Same as the spectrogram, with a resolution that adapts to each frequency. Best for short transients. .cwt Cepstrum Does the signal contain a pattern that repeats (echoes, pulse trains, harmonics)? With which period? .cep Cepstrogram How does that repetition period change with time? .ceps Cross-spectrum Are two traces related at each frequency (coherence)? How does one transform into the other (transfer function)? .coh

Each tool can be used in three ways:

  1. Interactively, from the command prompt of the plot (surfquake quick, then v), to explore your data.
  2. In a config file, to compute and save the results of many traces automatically.
  3. Plotting the saved results with surfquake specplot, or reading them in Python for your own analysis.

A step-by-step example is the Time-Frequency Tutorial.

docs.title: Time and frequency resolution
docs.text:
A spectrum computed from a window of length \(T\) seconds has a frequency resolution of about \(\Delta f \approx 1/T\) Hz. Long windows separate close frequencies, short windows locate events precisely in time, but no window does both: this is the time–frequency uncertainty principle. Each time-frequency method is a different way of choosing this compromise:

  • Spectrogram: one window length for all frequencies (you choose it with win).
  • CWT: long windows for low frequencies and short windows for high frequencies, automatically.

docs.title: Tapering and spectral leakage
docs.text:
The FFT assumes that the window repeats periodically. If the signal does not start and end at zero, the jump at the edges spreads energy over all frequencies: this is spectral leakage, which hides weak peaks next to strong ones. SurfQuake always removes the mean and applies a taper:

  • FFT: a single 5 % cosine taper on each side of the window.
  • Multitaper: several orthogonal tapers (Slepian sequences), each one giving an independent estimate; their average has much less variance (less "noisy" spectra) and very little leakage. It is slower.

The data are also zero-padded to the next power of 2, which interpolates the spectrum (more frequency samples), but does not improve the real resolution, which depends only on the window length.

docs.title: Units: Fourier amplitude or spectral density
docs.text:
The spectrum is given in one of two physical scalings, the same for every method, so spectra computed with different methods can be compared directly:

scaling Units Use it for fourier (default) trace unit × s (e.g. m/s · s) Transients (earthquakes, explosions): $ asd trace unit / √Hz Continuous signals (noise, microseism, tremor): amplitude spectral density, \(\sqrt{\text{PSD}}\). The value does not depend on the record length, so it can be compared with noise models.

The spectrograms store the power spectral density (PSD, unit²/Hz) of each window. In the figures, spectrograms and scalograms are shown in dB relative to their maximum:

\[P_{\mathrm{dB}}(f,t) = 10\log_{10}\left(\frac{P(f,t)}{P_{\max}}\right)\]

so 0 dB is the strongest point, and −60 dB is a million times weaker in power.

Tip

Remove the instrument response first (remove_response) if you want the spectra in ground-motion units (m/s, m). Otherwise they are in counts.

docs.title: Spectrum
docs.text: The spectrum shows how the energy of the whole trace (or of the selected window) is distributed in frequency. It is the tool to measure the corner frequency and the high-frequency decay of an earthquake, to identify the frequency band of a signal before filtering, or to find spectral lines (tones) in continuous data.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
method Description fft Fast Fourier transform with a 5 % cosine taper. Fast, keeps the full resolution and also stores the phase. The standard choice for transients. multitaper Adaptive multitaper estimate. Smoother, lower variance, very little leakage. The best choice for noise and for weak peaks. burg, yule, covar, modcovar Parametric (autoregressive, AR) methods: they fit a model of order poles to the samples and draw the spectrum from the model. They give smooth spectra and sharp peaks from short records. burg is the recommended one; yule is the smoothest and least resolving. minvar Minimum variance (Capon) spectrum. music, ev Pseudo-spectra: they separate signal and noise subspaces to find the frequencies of pure tones with very high resolution. Their amplitudes have no physical meaning: look at where the peaks are, not at how high they are.

The parametric methods need the optional package spectrum (pip install spectrum). The data are not tapered or zero-padded for them.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description method One of the methods above (default fft). scaling fourier (default) or asd, see Units. Ignored by music and ev. order Parametric methods: model order (default 20). Each spectral peak needs about 2 poles, and they are spread from 0 Hz to Nyquist; to study low frequencies, decimate the trace first rather than raising the order a lot. Capped at 1/3 of the number of samples. nsig music and ev only (required): 2 per pure tone you expect in the data (1 tone → 2, 3 tones → 6). Must be smaller than order. output_path Folder for the results (created if missing).

docs.title: Config Example
docs.text:
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'spectrum'
    method: 'fft'
    scaling: 'fourier'
    output_path: './spectral'

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'spectrum'
    method: 'multitaper'
    scaling: 'asd'
    output_path: './spectral'

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'spectrum'
    method: 'music'
    order: 30
    nsig: 4
    output_path: './spectral'

docs.title: Interactive
docs.text:
help spectrum
spectrum 0                                  # first trace, log-log axes, FFT
spectrum all loglog --mode multitaper       # all displayed traces
sp 2 xlog --mode burg --order 30            # 'sp' is an alias
sp 0 --mode music --order 20 --nsig 4

axis_type: loglog (default), xlog, ylog or linlin.

docs.title: Spectrogram
docs.text: The spectrogram cuts the trace into overlapping windows and computes the spectrum of each one (short-time Fourier transform). The result is a picture of power as a function of time and frequency. It shows how a signal evolves: the arrival of P and S waves with their different frequency content, the dispersion of surface waves, the gliding tones of tremor, the passage of a ship, the daily cycle of cultural noise.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description win Window length in seconds (required). Longer → finer frequency resolution (about 1/win Hz) but coarser time resolution. It should contain several cycles of the lowest frequency of interest. overlap Overlap between consecutive windows, in percent (default 50). Larger values give a smoother image in time (more windows), not more resolution. method multitaper (default): smoother, less noisy, slower. fft: fast, 5 % cosine taper per window, also stores the phase. nw Multitaper only: time-bandwidth product. Larger = smoother spectrum, lower frequency resolution. If not set, an adaptive low-bias estimate is used (recommended: nw < 4). output_path Folder for the results.

docs.title: Config Example
docs.text:
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'spectrogram'
    method: 'multitaper'
    win: 5.0
    overlap: 50
    output_path: './spectral'

docs.title: Interactive
docs.text:
help spectrogram
spectrogram 0                                       # first trace, defaults (5 s, 50 %)
spec 0 3.0 75                                       # 3 s windows, 75 % overlap
spec 0 5.0 50 -120                                  # clip the colour scale at -120 dB
spectrogram 0 5.0 50 --method fft --dates           # dates on the time axis
spectrogram 0 5.0 50 --method multitaper --nw 3.5

docs.title: Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT)
docs.text:
The CWT compares the trace with a wavelet, a short oscillation, stretched and compressed to many frequencies. At high frequencies the wavelet is short, so the CWT is sharp in time; at low frequencies it is long, so the CWT is sharp in frequency. This adaptive resolution makes it the best tool for transient signals: onsets, short bursts, dispersed wave trains, and signals with energy over a wide band. The result is called a scalogram.

The frequencies are sampled logarithmically (voices_per_octave frequencies per octave, i.e. per doubling of frequency), which matches the adaptive resolution.

Cone of influence: near the beginning and the end of the trace, the wavelet partially falls outside the data and the scalogram is unreliable. This edge region is wider at low frequencies (longer wavelets) and is marked in the figure.

docs.title: Wavelets
docs.text: wavelet Shape Use it for cm Complex Morlet: a sine wave inside a Gaussian envelope. Good balance between time and frequency resolution; with param: 6 its scales match Fourier frequencies. The default and recommended choice. mh Mexican Hat: real wavelet, second derivative of a Gaussian. Very short, excellent time resolution, poor frequency resolution. Locating sharp onsets. pa Paul: complex, asymmetric, short. Good time resolution. Impulsive signals.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description wavelet cm, mh or pa (required). param Main wavelet parameter (required). For cm it is the number of cycles (6 = standard; larger = better frequency resolution, worse time resolution). fmin, fmax Frequency band analysed (Hz). fmax must be below Nyquist. Defaults: 4 cycles in the trace length, and Nyquist. voices_per_octave Frequency sampling: 8 = coarse, 16 = standard (default), 32 = fine. output_path Folder for the results (required).

docs.title: Config Example
docs.text:
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'cwt'
    wavelet: 'cm'
    param: 6.0
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 20.0
    voices_per_octave: 16
    output_path: './spectral'

docs.title: Interactive
docs.text:
help cwt
cwt 0 cm 6                         # first trace, complex Morlet
cwt 2 mh 6 0.5 10                  # Mexican hat between 0.5 and 10 Hz
cwt 2 pa 6 0.5 10 -120 --dates     # clip at -120 dB, dates on the time axis

docs.title: Cepstrum and Cepstrogram
docs.text:
The cepstrum is the "spectrum of the log-spectrum". When a signal contains a pattern that repeats every \(T\) seconds (an echo, a reverberation in a water or sediment layer, a train of pulses, the harmonics of a ship's propeller or of volcanic tremor), its spectrum shows regularly spaced ripples, every \(1/T\) Hz. The cepstrum turns these ripples into a single peak at quefrency \(T\) (in seconds), which is much easier to detect and measure.

The cepstrogram computes the cepstrum in sliding windows, like the spectrogram, to follow how the repetition period changes with time (for example a ship approaching and moving away).

docs.title: Kinds
docs.text:
kind Definition Use it for real \(c = \mathrm{IFFT}(\log\lvert X(f)\rvert)\). Keeps the sign. Harmonic combs (propellers, tremor). power \(c = \lvert\mathrm{IFFT}(\log\lvert X(f)\rvert^2)\rvert^2\). Always positive. Echoes and multipath, where the reflection can make the peak negative in real. complex Uses the unwrapped phase too. Cepstrum only. Separating a signal from its echoes (deconvolution).

The low quefrencies (the first few samples) describe the smooth shape of the spectrum, not repetitions; they are hidden in the plots by default.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description kind real, power (or complex for the cepstrum). win Cepstrogram: window length in seconds. It must hold several repetitions: the longest detectable period is about win. overlap_percent Cepstrogram: overlap between windows, in percent. qmin, qmax Cepstrogram (optional): quefrency range kept, in seconds. output_path Folder for the results.

docs.title: Config Example
docs.text:
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'cepstrum'
    kind: 'real'
    output_path: './spectral'

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'cepstrogram'
    kind: 'real'
    win: 20
    overlap_percent: 75.0
    output_path: './spectral'

docs.title: Cross-spectrum: coherence and transfer function
docs.text:
The cross-spectrum compares a reference trace with every other trace, frequency by frequency:

  • Coherence (0–1): how linearly related the two traces are at each frequency. 1 = one trace is a filtered version of the other; 0 = unrelated. It shows the band where two sensors record the same signal, and a dashed line marks the significance threshold.
  • Transfer function \(H(f) = G_{xy}/G_{xx}\): the amplitude and phase of the filter that transforms the reference into the other trace. Use it to compare two sensors (huddle tests), to measure site amplification against a rock station, or to check the response of an instrument.

It needs averaging to be meaningful (coherence of a single window is always 1): welch averages overlapping windows, multitaper averages over tapers. It is a stream method; see Processing Stream for all its parameters.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'cross_spectrum'
    reference_idx: 0
    method: 'welch'
    win: 20.0
    overlap_percent: 75.0
    output_path: './spectral'

Interactive:

help coh
coh --ref 0 --kind both --win 20

docs.title: Interactive commands
docs.text:
Open the plot with surfquake quick, select a time window with u (start) and i (end) if you want to analyse only a part of the traces, and press v to open the command prompt. The traces are referred to by their position in the current page (0, 1, ...) or all.

Command Description spectrum / sp Amplitude spectrum spectrogram / spec Spectrogram cwt Continuous wavelet transform coh / tf Coherence and transfer function save_tf Save one of the above to disk

These commands only compute and display: the traces are not modified. To keep a result, save it with save_tf:

help save_tf
save_tf spectrum all --folder_path ./spectral
save_tf spectrogram 0 --win 5.0 --overlap 50 --method fft --folder_path ./spectral
save_tf cwt 0 --wavelet cm --param 6 --fmin 0.5 --fmax 10 --folder_path ./spectral
save_tf coh all --ref 0 --folder_path ./spectral

If a time window is selected (u, i), only that window is saved.

docs.title: Config file (automatic)
docs.text:
surfquake make_config -c spectral_config -o ./configs
surfquake quick -w "./data/*" -c ./configs/spectral_config.yaml -a

The template contains commented examples of every tool. The spectral steps can follow any pre-processing step (detrend, filter, remove response...) and they do not modify the traces: the next steps receive the same waveforms.

The results are saved in output_path as:

Tool File name spectrum <trace_id>.D.<year>.<julday>.sp spectrogram <trace_id>.D.<year>.<julday>.spec cwt <trace_id>.D.<year>.<julday>.cwt cepstrum <trace_id>.D.<year>.<julday>.cep cepstrogram <trace_id>.D.<year>.<julday>.ceps cross-spectrum <ref_id>__<trace_id>.D.<year>.<julday>.coh

If a file already exists, a number is added (_1, _2...).

docs.title: Plotting and CLI Usage
docs.text:
All the saved results are plotted with surfquake specplot. The type of result is recognised from the file extension.

surfquake specplot -h

# Spectrum
surfquake specplot -f ./spectral/IU.HKT.00.BHZ.D.2024.123.sp -a xlog

# Spectrogram, split into low/high frequency panels, dates on the x axis
surfquake specplot -f ./spectral/IU.HKT.00.BHZ.D.2024.123.spec --clip -120 --split -d

# Scalogram, smoothed, saved to a folder
surfquake specplot -f ./spectral/WM.OBS01..SHZ.D.2015.260.cwt -d --split --smooth --save_path ./figures --cmap gnuplot2

# Cepstrogram, repetition periods between 0.05 and 2 s, with the dominant period tracked
surfquake specplot -f ./spectral/IU.HKT.00.BHZ.D.2024.123.ceps --qmin 0.05 --qmax 2 --track

# Coherence and transfer function
surfquake specplot -f ./spectral/IU.HKT.00.BHZ__IU.HKT.10.BHZ.D.2024.123.coh

To save all the figures of a folder, loop over the files in a bash script:

for file in ./spectral/*.spec; do
    surfquake specplot -f "$file" --split --smooth -d --save_path ./figures
done

docs.title: CLI Options
docs.text:
Option Applies to Description -f, --file all (required) Path to the .sp, .spec, .cwt, .cep, .ceps or .coh file. -a, --axis_type .sp, .coh Axes: loglog (default), xlog, ylog, linlin. -c, --clip .spec, .cwt, .ceps Minimum displayed power, in dB (e.g. -120). -v, --vmax_db .spec, .cwt, .ceps Maximum displayed power, in dB (default 0). --split .spec, .cwt Split the plot into low and high frequency panels, each with its own colour scale. Cutoff 1 Hz by default, or --split 0.5. Useful when the microseism dominates the colour scale. -s, --smooth .spec, .cwt, .ceps Smooth the time-frequency image (slower, prettier). -d, --dates .spec, .cwt, .ceps Dates on the x axis instead of seconds. --cmap .spec, .cwt, .ceps Matplotlib colormap (default rainbow). --qmin, --qmax .cep, .ceps Quefrency range shown, in seconds. --track .ceps Overlay the dominant quefrency of every window. --save_path all Folder where the figure is saved (named automatically); the figure is then not shown. --extension all Image format: png (default), pdf, svg...

The plotting options change the figure only, never the stored values.

docs.title: Accessing the results in Python
docs.text:
SurfQuake does not store only an image. Each file contains a Python object with the numerical arrays and the original ObsPy Trace. You can load it, select frequencies or time windows, and continue your analysis without extracting data from a figure.

All the classes have from_pickle(filepath) to load a file, to_pickle(folder_path) to save it, and a plotting method. The files are gzip-compressed by default.

File Class Import .sp TraceSpectrumResult from surfquakecore.spectral.specrun import TraceSpectrumResult .spec TraceSpectrogramResult from surfquakecore.spectral.specrun import TraceSpectrogramResult .coh TraceCrossSpectralResult from surfquakecore.spectral.specrun import TraceCrossSpectralResult .cwt TraceCWTResult from surfquakecore.spectral.cwtrun import TraceCWTResult .cep TraceCepstrumResult from surfquakecore.spectral.ceprun import TraceCepstrumResult .ceps TraceCepstrogramResult from surfquakecore.spectral.ceprun import TraceCepstrogramResult

docs.title: 1. Spectrum (.sp)
docs.text:
Attribute Contents trace, stats The analysed ObsPy Trace and its header. freq Frequencies (Hz). spectrum Spectral amplitudes, paired with freq by index, in the units given by scaling. phase Phase (radians) of each frequency, fft method only (otherwise None). method, scaling Method and scaling used. order, nsig for the parametric methods. 
import numpy as np
from surfquakecore.spectral.specrun import TraceSpectrumResult

result = TraceSpectrumResult.from_pickle("./spectral/IU.HKT.00.BHZ.D.2024.123.sp")

print(result.trace.id, result.method, result.scaling)
freq = np.asarray(result.freq)
amp = np.asarray(result.spectrum)

# Amplitude at the frequency nearest to 5 Hz
i = np.argmin(np.abs(freq - 5.0))
print(f"{freq[i]:.3f} Hz: {amp[i]:.6g}")

# Frequency of the spectral peak between 1 and 20 Hz
band = (freq >= 1) & (freq <= 20)
print("Peak at", freq[band][np.argmax(amp[band])], "Hz")

docs.title: 2. Spectrogram (.spec)
docs.text:
Attribute Contents trace, stats The analysed ObsPy Trace and its header. time Centre of each window, in seconds from the trace start. freq Frequencies (Hz). spectrogram 2D array of power spectral density (linear, unit²/Hz), indexed [frequency, time]. phase 2D phase array (radians), fft method only. num_steps Number of windows. 
import numpy as np
from surfquakecore.spectral.specrun import TraceSpectrogramResult

result = TraceSpectrogramResult.from_pickle("./spectral/IU.HKT.00.BHZ.D.2024.123.spec")

power = np.asarray(result.spectrogram)
freq = np.asarray(result.freq)
time = np.asarray(result.time)
assert power.shape == (len(freq), len(time))

# Power at the nearest frequency and time
fi = np.argmin(np.abs(freq - 2.0))
ti = np.argmin(np.abs(time - 60.0))
print(f"PSD at {freq[fi]:.2f} Hz and {time[ti]:.1f} s:", power[fi, ti])

# Energy in the 1-5 Hz band as a function of time
band = (freq >= 1.0) & (freq <= 5.0)
band_energy = np.trapezoid(power[band, :], freq[band], axis=0)

# Absolute UTC times of the windows
utc_times = [result.stats.starttime + float(t) for t in time]

# Relative dB, as in the figure
with np.errstate(divide="ignore"):
    db = 10 * np.log10(power / np.nanmax(power))

docs.title: 3. Continuous Wavelet Transform (.cwt)
docs.text:
The result is stored in the tuple cwt_data:

Element Contents cwt_data[0] t: time in seconds from the trace start. cwt_data[1] f: frequencies (Hz), logarithmically spaced. cwt_data[2] Scalogram: complex wavelet coefficients, indexed [frequency, time]. The power is abs(...)**2. cwt_data[3], cwt_data[4] Left and right limits of the cone of influence (times, in seconds). 
import numpy as np
from surfquakecore.spectral.cwtrun import TraceCWTResult

result = TraceCWTResult.from_pickle("./spectral/WM.OBS01..SHZ.D.2015.260.cwt")
t, f, W, coi_left, coi_right = result.cwt_data

power = np.abs(W) ** 2
assert power.shape == (len(f), len(t))

# Power between 1 and 5 Hz
band = (f >= 1.0) & (f <= 5.0)
band_power = power[band, :]

# Instantaneous phase at 2 Hz (complex wavelets only)
fi = np.argmin(np.abs(f - 2.0))
phase = np.angle(W[fi, :])

# Plot again with other options
result.plot_cwt(split=1.0, clip=-80)

The cone-of-influence limits are times computed with a linear frequency axis, not boolean masks: use them as an approximate guide of the region affected by the edges.

docs.title: 4. Cepstrum (.cep) and Cepstrogram (.ceps)
docs.text:
Class Attributes TraceCepstrumResult quefrency (s), cepstrum, kind, and find_peaks() TraceCepstrogramResult time (window centres, s), quefrency (s), cepstrogram (2D, [quefrency, time]), kind, win, and track_peak() 
from surfquakecore.spectral.ceprun import TraceCepstrumResult, TraceCepstrogramResult

cep = TraceCepstrumResult.from_pickle("./spectral/IU.HKT.00.BHZ.D.2024.123.cep")
for peak in cep.find_peaks(qmin=0.05, qmax=2.0, n_peaks=3):
    print(f"Repetition every {peak['quefrency']:.3f} s ({peak['frequency']:.2f} Hz), SNR {peak['snr']:.1f}")

ceps = TraceCepstrogramResult.from_pickle("./spectral/IU.HKT.00.BHZ.D.2024.123.ceps")
time, period, value = ceps.track_peak(qmin=0.05, qmax=2.0)   # dominant period in each window

find_peaks() returns the strongest repetition periods, as dictionaries with quefrency (s), frequency (= 1 / quefrency, Hz), value and snr (height above the median, in robust standard deviations).

docs.title: 5. Cross-spectrum (.coh)
docs.text:
Attribute or property Contents ref_trace, trace Reference (input) and target (output) traces. freq Frequencies (Hz). gxx, gyy Auto-spectra of the reference and the target. gxy Complex cross-spectrum, \(E[X^* Y]\). n_avg Number of averages, used for the significance threshold. coherence Magnitude-squared coherence (0–1). transfer Complex transfer function \(G_{xy}/G_{xx}\). amplitude, phase_deg Amplitude and phase (degrees) of the transfer function. coherence_threshold(alpha) Coherence below which the result is not significant at level alpha (default 0.05). 
from surfquakecore.spectral.specrun import TraceCrossSpectralResult

result = TraceCrossSpectralResult.from_pickle("./spectral/IU.HKT.00.BHZ__IU.HKT.10.BHZ.D.2024.123.coh")

threshold = result.coherence_threshold(alpha=0.05)
reliable = result.coherence > max(threshold, 0.8)
print("Reliable band:", result.freq[reliable].min(), "-", result.freq[reliable].max(), "Hz")
print("Mean amplification there:", result.amplitude[reliable].mean())

coherence, transfer, amplitude and phase_deg are computed from gxx, gyy and gxy when you access them. High coherence means a strong linear relationship, not necessarily causality.

docs.title: Computing in Python
docs.text:
The same classes compute the results directly from ObsPy traces:

from obspy import read
from surfquakecore.spectral.specrun import TraceSpectrumResult, TraceSpectrogramResult

tr = read("./data/IU.HKT.00.BHZ.D.2024.123")[0]

sp = TraceSpectrumResult(tr)
sp.compute_spectrum(method="multitaper", scaling="asd")
sp.to_pickle("./spectral")

sg = TraceSpectrogramResult(tr)
sg.compute_spectrogram(win=5.0, overlap_percent=50, method="fft")
sg.plot_spectrogram(clip=-100, split=1.0)

docs.title: Scientific References
docs.text:
• Percival, D. B., & Walden, A. T. (1993). Spectral Analysis for Physical Applications: Multitaper and Conventional Univariate Techniques. Cambridge University Press.
  • Thomson, D. J. (1982). Spectrum estimation and harmonic analysis. Proceedings of the IEEE, 70(9), 1055–1096.
  • Torrence, C., & Compo, G. P. (1998). A practical guide to wavelet analysis. Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, 79(1), 61–78.
  • Bogert, B. P., Healy, M. J. R., & Tukey, J. W. (1963). The quefrency alanysis of time series for echoes. Proceedings of the Symposium on Time Series Analysis, 209–243.
  • Bendat, J. S., & Piersol, A. G. (2010). Random Data: Analysis and Measurement Procedures (4th ed.). Wiley.

docs.title: Synthetic Test Signals Tutorial 4
docs.text:
In this tutorial, we will learn how to generate synthetic signals with surfquake and use them to test what the processing methods do. We will work with the commands make_config, quick and specplot.

Why synthetic signals? With real data we never know exactly what the "true" signal is, so it is difficult to tell whether a result comes from the Earth, from the noise, or from the processing itself. With a synthetic signal we know the answer in advance: we know where the spike is, which frequencies the signal contains, and how many seconds one trace is delayed with respect to another. So we can check, step by step, that each method does what we expect, and learn what it does before applying it to real data.

In this tutorial we will:

  1. Generate and look at all the types of synthetic signals.
  2. See the impulse response of a filter, with and without phase shift.
  3. Check how detrending (rmean) removes trends.
  4. Watch aliasing happen when resampling without an anti-alias filter.
  5. Bury a wavelet in noise and recover it by filtering.
  6. Measure a time delay between two stations with cross-correlation.
  7. Combine synthetic signals with real data.

No data download is needed: all the traces are created by surfquake.

We will follow this structure:

  • Config Files: tutorial4/configs
  • Folder for the tutorial output: tutorial4/output, this will be created by surfquake.
--tutorial4
    --configs
        --test_sign_config.yaml
        --plotting_config.yaml
        --ex1_impulse.yaml
        --ex2_trends.yaml
        --ex3_aliasing.yaml
        --ex4_noise.yaml
        --ex5_delay.yaml

All the commands of this tutorial are run from the folder that contains tutorial4.

Please, first open a terminal, activate your environment and type the following command to overview all surfquake capabilities:

surfquake -h

docs.title: How synthetic signals work
docs.text:
A normal config file has an Analysis section with the processing steps. To generate synthetic traces, the config file has a Source section instead of (or in addition to) the Analysis section, and the command quick is run without -w: instead of reading files, surfquake builds the traces described in Source, and then processes them with the Analysis steps exactly as it would process real data.

Source:                 # what traces to create
  trace_1:
    ...
  trace_2:
    ...
Analysis:               # (optional) how to process them, as with real data
  process_1:
    ...

Each entry of Source (trace_1, trace_2, ...) creates one trace, in numerical order. An entry has two parts:

1. The header, which identifies the trace as in real data:

Key Description network, station, location, channel Trace codes, e.g. 'XX', 'IMP', '', 'BHZ'. Use a different station code for each trace: the output files are named after them. XX is the usual code for test networks. starttime UTC time of the first sample, 'YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS' (default 1970-01-01). sampling_rate Samples per second, in Hz (default 100). duration Length of the trace, in seconds (default 60).

2. The signal: signal_type and its parameters.

signal_type Signal Parameters Good for testing impulse A single spike amplitude, sample Impulse response of filters and instruments. impulse_train Several spikes samples, amplitudes Repetitions, cepstrum, stacking. step 0, then amplitude from the middle on amplitude Step response, integration, offsets. boxcar Rectangular pulse (1/3 to 2/3 of the trace) amplitude Spectra (sinc), tapers, convolution. triangle Triangular pulse (25 % to 75 %) amplitude Source time functions, smoothing. sine \(A \sin(2\pi f t + \phi)\) frequency, phase, amplitude Filters, spectra, polarity. line \(\text{slope}\cdot t + \text{intercept}\) slope, intercept Detrending. quadratic \(a t^2 + b t + c\) a, b, c Polynomial detrending, integration. cubic \(a t^3 + b t^2 + c t + d\) a, b, c, d Polynomial detrending. random Gaussian white noise mean, std, seed Noise, spectral methods, coherence. ricker Ricker wavelet (zero phase) frequency, time, amplitude A simple seismic "arrival": picking, correlation, detection. chirp Sine sweeping from f0 to f1 f0, f1, method, amplitude, phase Time-frequency analysis, aliasing, filter bands. damped_sine Decaying oscillation from time on frequency, decay, amplitude, phase, time Resonances, spectral peaks, wavelets. gaussian Bell-shaped pulse sigma, time, amplitude Smooth pulses, smoothing, envelopes.

Rules for the parameters:

  • time is in seconds from the first sample, and sample / samples are sample indices starting at 0. Both must lie inside the trace.
  • Frequencies are in Hz and must not exceed the Nyquist frequency (sampling_rate / 2).
  • Phases are in degrees.
  • seed (for random): an integer gives the same noise every run (reproducible), null a different noise each time.

docs.title: Generate Config Files
docs.text:
The template contains one example of every signal type, all documented. Let's prepare it, together with the plotting configuration:

surfquake make_config -h
surfquake make_config -c test_sign_config -o "./tutorial4/configs"
surfquake make_config -c plotting_config -o "./tutorial4/configs"

The plotting configuration is commented to explain the functionality, and the processing methods are described here for traces and here for streams.

docs.title: Step 1: Generate and look at all the signals
docs.text:
The template can be run as it is: it creates 14 traces, one per signal type.

surfquake quick -h
surfquake quick -c "./tutorial4/configs/test_sign_config.yaml" --plot_config "./tutorial4/configs/plotting_config.yaml"

Note that there is no -w: the traces come from the Source section. Move through the pages with n and b.

To save the traces as files, use the automatic mode with an output folder:

surfquake quick -c "./tutorial4/configs/test_sign_config.yaml" -o "./tutorial4/output" -a

The files are written in HDF5 format, named network.station.location.channel.D.year.julday.h5, for example XX.RCK..BHZ.D.2024.1.h5. They can be read like any other waveform file, with -w:

surfquake info -w "./tutorial4/output/*" -c 3

docs.title: Step 2: The impulse response of a filter
docs.text:
An impulse contains all the frequencies with the same amplitude. So, if we filter an impulse, what comes out is exactly the filter itself: its impulse response. Its spectrum is the frequency response of the filter.

Create the file ex1_impulse.yaml:

Source:
  trace_1:
    network: 'XX'
    station: 'IMP'
    location: ''
    channel: 'BHZ'
    starttime: '2024-01-01T00:00:00'
    sampling_rate: 100.0
    duration: 60.0
    signal_type: 'impulse'
    amplitude: 1.0
    sample: 3000          # the spike is at 30 s
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 1.0
    fmax: 10.0
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True

surfquake quick -c "./tutorial4/configs/ex1_impulse.yaml" --plot_config "./tutorial4/configs/plotting_config.yaml"

Zoom around 30 s. Then open the prompt with v and look at its spectrum, which is the frequency response of the filter:

spectrum 0 loglog

Now change zerophase: True to zerophase: False, and run it again. Close the window and type r in the terminal to reprocess with the new config, or run the command again.

What you should see:

zerophase Result True A symmetric wavelet centred exactly at 30.000 s, with energy before the impulse. False Nothing before 30 s; the wavelet starts at the impulse, its maximum is delayed (about 30.10 s) and it is not symmetric.

What does this mean for real data?

A zero-phase filter (applied forwards and backwards) does not move the arrivals, so it is the right choice for picking times. But it spreads energy before the onset, which can make a first motion look earlier, or create a small "precursor". A causal filter never puts energy before the onset, so it is the choice for first-motion polarities and for onsets of very impulsive signals, but it delays and distorts the waveform.

docs.title: Step 3: Removing trends
docs.text:
Real records often contain offsets and slow drifts. We will test the rmean methods with a line and a parabola, whose exact shape we know.

Create the file ex2_trends.yaml:

Source:
  trace_1:
    network: 'XX'
    station: 'LIN'
    location: ''
    channel: 'BHZ'
    starttime: '2024-01-01T00:00:00'
    sampling_rate: 100.0
    duration: 60.0
    signal_type: 'line'
    slope: 0.5
    intercept: 2.0
  trace_2:
    network: 'XX'
    station: 'QUA'
    location: ''
    channel: 'BHZ'
    starttime: '2024-01-01T00:00:00'
    sampling_rate: 100.0
    duration: 60.0
    signal_type: 'quadratic'
    a: 0.01
    b: 0.0
    c: 0.0
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'demean'

Run it, then change method to 'linear', and finally to 'polynomial' with order: 2:

surfquake quick -c "./tutorial4/configs/ex2_trends.yaml" --plot_config "./tutorial4/configs/plotting_config.yaml"

What you should see (maximum absolute value left in the trace):

method Line (LIN) Parabola (QUA) Why (no processing) 32 36 The original signals. demean 15 24 Only the mean is removed: the slope remains. linear ~0 6 A straight line is removed exactly; a parabola is not a line, so a curved residual remains. polynomial, order: 2 ~0 ~0 A second-order polynomial fits both.

Tip

Use the simplest method that removes your trend: high polynomial orders can also remove real long-period signals.

docs.title: Step 4: Aliasing
docs.text:
When the sampling rate is reduced, frequencies above the new Nyquist frequency (half the new sampling rate) cannot be represented. They do not disappear: they fold back into the band and appear as false, lower frequencies. This is aliasing, and once it has happened it cannot be undone. A chirp, which sweeps all frequencies from 1 to 20 Hz, makes it easy to see.

Create the file ex3_aliasing.yaml. We resample the chirp from 100 Hz to 20 Hz (new Nyquist: 10 Hz) with the correct method, resample, which applies an anti-alias filter first:

Source:
  trace_1:
    network: 'XX'
    station: 'CHP'
    location: ''
    channel: 'BHZ'
    starttime: '2024-01-01T00:00:00'
    sampling_rate: 100.0
    duration: 60.0
    signal_type: 'chirp'
    f0: 1.0
    f1: 20.0
    method: 'linear'
    amplitude: 1.0
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'resample'
    sampling_rate: 20
    pre_filter: True

surfquake quick -c "./tutorial4/configs/ex3_aliasing.yaml" --plot_config "./tutorial4/configs/plotting_config.yaml"

Open the prompt with v and look at the spectrogram:

spectrogram 0 2.0 75

Now replace the resample step with a plain decimation, raw, which keeps one sample out of 5 without any filter:

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'raw'
    factor: 5
    integers: False

Run it again and compare the spectrograms.

What you should see:

Time True frequency resample (with anti-alias filter) raw (no filter) 10–15 s ~5 Hz 5 Hz, full amplitude 5 Hz, full amplitude 40–45 s ~14.4 Hz removed (amplitude ~0) appears at 5.6 Hz (= 20 − 14.4), full amplitude 55–60 s ~19.2 Hz removed appears at 0.8 Hz (= 20 − 19.2), full amplitude

With raw, the spectrogram shows the sweep going up to 10 Hz and then coming back down, as if reflected by a mirror at the Nyquist frequency. Those false frequencies look perfectly real: in real data you could not tell them apart from true signals.

Warning

Always use resample (with pre_filter: True) to reduce the sampling rate for analysis. raw is only meant to speed up the plotting of long traces.

docs.title: Step 5: Recovering a signal from the noise
docs.text:
We bury a Ricker wavelet (a simple model of a seismic arrival, centred at 5 Hz) in white noise, and recover it with a band-pass filter.

Create the file ex4_noise.yaml:

Source:
  trace_1:
    network: 'XX'
    station: 'RCK'
    location: ''
    channel: 'BHZ'
    starttime: '2024-01-01T00:00:00'
    sampling_rate: 100.0
    duration: 60.0
    signal_type: 'ricker'
    frequency: 5.0
    time: 30.0
    amplitude: 1.0
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'add_noise'
    noise_type: 'white'
    SNR_dB: -10
  process_2:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_3:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 1.0
    fmax: 10.0
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True

First run it without the filter (delete or comment the process_3 block), then with it:

surfquake quick -c "./tutorial4/configs/ex4_noise.yaml" --plot_config "./tutorial4/configs/plotting_config.yaml"

What you should see (peak of the wavelet divided by the standard deviation of the noise):

SNR_dB Before filtering After the 1–10 Hz filter 10 ~100 ~220 0 ~32 ~72 −10 ~9 ~23

The filter removes the noise outside the band of the wavelet, while keeping the wavelet: the peak-to-noise ratio improves by more than 2 times. White noise has energy at all frequencies, and the wavelet only between ~1 and ~12 Hz, so the narrower the filter around the signal, the larger the gain.

About SNR_dB

SNR_dB compares the noise with the mean power of the whole trace. A short pulse in a long trace has a very small mean power, so even SNR_dB: 0 leaves the pulse clearly visible. To create a difficult test with short signals, use negative values (−10, −20 dB).

Try it: lower SNR_dB until you cannot see the wavelet before filtering, and check whether you can still see it after. You can also test the characteristic functions on it (see Characteristic Functions), for example by adding an STA/LTA step:

  process_4:
    name: 'snr'
    method: 'classic'
    sign_win: 0.5
    noise_win: 10

docs.title: Step 6: Measuring a time delay with cross-correlation
docs.text:
We create the same wavelet at two "stations", the second one 2.5 s later, as if the wave took 2.5 s to travel from one to the other. The cross-correlation should find that delay.

Create the file ex5_delay.yaml:

Source:
  trace_1:
    network: 'XX'
    station: 'STA1'
    location: ''
    channel: 'BHZ'
    starttime: '2024-01-01T00:00:00'
    sampling_rate: 100.0
    duration: 60.0
    signal_type: 'ricker'
    frequency: 5.0
    time: 30.0
  trace_2:
    network: 'XX'
    station: 'STA2'
    location: ''
    channel: 'BHZ'
    starttime: '2024-01-01T00:00:00'
    sampling_rate: 100.0
    duration: 60.0
    signal_type: 'ricker'
    frequency: 5.0
    time: 32.5
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'cross_correlate'
    mode: 'full'
    normalize: 'naive'
    reference_idx: 0
    trim: True

To see the result against the lag time, open the plotting configuration and set:

plot_type: record
record_option: egf

surfquake quick -c "./tutorial4/configs/ex5_delay.yaml" --plot_config "./tutorial4/configs/plotting_config.yaml"

What you should see:

  • XX.STA1_STA1..BXZ: the autocorrelation of the reference, with its maximum (1.0) at lag 0 s.
  • XX.STA1_STA2..BXZ: the cross-correlation, with its maximum (1.0) at lag +2.5 s: STA2 records the wave 2.5 s after STA1.

Try it: change time of the second trace, or add noise to both traces with add_noise before the correlation, and check that the peak stays at the right lag.

Why normalize: 'naive'?

With normalize: 'full', each lag is divided by the local energy of the traces. The synthetic traces are exactly zero far from the wavelet, so that energy is zero and the result is undefined (NaN). Real data, and synthetic traces with noise added, always have some energy, so full works for them.

docs.title: Step 7: Combining synthetic signals with real data
docs.text:
A powerful test is to inject a synthetic signal of known shape into real noise, for example to know the smallest event your detector can find. It is done in two runs:

  1. Generate the synthetic trace and save it. Give it a starttime inside the time window of your real data, and the same sampling_rate:

    surfquake quick -c "./tutorial4/configs/ex4_noise.yaml" -o "./tutorial4/output" -a

  2. Read the real data and the synthetic files together with -w (paths separated by a comma), and process them as usual:

    surfquake quick -w "./data/*,./tutorial4/output/*" -c "./tutorial4/configs/typical_config.yaml" --plot_config "./tutorial4/configs/plotting_config.yaml"

To add the synthetic signal onto a real trace (signal + real noise in the same trace), use the algebra method, e.g. expression: "tr1 + tr2". See Processing Stream.

Note

When -w is given, the Source section of the config file is ignored: generation only happens without -w.

docs.title: Using Bash script
docs.text:
Finally, we can run all the exercises at once and save their results with a bash script file. Create a file named run_synthetic.sh:

#!/bin/bash
set -e

# Activate your conda environment
eval "$(conda shell.bash hook)"
conda activate surfquake  # Replace with the name of your environment

for exercise in ex1_impulse ex2_trends ex3_aliasing ex4_noise ex5_delay; do
    echo "Running $exercise"
    surfquake quick -c "./tutorial4/configs/$exercise.yaml" -o "./tutorial4/output/$exercise" -a
done

Open a terminal in your working directory and run it:

chmod u+x run_synthetic.sh
./run_synthetic.sh

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text:
Synthetic signals turn processing into an experiment with a known answer:

  • Filters: an impulse shows what a filter really does, and the price of zero phase (energy before the onset) or causal filtering (delay and distortion).
  • Detrending: each method removes exactly the shape it assumes, and leaves the rest.
  • Resampling: without an anti-alias filter, high frequencies become false low frequencies that look completely real.
  • Noise: filtering in the band of the signal recovers signals that are invisible in the raw trace.
  • Correlation: a known delay is recovered exactly, which validates the timing of your whole processing chain.

Whenever you are not sure about a new method or a combination of parameters, test it first on a synthetic signal: if it does not give the expected answer on a signal you know, it will not give a reliable answer on real data.

docs.title: Trace Header
docs.text:
Every seismic trace carries two things: the samples (tr.data, a NumPy array) and the header (tr.stats), the metadata that gives the samples a meaning: which station and channel recorded them, when the first sample was taken, how many samples per second...

SurfQuake reads your files with ObsPy, so every trace is an ObsPy Trace with a tr.stats header. During processing and interaction, SurfQuake extends this header with the results of your analysis:

  • Picks: phase arrivals picked manually or automatically.
  • References: reference times marked on the plot, used to cut or align traces.
  • Geodetic information: event location, source–receiver distance, azimuths and theoretical arrival times.

The header is the memory of the workflow: what you add in one step can be used by the next one. A pick made on the plot is used by cut (method: phase) or shift (phase); the theoretical arrivals computed by surfquake processing are used by shift (phase_theo); the back-azimuth is used by rotate (GAC); and your own scripts can read and write any field.

docs.title: Why HDF5?
docs.text:
MiniSEED, the standard format of seismic archives, has a fixed header: it stores the station codes, the start time and the sampling rate, but there is no place for picks, references or event information. If a processed trace were written back to MiniSEED, all this information would be lost.

For this reason SurfQuake writes processed traces in HDF5 (.h5) format. HDF5 is a hierarchical format that stores the samples together with the whole tr.stats dictionary, including the SurfQuake fields. When you read the file again (with surfquake or with ObsPy), the trace comes back exactly as you left it: data, picks, references and geodetic information.

surfquake quick -w "./data/*" -c ./config.yaml -o ./processed -a

The output files are named <trace_id>.D.<year>.<julday>.h5, e.g. ES.EALB..HHZ.D.2018.233.h5. They can be read like any other waveform file by every surfquake command, and in Python:

from obspy import read

tr = read("./processed/ES.EALB..HHZ.D.2018.233.h5")[0]
print(tr.stats.picks)       # the picks are still there
print(tr.stats.geodetic)    # and the event information

ℹ️ Reading HDF5 in your own Python code needs the obspyh5 plugin, which is installed with surfquake.

docs.title: Core Header Fields (ObsPy Standard)
docs.text:
These fields are part of the default trace.stats dictionary and are filled when the file is read:

Field Description network Network code (e.g., IU, ES) station Station code (e.g., ANMO) location Location code (e.g., 00, 10, or empty) channel Channel code (e.g., BHZ, HHN) starttime Time of the first sample (UTCDateTime) endtime Time of the last sample (UTCDateTime) sampling_rate Samples per second, in Hz delta Time between samples, in s (1 / sampling_rate) npts Number of samples

The trace id is network.station.location.channel, e.g. ES.EALB..HHZ (the location is empty here). The channel code follows the SEED convention: the first letter is the band (sampling rate and period: H = high broadband, B = broadband, S = short period), the second the instrument (H = high-gain seismometer, N = accelerometer), and the third the component (Z, N, E, or 1, 2 for sensors not oriented to North and East).

docs.title: Header Info from Command Line
docs.text:
The info command prints the header of your files on screen, including the SurfQuake fields (picks, references and, when available, the event and geodetic information). It is the quickest way to check your data before processing: are all sampling rates the same? Do the start times match? Do the processed files keep their picks?

surfquake info -h
surfquake info -w [path to waveform files, e.g. './data/*Z' or './mseed1,./mseed2'] -c [number of traces (columns) shown side by side, default 1]

The files can be given with a wildcard ('./data/*Z') or as a list separated by commas.

Example:

> surfquake info -w './ES.ELOB..HHZ.D.2018.233,./ES.EMAZ..HHZ.D.2018.233' -c 2

File                 | ES.ELOB..HHZ.D.2018.233   | ES.EMAZ..HHZ.D.2018.233
Network              | ES                        | ES
Station              | ELOB                      | EMAZ
Location             |                           |
Channel              | HHZ                       | HHZ
Start Time           | 2018-08-21T00:12:58.4300  | 2018-08-21T00:12:56.3977
End Time             | 2018-08-21T00:47:06.6900  | 2018-08-21T00:47:03.5077
Sampling Rate (Hz)   | 100.0                     | 100.0
Delta (s)            | 0.01                      | 0.01
Npts                 | 204827                    | 204712
Picks                | None                      | None
References           | None                      | None

When the traces carry event information (files processed with surfquake processing and an event file), info also shows the rows Origin Time, Event Lat, Event Long, Distance (km), Az (°), Baz (°), Incidence (°) and Arrivals.

docs.title: SurfQuake-Extended Header Fields
docs.text: These fields are added during processing or interactive analysis. A trace that has never been picked has no picks field: always access them safely, e.g. getattr(tr.stats, "picks", []).

docs.title: trace.stats.picks (list of dicts)
docs.text:
Phase arrivals picked manually on the plot, or added by your scripts. Each entry contains:

Key Type Description time float Time of the pick, as a UTC timestamp (seconds since 1970-01-01). Convert it with UTCDateTime(p["time"]). phase str Phase name (e.g., P, S, Pg, Lg). amplitude float Amplitude of the trace at the pick time. polarity str First-motion polarity: U (up), D (down) or ? (unknown). 
{
  "time": 1727123830.321,
  "phase": "P",
  "amplitude": 3.21e-05,
  "polarity": "U"
}

The picks are also written to the CSV file set by pick_output_file in the plotting configuration (default ./picks.csv).

docs.title: trace.stats.references (list of floats)
docs.text: Reference times (UTC timestamps) marked on the plot with the key w. A reference is added to all the traces of the plot at the same time, so it is a common time mark: for example the origin time of an event, or the start of a window you want to cut (cut, method: reference, uses the last reference).

docs.title: trace.stats.geodetic (dict)
docs.text:
Event and source–receiver information. It is filled by surfquake processing when you give an event file (-e) and an inventory (-i), for each event and station:

Key Content otime Origin time of the event. event [latitude, longitude, depth] of the event (depth in km). geodetic [distance_km, azimuth, back_azimuth, incidence]: source–receiver distance (km); azimuth from the source to the station (°); back-azimuth from the station to the source (°); incidence angle of the first arrival (°). arrivals List of theoretical arrivals (TauP), one dict per phase: phase, time (UTC timestamp), ray_param (s/°) and incident_angle (°). 
trace.stats.geodetic = {
    "otime": UTCDateTime("2018-08-21T00:27:00.5"),
    "event": [42.51, 1.43, 10.0],
    "geodetic": [254.7, 303.4, 123.4, 31.5],
    "arrivals": [
        {"phase": "P", "time": 1534811249.2, "ray_param": 13.1, "incident_angle": 31.5},
        {"phase": "S", "time": 1534811264.0, "ray_param": 23.6, "incident_angle": 31.9},
    ],
}

With quick and processing_daily there is no event, so the geodetic values are set to -1 and the event to None.

SurfQuake also copies the back-azimuth and the incidence angle to the ObsPy fields trace.stats.back_azimuth and trace.stats.inclination, which are the ones used by rotate with method: 'GAC'.

docs.title: Who writes and who reads the header
docs.text:
Action Writes Read by Double left-click on a trace, keys 1–6, key e picks cut / cut_stream (phase), shift (phase), scripts Key w references (all traces) cut / cut_stream (reference), scripts surfquake processing -e events.txt -i inventory.xml geodetic, back_azimuth, inclination shift (phase_theo), rotate (GAC), info, scripts Your post-scripts anything you want the following steps, the plot, the HDF5 output

Interactive keys that edit the header (see Plotting):

Key Action Double left-click Add a pick (you are asked for the phase and polarity) 1 / 2 / 3 Quick P pick with polarity ? / U / D 4 / 5 / 6 Quick S pick with polarity ? / U / D e Manual pick (interactive input) d / Del Delete the pick under the cursor c Clear all picks w Add a reference time (all traces) p Remove the last reference time

docs.title: Trace header modification
docs.text:
To change the codes of your traces (network, station, location, channel), use the rename method with quick or processing_daily. It maps the original codes to the new ones, for example to harmonise data from different providers or to change 1/2 components into N/E:

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rename'
    networks:
      'IM': 'IH'
    stations:
      'IL02': 'XX02'
    channels:
      'SHZ': 'BHZ'      # whole channel replacement
    components:
      '1': 'N'          # only the last letter of the channel
      '2': 'E'

⚠️ Always quote the codes: unquoted 00 becomes 0, and NO (Norway) becomes False. See Processing Traces for all the options.

docs.title: Working with the header in Python
docs.text:
In your scripts, or in any Python session, the header is a dictionary-like object:

from obspy import UTCDateTime

for tr in stream:
    # read: always with a default, the field may not exist
    picks = getattr(tr.stats, "picks", [])
    p_picks = [p for p in picks if p["phase"] == "P"]

    # write a pick
    if "picks" not in tr.stats:
        tr.stats.picks = []
    tr.stats.picks.append({"time": UTCDateTime("2018-08-21T00:27:15").timestamp,
                           "phase": "P", "amplitude": 0.0, "polarity": "?"})

    # theoretical P arrival (only after surfquake processing with an event file)
    arrivals = tr.stats.get("geodetic", {}).get("arrivals", [])
    p_theo = next((UTCDateTime(a["time"]) for a in arrivals if a["phase"] == "P"), None)

    # your own fields
    tr.stats.quality = "good"

Best practices

  • Store times as UTC timestamps (floats), like SurfQuake does: they are simple, sortable and safe to write in HDF5.
  • Read optional fields with a default (getattr, .get), because traces without picks or events do not have them.
  • Keep the tr.stats when you create new traces in a script (tr.copy()), otherwise the picks and geodetic information are lost.
  • Write your results in HDF5 (-o with -a) to keep the header between runs.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The extended header turns each trace into a self-descriptive object: the waveform travels together with its acquisition information, its picks, its event and the results of your own analysis, from one processing step to the next and from one run to the next.

docs.title: Utilities
docs.text: In this section we show some useful utilities to make easier how to create a metadata file and manage a catalog.

docs.title: Create Metadata from CLI
docs.text:
The csv2xml tool allows users to generate StationXML metadata required by SurfQuake modules.

It supports two common scenarios:

  1. Only station coordinate file available → A valid StationXML is generated with default channel information.
  2. Station file + RESP/Inventory files available → Full response information is incorporated automatically.

docs.title: Minimum Required Station File
docs.text:
The station table must contain at least the following columns:

Net Station Lat Lon elevation start_date starttime end_date endtime

Example (space-separated or CSV format supported):

WM ARNO 37.0988 -6.7322 117.0 2007-01-01 00:00:00 2050-12-31 23:59:59
WM AVE 33.2981 -7.4133 230.0 2007-01-01 00:00:00 2050-12-31 23:59:59
WM CART 37.5868 -1.0012 65.0 2007-01-01 00:00:00 2050-12-31 23:59:59
  • Columns are case-insensitive.
  • The tool automatically detects whitespace or comma-separated files.
  • Date format must follow:

<!-- -->
YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS

Start/end times can be wide ranges (e.g., 2007 → 2050).

If no channel information is provided, a default channel is created: - Channel code: HHZ - Sample rate: 100.0 Hz

docs.title: Optional Columns (Advanced Metadata)
docs.text: The tool automatically uses additional columns if present.

docs.title: Station-Level Optional Columns
docs.text:
Column Name Description

site_name Human-readable station name

clock_drift Clock drift rate (seconds/second). Applied to all channels unless overridden

docs.title: Channel-Level Optional Columns
docs.text:
Column Name Description

channel Channel code (e.g., HHZ, HHN, HHE)

location_code SEED location code

sample_rate Sampling rate (Hz)

dip Channel dip (degrees)

azimuth Channel azimuth (degrees)

depth Sensor depth (meters)

clock_drift Channel-specific drift (overrides station-level drift)

If multiple rows exist for the same station with different channels, all channels will be included in the StationXML.

docs.title: Using RESP / Inventory Files
docs.text:
If a RESP (or StationXML inventory) directory is provided:

  • The tool scans recursively.
  • All channels found in RESP files are indexed by: (Network, Station, Location, Channel)
  • If the CSV does not specify channels, RESP channels are used automatically.
  • If the CSV specifies channels, matching RESP responses are attached when available.

RESP files must correspond to the correct Network and Station codes.

docs.title: Command Line Usage
docs.text: surfquake csv2xml     -c [csv_file_path]     -r [resp_files_path]     -o [output_path]     -n [stations_xml_name]

docs.title: Required Arguments
docs.text:
• -c, --csv_file_path → Path to station table
  • -o, --output_path → Directory for output StationXML
  • -n, --stations_xml_name → Output filename

docs.title: Optional Argument
docs.text: • -r, --resp_files_path → Directory containing RESP/Inventory files

docs.title: Interactive Help
docs.text: surfquake csv2xml -h

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The updated csv2xml tool now:

  • Accepts whitespace or comma-separated files
  • Validates numeric and date fields
  • Supports multi-channel stations
  • Integrates RESP metadata robustly
  • Supports OBS clock drift metadata
  • Applies intelligent defaults when optional columns are missing

This makes metadata creation flexible, robust, and suitable for both simple deployments and advanced OBS workflows.

docs.title: Run Create Metadatafrom CLI
docs.text: >> surfquake csv2xml -c ./stations_file.txt -r ./resp_files_folder -o ./output_path -n metadata.xml
