docs.title: Array Processing: Beamforming Tutorial 3
docs.text:
In this tutorial, we will learn how to work with the commands: explore, info, quick and beamplot to estimate the back-azimuth and the apparent slowness of a teleseismic P wave recorded by a seismic array.

The event is the North Korea nuclear test of 3 September 2017 (origin time 03:30:01 UTC), recorded at the ILAR array (network IM, Eielson, Alaska). ILAR is a small-aperture array (about 10 km across) of vertical short-period sensors, so it is a nice example to see how a plane wave crosses an array.

In this tutorial we will follow this structure:

  • Seismic files: tutorial3/data
  • Metadata: tutorial3/metadata
  • Config Files: tutorial3/configs
  • Folder for the tutorial output: tutorial3/beam, this will be created by surfquake.
--tutorial3
    --data
        --IM.IL02..SHZ
        --IM.IL03..SHZ
        --IM.IL04..SHZ
        ......
        --IM.IL19..SHZ
    --metadata
        --dataless.dlsv
    --configs
        --stream_config.yaml
        --plotting_config.yaml
        --beam_config.yaml

For this tutorial you need to download the seismic data here and the metadata here. In this tutorial the metadata is not optional: beamforming needs the coordinates of every station of the array.

Note

The metadata folder is called dataless_LASA, but the file dataless.dlsv contains the stations of the ILAR array (IM.IL01 to IM.IL31). It is the right file for this data.

Please, first open a terminal, activate your environment and type the following command to overview all surfquake capabilities:

surfquake -h

docs.title: A bit of theory
docs.text:
When a seismic wave arrives from far away, its wavefront is almost a plane when it crosses the array. Each station records the same signal, but shifted in time. These delays depend on two parameters:

  • Back-azimuth (BAz): direction from the array to the source, in degrees clockwise from North.
  • Apparent slowness (s): inverse of the apparent velocity of the wavefront along the surface, in s/km. Steep incident waves (teleseismic P) have small slowness, while waves travelling along the surface (Lg, Rg) have large slowness.

Beamforming tests a grid of slowness vectors, shifts and stacks the traces for each one, and looks for the one that gives the maximum coherent energy. The result for each time window is a pair (BAz, s) plus the relative power of the beam.

For this event we can compute what we expect to find (IASP91 model, epicentre 41.34°N 129.04°E):

Parameter Expected value Epicentral distance ~51° P arrival at ILAR ~03:39:05 UTC Back-azimuth ~286° P apparent slowness ~0.068 s/km (~14.7 km/s)

Keep this table at hand, we will compare our results with it.

Please review the following documentation:

Beamforming

Scientific Reference:

Rost, S., & Thomas, C. (2002). Array seismology: Methods and applications. Reviews of Geophysics, 40(3).

docs.title: Generate Config Files
docs.text:
The beamforming is a stream method, it uses all traces together. Its template is inside the stream configuration file. Let's prepare the necessary files.

surfquake make_config -h
surfquake make_config -c stream_config -o "./tutorial3/configs"
surfquake make_config -c plotting_config -o "./tutorial3/configs"

The plotting configuration is commented to explain the functionality. The parametrization for signal processing can be found here for traces and here for streams.

docs.title: Explore your data
docs.text:
First, let's check that all stations have data for the same time span.

surfquake explore -h
surfquake explore -w './tutorial3/data/*'

You should see 18 stations (IL02 to IL19) recording continuously for two hours, starting at the origin time of the test.

docs.title: Look at the files header
docs.text:
surfquake info -h
surfquake info -w './tutorial3/data/*' -c 3

File                 | IM.IL02..SHZ              | IM.IL03..SHZ              | IM.IL04..SHZ
Network              | IM                        | IM                        | IM
Station              | IL02                      | IL03                      | IL04
Location             |                           |                           |
Channel              | SHZ                       | SHZ                       | SHZ
Start Time           | 2017-09-03T03:30:01.0000  | 2017-09-03T03:30:01.0000  | 2017-09-03T03:30:01.0000
End Time             | 2017-09-03T05:30:01.0000  | 2017-09-03T05:30:01.0000  | 2017-09-03T05:30:01.0000
Sampling Rate (Hz)   | 20.0                      | 20.0                      | 20.0
Delta (s)            | 0.05                      | 0.05                      | 0.05
Npts                 | 144001                    | 144001                    | 144001

All traces have the same sampling rate (20 Hz) and the same start time. This is important: beamforming compares the traces sample by sample.

docs.title: Find the P wave
docs.text:
Let's plot the array and look for the P arrival. We pass the metadata with -i, it will be needed later by the beamforming.

surfquake quick -h
surfquake quick -w "./tutorial3/data/*" -i "./tutorial3/metadata/dataless.dlsv" --plot_config "./tutorial3/configs/plotting_config.yaml"
  • Open an interactive prompt pressing v.
  • Filter the traces in the band where the P wave is clear:
help filter
filter bandpass 0.8 2.2 --corners 4 --zerophase True

After filtering, the figure is redrawn and you are back in picking mode.

  • Zoom around 03:39 UTC, about 9 minutes after the origin time. You will see the P wave arriving at all stations almost at the same time.
  • Set the analysis time window: place the mouse a bit before the P wave (around 03:38:50) and press u (start time), then place it after the main P energy (around 03:39:40) and press i (end time).

Tip

The P wave of a teleseism crosses the 10 km of ILAR in less than one second, so you will not see the delays by eye. This is exactly why we need the beamforming.

docs.title: Interactive Beamforming
docs.text: With the time window set, open the prompt again pressing v.

docs.title: Beam: time evolution of slowness and back-azimuth
docs.text:
The command beam slides a short window (--win, in seconds) along the selected time window and computes the FK beamforming in each one.

help beam
beam --fmin 0.8 --fmax 2.2 --smax 0.3 --grid 0.01 --win 3 --overlap 0.05
  • --fmin, --fmax: frequency band of the analysis (Hz).
  • --smax: maximum slowness of the grid (s/km). 0.3 s/km covers all P and S phases.
  • --grid: slowness grid spacing (s/km). With 0.01 we can separate 0.06 from 0.07 s/km, the default 0.05 is too coarse for a teleseismic P.
  • --win: length of each sliding window (s). It should contain a few cycles of the lowest frequency.
  • --overlap: step between consecutive windows, as a fraction of --win. With 0.05 the window moves 5 % of its length each time (0.15 s), i.e. consecutive windows overlap by 95 %.

The figure shows, from top to bottom, the relative power, the slowness and the back-azimuth of each window, colored by relative power.

Look at the windows with the highest relative power at the P arrival. The back-azimuth should be close to 286° and the slowness close to 0.068 s/km.

docs.title: Slowness map of a single window
docs.text:
The beam figure is interactive. Point with the mouse at a power peak, press a number to select the method and then press e to plot the slowness map of that window:

KEY             | ACTION
---             | ------
1               | Conventional FK
2               | Capon
3               | Multitaper Coherence
4               | Music for 1 signal
5               | Music for 2 signals
6               | Music for 3 signals

The maximum of the map gives the slowness vector of the wave: its distance to the centre is the slowness, and its direction is the back-azimuth.

Alternatively, you can compute the slowness map of the whole selected time window directly from the prompt with smap. Write the method in capital letters (FK, CAPON, MTP.COHERENCE, MUSIC):

help smap
smap --method FK --fmin 0.8 --fmax 2.2 --smax 0.3 --grid 0.01
smap --method CAPON --fmin 0.8 --fmax 2.2 --smax 0.3 --grid 0.01

Compare both maps. Capon gives a sharper maximum than the conventional FK, because it suppresses the energy coming from other directions.

Note

For smap, select a short time window around the P onset (a few seconds) with u and i. A long window mixes the P wave with the coda and the noise, and the maximum becomes wider.

To close the interactive session:

exit

docs.title: Automatic
docs.text:
In this section we compute the same beamforming, but using a config file. The advantage is that we can automate the process for many events and save the results for later use.

Make a copy of stream_config.yaml and name it beam_config.yaml. Keep the pre-processing, cut the traces around the P wave and enable the beam step:

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'cut_stream'
    method: 'absolute'
    start: 2017-09-03T03:38:30
    end: 2017-09-03T03:41:30
  process_4:
    name: 'beam'
    method: 'FK'
    timewindow: 3.0
    overlap: 0.05
    fmin: 0.8
    fmax: 2.2
    smax: 0.3
    slow_grid: 0.01
    output_folder: './tutorial3/beam'
  • cut_stream keeps three minutes around the P wave. Without it, the beamforming would run along the two hours of data.
  • method can be FK or CAPON.
  • The beamforming filters the traces in the band fmin–fmax, so we do not need a filter step.

Run the quick command in automatic mode. Remember to pass the metadata:

surfquake quick -w "./tutorial3/data/*" -i "./tutorial3/metadata/dataless.dlsv" -c "./tutorial3/configs/beam_config.yaml" -a

The result is saved in ./tutorial3/beam as a binary file named after the year and the julian day of the first trace, 2017.246.beam.

docs.title: Plot the results and find the P wave automatically
docs.text:
Open the result with the command beamplot:

surfquake beamplot -h
surfquake beamplot -f "./tutorial3/beam/2017.246.beam"

You will get the same figure as in the interactive section, and you can also open the slowness maps with the keys 1–6 and e.

Now let's ask surfquake to find the power peaks that match a P wave. The option --find_solutions accepts the shortcuts regional and teleseismic, or your own slowness ranges in JSON format. The teleseismic shortcut uses 0.04–0.07 s/km for P, and our expected value (0.068 s/km) is very close to the limit, so we define our own range:

surfquake beamplot -f "./tutorial3/beam/2017.246.beam" --find_solutions '{"P": [0.05, 0.08]}' --baz_range 260 310 --min_power 0.6 --write_path "./tutorial3/beam/solutions.txt"
  • --baz_range: only accept back-azimuths between 260° and 310°.
  • --min_power: minimum relative power to accept a peak.
  • --write_path: the solutions are appended to this text file.

The terminal shows the detected peaks:

[INFO] Found N beam peaks:
  2017-09-03T03:39:... | Phase: P        | BAz: ...° | S: ... s/km | Pow: ...

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text:
Compare your solution with the expected values of the table at the beginning of the tutorial.

  • Back-azimuth: the measured value is usually a few degrees off the theoretical one. The difference comes from the structure under the array and along the path, which the 1D model does not include.
  • Slowness: the measured slowness depends on the slowness grid. With slow_grid: 0.05 you would only obtain 0.05 or 0.10 s/km, so always use a grid fine enough for the phase you are looking for.
  • Phase identification: a slowness of ~0.068 s/km together with a back-azimuth pointing to the Korean peninsula confirms that this is the P wave from the test, and not a local or regional event.

As an exercise, try:

  • Change the band to fmin: 2.0 and fmax: 4.0. What happens with the relative power? Why?
  • Change method to CAPON and compare the solutions.
  • Move the cut_stream window to the PcP and PP arrivals (about 1.5 and 2 minutes after P). Can you find them? Which slowness do they have?

docs.title: Using Bash script
docs.text:
Finally, we can concatenate the automatic steps in a bash script file. Create a file named run_beam.sh:

#!/bin/bash

# Activate your conda environment
eval "$(conda shell.bash hook)"
conda activate surfquake  # Replace with the name of your environment

surfquake quick -w "./tutorial3/data/*" -i "./tutorial3/metadata/dataless.dlsv" -c "./tutorial3/configs/beam_config.yaml" -a
surfquake beamplot -f "./tutorial3/beam/2017.246.beam" --find_solutions '{"P": [0.05, 0.08]}' --baz_range 260 310 --write_path "./tutorial3/beam/solutions.txt" --save_path "./tutorial3/beam/beam.png"

Open a terminal in your working directory and run it:

chmod u+x run_beam.sh
./run_beam.sh

docs.title: Event Analysis: Automatic Phase Picking Tutorial 5
docs.text:
In the previous tutorials, we always knew when the earthquakes happened: the event file told surfquake where to cut. In real life, the first problem is the opposite: we have hours or days of continuous data, and we need to find the arrival times of the P and S waves of every earthquake inside it. Doing it by hand is impossible when a seismic sequence produces hundreds of events. In this tutorial, we will learn how to work with the commands project, pick and quick to:

  1. Organise continuous data in a project.
  2. Run the deep-learning picker PhaseNet on all the stations.
  3. Understand the three output files of the picker.
  4. Read the picks of one earthquake and check that they make sense.
  5. Draw the picks on top of the waveforms.
  6. Choose the probability thresholds and select stations, channels and dates.
  7. Run the picker from Python and from a bash script.

The data is from the Granada seismic sequence (southern Spain) of January 2021. We will use 1.5 hours of continuous data, from 21:00 to 22:30 UTC on 26 January 2021, recorded by 19 stations of the Spanish network (ES). During that time, three earthquakes of magnitude around 4 (ML 4.1, 4.1 and 4.3) happened very close to each other, near 37.19° N, 3.69° W and about 5 km deep, at 21:36:32, 21:44:18 and 21:54:55 UTC, together with many smaller aftershocks.

In this tutorial we will follow this structure:

  • Seismic files: tutorial5/data
  • Metadata: tutorial5/metadata
  • Config Files: tutorial5/configs
  • Project: tutorial5/project
  • Folder for the picks: tutorial5/picks, this will be created by surfquake.
--tutorial5
    --data
        --ES.E0802..HHE.D.2021.26
        --ES.E0802..HHN.D.2021.26
        --ES.E0802..HHZ.D.2021.26
        ......
        --ES.UMV15..EHZ.D.2021.26
    --metadata
        --ES_network.xml
    --configs
        --typical_config.yaml
        --plotting_config.yaml
    --project

For this tutorial you need to download the seismic data here (52 files, about 30 MB). The metadata is not needed to pick, because PhaseNet only looks at the waveforms, but download it too: you will need it in the next steps of the workflow (association and location).

The config files are the same as in Tutorial 1. All the commands of this tutorial are run from the folder that contains tutorial5.

Note

PhaseNet is a neural network: running it takes some time and memory. With this small dataset it takes from a few seconds to a few minutes, depending on your computer. If you have a GPU configured for TensorFlow, surfquake uses it automatically.

docs.title: Step 1: What does PhaseNet do?
docs.text:
PhaseNet (Zhu and Beroza, 2019) is a neural network trained with hundreds of thousands of P and S arrivals picked by analysts. It reads a seismogram and returns, for every sample, three probabilities that add up to 1:

  • the probability that a P wave arrives at that sample,
  • the probability that an S wave arrives at that sample,
  • the probability that it is noise.

When an earthquake arrives, the P probability rises to a sharp peak at the onset of the P wave, and the S probability rises at the onset of the S wave. A pick is a peak of the probability curve that is higher than a threshold (0.3 by default). Its time is the arrival time, and its height, the probability (between 0 and 1), tells how confident the network is.

Before the network, surfquake prepares every file:

  1. Removes slow trends (a spline detrend) and merges gaps, filling them with zeros.
  2. Resamples the data to 100 Hz if needed, and applies a high-pass filter at 0.5 Hz to remove long-period noise.
  3. Keeps the UTC day that contains most of the samples of the file.

Three things are important to know about how surfquake runs PhaseNet:

  • Each file is picked alone. The network is given one component at a time, so the same P wave is usually picked on Z, N and E: you will see up to three picks of the same arrival. This is normal, and the associator handles it later.
  • PhaseNet was trained with data at 100 Hz. The Granada data is already 100 Hz; data with another sampling rate is resampled automatically before picking.
  • All the files should cover the same time span. The network uses the length of the first file for all of them, so a longer file is cut. Daily files (or, like here, files cut to the same window) are the ideal input.

docs.title: Step 2: Create a project
docs.text:
As in Tutorial 1 (Part 2), the first step is to index the files in a project.

Please review the following documentation:

Project

surfquake project -d ./tutorial5/data -s ./tutorial5/project -n granada
  • -d: folder with the waveform files.
  • -s: folder where the project is saved.
  • -n: name of the project (the file name).

The terminal shows a summary of the project: 1 network, 19 stations and 52 files, from 21:00 to 22:30 on 26 January 2021. Not every station has three components: EMIN and EMLI have only two, and ENIJ only the vertical one. The picker works with whatever is available.

The project is saved as ./tutorial5/project/granada.

docs.title: Step 3: Run the picker
docs.text:
Please review the following documentation:

Phase Picker

surfquake pick -h
surfquake pick -f ./tutorial5/project/granada -o ./tutorial5/picks -pt 0.3 -st 0.3 --verbose
  • -f: the project file.
  • -o: folder where the picks are written. It is created if it does not exist.
  • -pt, -st: minimum probability of a P pick and of an S pick (0.3 is the default).
  • --verbose: prints the number of P and S picks of every file.

While it runs, surfquake shows the device it uses and the progress:

[PhaseNet] 52 files | device: CPU | batch size: 3 | min prob P/S: 0.3/0.3
    ES.E0802..HHE.D.2021.26: ... P, ... S picks
    ......
[PhaseNet] 3/52 files (6%) | elapsed 0:00:04 | remaining ~0:01:05

At the end, it prints a summary similar to this one (the time depends on your computer):

============================================================
 PhaseNet summary
============================================================
 Files processed     : 52
 Stations with picks : 19
 P picks             : 1140
 S picks             : 1123
 Total time          : 0:01:10
 Results saved in    : .../tutorial5/picks
   original_picks.csv, nll_picks.txt and one folder per day (REAL format)
============================================================

More than 2000 picks in only 1.5 hours! Do not worry: three large earthquakes and their aftershocks produce many real arrivals, each arrival is often picked on three components, and some picks are noise. The next steps show how to read them.

Tip

To force the CPU (for example if your GPU does not have enough memory), add --device cpu. With --device gpu, surfquake stops with an error if no GPU is found.

docs.title: Step 4: The output files
docs.text:
The picker writes the same picks in three formats, each one for a different use:

--tutorial5
    --picks
        --original_picks.csv
        --nll_picks.txt
        --20210126
            --ES.E0802.P.txt
            --ES.E0802.S.txt
            --ES.EADA.P.txt
            ......

docs.title: original_picks.csv: the complete table
docs.text:
One line per pick, with all the information. This is the file to open with a spreadsheet or with pandas:

date,fname,year,month,day,net,station,flag,tt,date_time,weight,amplitude,phase,channel
20210126,ES.E0802.P,2021,1,26,ES,E0802,1,77809.42,2021-01-26T21:36:49.420000,0.7245163321495056,498471187.5,P,HHE

The important columns are:

  • date_time: the arrival time (UTC).
  • phase: P or S.
  • weight: the probability of the pick, given by PhaseNet.
  • net, station, channel: where it was picked.
  • tt: the arrival time in seconds from 00:00 of that day (77809.42 s = 21:36:49.42).
  • amplitude: the maximum amplitude of the waveform just after the pick (10 s after a P, 5 s after an S). It is measured in counts and multiplied by a fixed factor, so it is not a physical amplitude: use it only to compare picks of the same channel.

docs.title: 20210126/: input for the associator
docs.text:
One folder per day, and one file per station and phase (ES.EADA.P.txt), with three columns: tt, probability and amplitude. This is the input format of the associator REAL, used by surfquake associate. Here are the first P picks of EADA. The first three are the same P wave of the first earthquake, picked on HHE, HHN and HHZ:

77815.05 0.753131 5.795099e+08
77815.05 0.760775 5.920444e+08
77815.07 0.766324 8.130278e+08
78030.83 0.535015 1.220437e+07

docs.title: nll_picks.txt: the NonLinLoc format
docs.text:
All the picks in the phase format of the location program NonLinLoc, one per line:

Station_name    Instrument  Component   P_phase_onset   P_phase_descriptor  First_Motion    Date    Hour_min    Seconds Err ErrMag  Coda_duration   Amplitude   Period
E0802  ?    HHE  ? P      ? 20210126 2136 49.4200 GAU 1.50e-01 -1.00e+00 4.98e+08 -1.00e+00

The column ErrMag is the uncertainty of the pick in seconds, translated from the probability: the more confident the pick, the smaller the error (0.02 s above 0.95, up to 0.5 s below 0.6). This file can also be loaded in the interactive plot (Step 6) and is the input of surfquake polarity.

docs.title: Step 5: The picks of one earthquake
docs.text:
Let's look at the first earthquake, at 21:36:32.6 UTC. Open original_picks.csv and keep the picks between 21:36:32 and 21:37:20. For every station, this table shows the P and the S pick with the highest probability, ordered by time:

Station P pick (21:3x:xx) Prob. P S pick Prob. S S − P (s) UMV15 36:33.98 (EHZ) 0.97 36:35.89 (EHE) 0.83 1.9 EQTA 36:36.33 (HHZ) 0.96 36:40.00 (HHE) 0.78 3.7 EGOR 36:38.37 (HHZ) 0.92 36:44.18 (HHZ) 0.43 5.8 ELGU 36:38.61 (HHZ) 0.82 36:44.25 (HHE) 0.52 5.6 EBER 36:46.14 (HHZ) 0.88 – – – E0802 36:49.29 (HHZ) 0.93 37:01.90 (HHE) 0.65 12.6 EADA 36:55.07 (HHZ) 0.77 37:12.09 (HHN) 0.48 17.0 ENIJ 36:55.08 (HHZ) 0.83 37:19.06 (HHZ) 0.44 24.0 ⚠ EALB 36:56.75 (HHZ) 0.83 37:15.70 (HHN) 0.31 19.0 ECAB 37:00.66 (HHZ) 0.65 – – – TLOR 37:04.22 (HHZ) 0.67 – – – ESPR 37:04.71 (HHZ) 0.63 – – – EZAR 37:05.31 (HHZ) 0.68 – – – EMUR 37:09.70 (HHE) 0.81 – – – ETOB 37:11.25 (HHZ) 0.90 37:17.21 (HHE) 0.42 6.0 ⚠ EMIN 37:11.82 (HHZ) 0.93 – – –

What can we learn from this table?

  • The P picks are very good. Almost all the stations have a P pick, most of them with probability above 0.8, and the same arrival is picked on the three components within a few hundredths of a second.
  • The arrivals follow the distance. The closest station, UMV15, records the P wave 1.4 s after the origin time, and the furthest ones about 40 s later.
  • S − P grows with distance. A simple rule for local earthquakes is that the distance (in km) is about 8 times S − P (in s): UMV15 is about 15 km from the earthquake, EQTA about 30 km and E0802 about 100 km.
  • The S picks are fewer and less confident. The S wave arrives in the coda of the P wave, so it is harder to recognise: many stations have no S pick, and their probabilities are usually lower. The S is picked mostly on the horizontal components, where it is larger.
  • Not every pick is right. Two S picks are suspicious (⚠). ENIJ has almost the same P time as EADA, so its S − P should also be about 17 s, not 24 s. ETOB has an S − P of only 6 s while its P arrives 40 s after the origin time: it is probably a pick of another arrival. These are the picks that the associator and the location will reject, because they do not fit with the other stations.

Notice also TLOR, which has several P picks within one second with low probabilities (0.3 to 0.4) on its horizontal components: when the onset is not sharp, PhaseNet can give more than one peak.

docs.title: Step 6: Draw the picks on the waveforms
docs.text:
A table is useful, but it is always worth looking at the picks on the waveforms. Let's open the first earthquake at EQTA, the second closest station, with quick, cutting a window of 70 s with --min_date and --max_date:

surfquake quick -w "./tutorial5/data/ES.EQTA*" -c ./tutorial5/configs/typical_config.yaml --plot_config ./tutorial5/configs/plotting_config.yaml --min_date "2021-01-26 21:36:25" --max_date "2021-01-26 21:37:35"

The pattern ES.EQTA* selects the three components of EQTA. Change it to see other stations, for example "./tutorial5/data/ES.UMV15*", or "./tutorial5/data/*HZ*" for the vertical component of all the stations.

In the interactive prompt, load the picks:

>> load_picks --file ./tutorial5/picks/nll_picks.txt

surfquake draws every pick on the trace of the same station and channel, and stores it in the trace header (picks). The picks of the whole 1.5 hours are read, but only those inside the window are visible.

Look at EQTA: the P pick is exactly at the sharp onset of the P wave on the three components, and the S pick on the horizontal components at the start of the larger S wave, 3.7 s later. You can now move, delete or add picks by hand, as explained in Plotting Interaction, and save them.

Tip

To see the picks of the second and third earthquakes, change the window to 21:44:10–21:45:20 and 21:54:50–21:56:00.

docs.title: Step 7: Choosing the thresholds
docs.text:
The thresholds -pt and -st decide which peaks of the probability curve become picks. It is a compromise:

  • A low threshold finds the arrivals of small earthquakes, but also picks noise.
  • A high threshold keeps only clear arrivals, but misses the small events and many S waves.

With the Granada picks, this is the number of picks that you would keep with each threshold:

Threshold P picks S picks 0.3 1140 1123 0.5 702 544 0.7 388 188 0.9 128 15

The S picks fall much faster than the P picks: above 0.9 almost no S wave survives. In the table of Step 5, a threshold of 0.5 would remove the suspicious S of ENIJ and ETOB, but also the good S picks of EADA and EALB.

The usual strategy is to keep low thresholds (0.3) and let the associator and the location clean the false picks: a false pick that does not match other stations is simply not associated to any event. Raise the threshold only if the noisy picks are so many that the association becomes slow, or if you want only the best picks (for example, for a tomography).

surfquake pick -f ./tutorial5/project/granada -o ./tutorial5/picks_05 -pt 0.5 -st 0.4

docs.title: Picking only some stations, channels or times
docs.text:
You do not need to pick the whole project. The same filters as in other commands are available:

# Only the vertical components (HHZ and EHZ)
surfquake pick -f ./tutorial5/project/granada -o ./tutorial5/picks_Z -ch "?HZ"

# Only three stations
surfquake pick -f ./tutorial5/project/granada -o ./tutorial5/picks_sta -s "UMV15|EQTA|EGOR"

A filter can be a pattern with * and ?, or a list of names separated by |. Always write it between quotes, because *, ? and | have a special meaning in the terminal.

Picking only the vertical components is faster and gives one P pick per arrival, but you lose most of the S picks, which are better seen on the horizontal components.

With a long archive of daily files, --min_date and --max_date select the days to pick. They select files, they do not cut them: in this tutorial all the files cover the same 1.5 hours, so a date filter would keep all of them.

docs.title: Step 8: Picking from Python
docs.text:
The same can be done from a Python script, using the library. Create a file named run_picking.py:

from multiprocessing import freeze_support
from surfquakecore.phasenet.phasenet_handler import PhasenetISP, PhasenetUtils
from surfquakecore.project.surf_project import SurfProject

project_file = "./tutorial5/project/granada"
output_picks = "./tutorial5/picks"

if __name__ == '__main__':
    freeze_support()

    # Load the project and keep only the vertical components
    sp = SurfProject.load_project(path_to_project_file=project_file)
    sp.filter_project_keys(channel="?HZ")

    # Run PhaseNet
    picker = PhasenetISP(sp.project, amplitude=True, min_p_prob=0.3, min_s_prob=0.3, output=output_picks)
    picks = picker.phasenet()

    # Convert the predictions to a table and write the three formats
    picks_results = PhasenetUtils.split_picks(picks)
    PhasenetUtils.convert2real(picks_results, output_picks)
    PhasenetUtils.save_original_picks(picks_results, output_picks)
    PhasenetUtils.write_nlloc_format(picks_results, output_picks)

    # The table is a pandas DataFrame: you can work with it directly
    best = picks_results[picks_results["weight"] > 0.8]
    print(best[["station", "channel", "phase", "date_time", "weight"]])

python run_picking.py

The lines if __name__ == '__main__': and freeze_support() are needed because the reading of the files runs in parallel; without them, the script may fail on Windows and macOS.

docs.title: Step 9: The bash script
docs.text:
Finally, the whole workflow in a bash script file. Create a file named run_picking.sh:

#!/bin/bash
# Activate your conda environment
eval "$(conda shell.bash hook)"
conda activate surfquake  # Replace with the name of your environment

BASE=./tutorial5

surfquake project -d $BASE/data -s $BASE/project -n granada
surfquake pick -f $BASE/project/granada -o $BASE/picks -pt 0.3 -st 0.3 --verbose

chmod u+x run_picking.sh
./run_picking.sh

docs.title: What comes next?
docs.text:
The picks are only the first step of the automatic workflow. With the same Granada data, the next steps are:

  1. Association (surfquake associate): groups the picks of different stations that belong to the same earthquake, using the daily folders and the metadata. Here, it finds the earthquakes of the sequence and discards the isolated false picks. See Clustering Associate.
  2. Location (surfquake locate): computes the hypocentre of every event with NonLinLoc. See Event Location.
  3. Source parameters and moment tensor (surfquake source, surfquake mti): magnitudes and focal mechanisms.

The results of the complete workflow with this data can be found in the Granada example.

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text:
• PhaseNet turns every seismogram into probability curves for P, S and noise; a pick is a peak above the threshold, and its height is the probability.
  • Each file is picked alone, so the same arrival can be picked on the three components.
  • PhaseNet works at 100 Hz (other rates are resampled automatically), and all the files should cover the same time span.
  • The picks are written in three formats: original_picks.csv (complete table), daily folders (input of the associator REAL) and nll_picks.txt (NonLinLoc, interactive plot and polarities).
  • P picks are usually precise and confident; S picks are fewer, less confident and found mostly on the horizontal components.
  • Some picks are wrong: keep low thresholds and let the associator and the location reject the picks that do not fit.
  • Always check a few events on the waveforms with load_picks.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Zhu, Weiqiang, and Gregory C. Beroza. "PhaseNet: a deep-neural-network-based seismic arrival-time picking method." Geophysical Journal International 216.1 (2019): 261-273.

docs.title: Basic Signal Processing Tutorial 1
docs.text:
In this tutorial, we will learn how to work with the commands: make_config, explore, info and quick to process your seismic waveforms.

In this tutorial we will follow this structure:

  • Seismic files: tutorial1/data
  • Metadata: tutorial1/metadata
  • Config Files: tutorial1/configs
  • Folder for the tutorial output: tutorial1/output, this will be created by surfquake.
--tutorial1
    --data
        --CA.ARBS..HH1.D.2022.32
        --CA.ARBS..HH2.D.2022.32
        --CA.ARBS..HHZ.D.2022.32
        ......
    --metadata
        --inv_all.xml
    --configs
        --typical_config.yaml
        --plotting_config.yaml

For this tutorial you need to download the seismic data here. Optionally, download the corresponding metadata.

All the commands of this tutorial are run from the folder that contains tutorial1.

Please, first open a terminal, activate your environment and type the following command to overview all surfquake capabilities:

surfquake -h

docs.title: Generate Config Files
docs.text:
When working with seismic waveforms, it is useful to describe the signal processing workflow and the plotting options in configuration files. Let's prepare the necessary files.

surfquake make_config -h
surfquake make_config -c typical_config -o "./tutorial1/configs"
surfquake make_config -c plotting_config -o "./tutorial1/configs"

The plotting configuration is commented to explain the functionality. The parametrization for signal processing can be found here for traces and here for streams.

docs.title: Explore your data
docs.text:
Sometimes we have really big datasets. Before processing, it is good to have a first view of the data coverage, including gaps.

surfquake explore -h
surfquake explore -w './tutorial1/data/*'

In this example we use the wildcard *, which means all files. No worries, only seismic files will be read.

Other useful wildcards are *Z* (all vertical components) or *VALC* (only station VALC). Keep in mind that wildcards work on the file names, not on the file headers.

docs.title: Look at the files header
docs.text:
Now let's look at the header of your files. It tells you a lot about what is inside them, such as the sampling rate, the number of points or the start time.

Please review the following documentation:

Trace Header

surfquake info -h
surfquake info -w './tutorial1/data/*' -c 3

[INFO] 30 files retained after filtering.
File                 | CA.ARBS..HH1.D.2022.32    | CA.ARBS..HH2.D.2022.32    | CA.ARBS..HHZ.D.2022.32
Network              | CA                        | CA                        | CA
Station              | ARBS                      | ARBS                      | ARBS
Location             |                           |                           |
Channel              | HH1                       | HH2                       | HHZ
Start Time           | 2022-02-01T01:15:00.6200  | 2022-02-01T01:15:00.6200  | 2022-02-01T01:15:00.6200
End Time             | 2022-02-01T02:35:00.2100  | 2022-02-01T02:35:00.2100  | 2022-02-01T02:35:00.2100
Sampling Rate (Hz)   | 100.0                     | 100.0                     | 100.0
Delta (s)            | 0.01                      | 0.01                      | 0.01
Npts                 | 479960                    | 479960                    | 479960
Picks                | None                      | None                      | None
References           | None                      | None                      | None

The option -c sets how many traces (columns) are shown side by side.

docs.title: Process your waveforms
docs.text:
Finally, it is time to play with processing. The file typical_config.yaml removes the mean, applies a taper and filters the traces between 0.5 and 8.5 Hz with a zero-phase Butterworth bandpass filter:

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 8.5
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True

Please review the following documentation:

Trace processing and plotting

surfquake quick -h
surfquake quick -w "./tutorial1/data/*" -c "./tutorial1/configs/typical_config.yaml" --plot_config "./tutorial1/configs/plotting_config.yaml"

Note

You can also select the specific files that you want to process surfquake quick -w "./file1,./file2,./file3"

Navigate and process your data interactively. The keyboard shortcuts are printed in the terminal:

=======================================================
Plot Interaction Help
=======================================================
KEY             | ACTION
---             | ------
n               | Next page
b               | Previous page
w               | Add reference time
p               | Remove last reference
c               | Clear all picks
e               | Manual pick (interactive input)
1–6             | Quick picks (P/S + polarity)
d / Del         | Delete pick under cursor
v               | Open command prompt
u               | Set start time at cursor
i               | Set end time at cursor
Right-click drag | Select time window
Double left-click | Add pick
ESC / Enter     | Exit current mode
=======================================================

Your picks are saved in the file set by pick_output_file in plotting_config.yaml (default ./picks.csv).

docs.title: Automatic processing
docs.text:
Sometimes we do not want to plot the seismograms, only to process them and write the output files to disk. This is done by adding the option -a (automatic mode) and an output folder with -o:

surfquake quick -w "./tutorial1/data/*" -c "./tutorial1/configs/typical_config.yaml" -o "./tutorial1/output" -a

The processed traces are saved in H5 format. Picks, reference times and geodesic information travel with the traces in the header.

If you also want to save the figures automatically, edit these fields in ./tutorial1/configs/plotting_config.yaml:

plot_output_path: ./tutorial1/figures
show_plot: false

and run the command again, now passing the plotting configuration:

surfquake quick -w "./tutorial1/data/*" -c "./tutorial1/configs/typical_config.yaml" --plot_config "./tutorial1/configs/plotting_config.yaml" -o "./tutorial1/output" -a

With show_plot: false nothing is displayed on screen: all pages are written to plot_output_path and surfquake does not ask any question. This is the mode to automate your plots.

show_plot plot_output_path Result true null displayed, not saved true ./figures displayed and saved false ./figures not displayed, saved (batch) false null nothing shown or saved

Note

In automatic mode (-a) the figures are only saved when show_plot: false and plot_output_path is set.

docs.title: Using Bash script
docs.text:
Now, how can you chain several surfquake commands? The answer is a bash script file. Please, create a file named run_commands.sh and write the following commands in it:

#!/bin/bash

# Activate your conda environment
eval "$(conda shell.bash hook)"
conda activate surfquake  # Replace with the name of your environment

surfquake explore -w './tutorial1/data/*'
surfquake quick -w "./tutorial1/data/*" -c "./tutorial1/configs/typical_config.yaml" -o "./tutorial1/output" -a

Ok, let's run the bash script. Open a terminal in your working directory, where the run_commands.sh file is, and type:

chmod u+x run_commands.sh
./run_commands.sh

Tip

Run the script with ./run_commands.sh or bash run_commands.sh. On many Linux systems sh is not bash, and the activation of the environment fails.

docs.title: Interactive Processing
docs.text:
Open again the plot with the quick command (interactive mode, without -a):

surfquake quick -w "./tutorial1/data/*" -c "./tutorial1/configs/typical_config.yaml" --plot_config "./tutorial1/configs/plotting_config.yaml"
  • Open an interactive prompt pressing v. The directions for interacting with the traces are printed in the terminal.
  • In the new prompt type help to open the interactive signal processing menu. To get details and examples of one command, type for example help filter.

This is an excerpt of the menu (type help to see the full and updated list):

▸ Navigation
  n                      Next trace page
  b                      Previous trace page
  p                      Return to picking mode
  back2future / b2f      Restore original waveforms (undo all processing)
  exit                   Close interactive session

▸ Signal Processing
  algebra                Apply a Math expression on traces
  rmean                  Remove mean on traces
  taper                  Apply taper window on traces
  normalize / norm       Normalize traces
  remove_spikes          Remove spikes from traces
  filter                 Apply signal filtering
  cut                    Trim traces using picks or UTC times
  concat                 Merge trace segments
  rotate                 Rotate seismic components
  shift                  Align traces by phase arrivals
  write                  Export traces to HDF5

▸ Spectral Analysis
  spectrum / sp          Plot amplitude spectrum
  spectrogram / spec     Plot spectrogram
  cwt                    Continuous wavelet transform
  save_tf                Save Time-Frequency Analysis

▸ Array Processing
  beam                   FK beamforming analysis
  smap                   Slowness map estimation
  stack                  Trace stacking
  xcorr                  Cross-correlate traces

Let's try a few commands. First, filter the displayed traces between 1 and 5 Hz:

help filter
filter bandpass 1.0 5.0 --corners 4 --zerophase True

The commands that modify the traces (filter, rmean, taper, back2future...) redraw the figure and take you back to picking mode. Look at the result and press v again to reopen the prompt.

Now restore the original waveforms, undoing all the processing:

back2future

Press v again. To export the traces you have processed interactively:

write --folder_path ./tutorial1/output

To go back to picking mode without modifying the traces type p, and to close the session type exit.

docs.title: Basic Signal Processing Tutorial 2: Events and Record Sections
docs.text:
In the first part we processed whole files with quick. In seismology, however, we usually want to look at earthquakes: a short window of every station around the arrival of the waves of a known event. In this tutorial, we will learn how to work with the commands project and processing to:

  1. Organise the data in a project.
  2. Describe the earthquakes in an event file.
  3. Cut the waveforms of every station around the arrival of the waves, automatically.
  4. Plot record sections: all the stations ordered by distance, with the theoretical arrival times.
  5. Choose the phases and the cutting strategy.
  6. Measure amplitudes of all the events with your own script.

We will use the same data as in Part 1: 10 stations around Andorra, recording between 01:15 and 02:35 UTC on 1 February 2022, during a seismic sequence. We will follow this structure:

  • Seismic files: tutorial1/data
  • Metadata: tutorial1/metadata (required in this tutorial)
  • Config Files: tutorial1/configs
  • Event file: tutorial1/events
  • Project: tutorial1/project
  • Folder for the tutorial output: tutorial1/output, this will be created by surfquake.
--tutorial1
    --data
        --CA.ARBS..HH1.D.2022.32
        --CA.ARBS..HH2.D.2022.32
        --CA.ARBS..HHZ.D.2022.32
        ......
    --metadata
        --inv_all.xml
    --configs
        --typical_config.yaml
        --plotting_config.yaml
        --velocity_config.yaml
    --events
        --events.txt
    --project

If you have not done Part 1, download the seismic data here and the metadata here, and create the config files as explained there. This time the metadata is required: surfquake needs the coordinates of the stations to compute their distance to the earthquakes.

All the commands of this tutorial are run from the folder that contains tutorial1.

docs.title: Step 1: Create a project
docs.text:
A project is a small file that indexes all your waveform files: which networks, stations and channels you have, and which time span every file covers. Once it is created, surfquake knows where to find the data of any station at any time, without scanning the folders again. This is important with large archives, and it lets you select stations and channels by name.

Please review the following documentation:

Project

surfquake project -h
surfquake project -d ./tutorial1/data -s ./tutorial1/project -n andorra
  • -d: folder with the waveform files.
  • -s: folder where the project is saved.
  • -n: name of the project (the file name).

The terminal shows a summary of the project:

Num Networks:  2 Num Stations:  10 Num Channels:  5 Num Total Files:  30
Start Project:  2022-02-01 01:15:00 , End Project:  2022-02-01 02:35:00

Project successfully saved.

The project is saved as ./tutorial1/project/andorra.

docs.title: Step 2: The event file
docs.text:
The event file lists the earthquakes, one per line, with the columns separated by ;:

date;hour;latitude;longitude;depth;magnitude
  • date: YYYY-MM-DD, and hour: HH:MM:SS.s, the origin time in UTC.
  • latitude, longitude in degrees, depth in km.
  • magnitude: optional information, kept with the event.

Create the file ./tutorial1/events/events.txt with three earthquakes of the sequence, located with surfquake (a magnitude 3.5 and two small events):

date;hour;latitude;longitude;depth;magnitude
2022-02-01;02:03:00.3;42.5003;1.4619;5.3;3.49
2022-02-01;02:10:10.1;42.5024;1.4581;4.6;1.11
2022-02-01;02:23:34.4;42.5003;1.4728;6.2;0.48

A template is available with surfquake make_config -c events -o ./tutorial1/events.

docs.title: Step 3: Cut and process the waveforms of each event
docs.text:
Let's run the processing command with the project, the metadata, the event file and the usual processing config:

surfquake processing -h
surfquake processing -p ./tutorial1/project/andorra -i ./tutorial1/metadata/inv_all.xml -e ./tutorial1/events/events.txt -c ./tutorial1/configs/typical_config.yaml -cs 10 -ce 50 --plot_config ./tutorial1/configs/plotting_config.yaml

For each event and each station, surfquake:

  1. Computes the epicentral distance and the back-azimuth from the station coordinates (inventory) and the event location.
  2. Computes the theoretical arrival times of the seismic phases with the IASP91 Earth model (TauP).
  3. Cuts the waveform around the first arrival: -cs 10 seconds before and -ce 50 seconds after it.
  4. Applies the processing of the config file (detrend, taper, filter).
  5. Stores the event, the distance, the back-azimuth and the arrival times in the header of every trace.

The plot opens with the 30 traces (10 stations × 3 components) of the first event, each one starting 10 s before its first arrival:

You can pick, process and analyse the traces as in Part 1. When you close the figure window, the terminal asks:

[Prompt] Finished processing. Type 'c' to continue, 'r' to reprocess this event, or 'e' to exit:

Type c to go to the next event, r to process the same event again (after changing the config file, for example), or e to exit.

Cutting options:

Option Description -cs, -ce Seconds before and after the first arrival. -t The same number of seconds before and after (e.g. -t 30). (none) 300 s before and after.

docs.title: Step 4: Record sections
docs.text:
A record section plots all the stations of an event in a single figure, each one at its distance from the epicentre. It is one of the most useful figures in seismology: the arrivals of every wave line up along a curve (the moveout), the further the station, the later the arrival, and the slope tells the speed of the wave. Phases, noisy stations and timing errors are recognised at a glance.

Open ./tutorial1/configs/plotting_config.yaml and set:

plot_type: record
sort_by: distance
record_option: dates
show_arrivals: true
  • plot_type: record: record section.
  • sort_by: distance: stations ordered by epicentral distance.
  • record_option: dates: absolute UTC time on the x axis.
  • show_arrivals: true: draw the theoretical arrival times.

To make the figure clearer, we use only the vertical components (-ch HHZ) and a shorter window:

surfquake processing -p ./tutorial1/project/andorra -i ./tutorial1/metadata/inv_all.xml -e ./tutorial1/events/events.txt -c ./tutorial1/configs/typical_config.yaml -cs 5 -ce 25 -ch HHZ --phases p,s,P,S --plot_config ./tutorial1/configs/plotting_config.yaml

What you should see for the first event (magnitude 3.5):

  • The stations from 7 km (PAND) to 69 km (FNEB).
  • The P waves arrive first, along the blue dashed curve p, about 2 s after the origin at 7 km and 12 s at 69 km.
  • The S waves, larger, arrive later along the orange curve s, and the gap between P and S grows with distance (that is how the distance of an earthquake is estimated from a single station).
  • The observed arrivals follow the theoretical curves closely: the event location and the station timing are consistent.

Now change record_option: dates to record_option: seconds and run it again. Each trace is now plotted against the seconds from its own start, and since every trace was cut 5 s before its own first arrival, all the P waves are aligned at 5 s: the moveout disappears, and the waveforms can be compared directly.

Tip

Use scale_factor in the plotting configuration to make the traces larger or smaller, and sort_by: backazimuth to order the stations by direction instead of distance.

docs.title: Step 5: Choosing the phases
docs.text:
By default, surfquake computes all the phases of the IASP91 model, and cuts around the first one. With --phases you choose which ones are computed and stored in the header (and drawn with show_arrivals).

Uppercase and lowercase phase names

In the TauP convention used by surfquake, P and S are the waves that leave the source downwards, while p and s leave it upwards. For local earthquakes, the direct waves to the stations are usually p and s: in our example, every station has p and s arrivals, and only the most distant one, FNEB (69 km), also has a P arrival. If you write --phases P,S, the other nine stations have no arrival and they are removed (only 1 of the 10 traces is kept). For local and regional events, always include both: --phases p,s,P,S. Other useful phases are Pn and Sn (head waves along the Moho, at larger distances).

The theoretical arrivals stored in the header can be used later, for example to align the traces on the S wave from the interactive prompt:

shift --phase_theo s

docs.title: Around a wave speed (--vel)
docs.text:
Instead of the theoretical arrivals, the cut can be centred on the time a wave travelling at a given speed (km/s) needs to reach each station: distance / vel. It is very useful for surface waves and for the crustal S waves (Lg), which are not well predicted by a global model:

surfquake processing -p ./tutorial1/project/andorra -i ./tutorial1/metadata/inv_all.xml -e ./tutorial1/events/events.txt -c ./tutorial1/configs/typical_config.yaml --vel 3.4 -cs 5 -ce 15 -ch HHZ --plot_config ./tutorial1/configs/plotting_config.yaml

For CARF, at 57.9 km, the window starts 57.9 / 3.4 − 5 = 12.0 s after the origin time. The distance is stored in the header, so the record section works, but no theoretical arrivals are computed.

docs.title: Around the origin time (-r)
docs.text:
With -r the cut is made around the origin time of the event (-cs seconds before, -ce seconds after), the same for all the stations:

surfquake processing -p ./tutorial1/project/andorra -e ./tutorial1/events/events.txt -c ./tutorial1/configs/typical_config.yaml -r -cs 5 -ce 60 -s CARF -ch HHZ

With -r the location of the event is not used: only the date and hour columns matter, and the inventory is not needed. It is the option to chop waveforms around a list of times (detections, picks, any time of interest). As a consequence, no distance is stored in the headers, so record sections and sort_by cannot be used with -r.

docs.title: Selecting stations and channels
docs.text:
The options -n, -s and -ch select networks, stations and channels of the project, as comma-separated lists:

-s CARF,PAND -ch HHZ,HHN

docs.title: Step 7: Measuring all the events with your own script
docs.text:
Finally, let's process all the events automatically and measure the peak amplitude of every station, writing a table with your own Python script. With processing, the script receives the stream of each event and the event information.

Create the file ./tutorial1/peak_table.py:

import csv
import os

OUTPUT = "./tutorial1/peak_amplitudes.csv"

def run(stream, **kwargs):
    event = kwargs.get("event") or {}
    new_file = not os.path.exists(OUTPUT)
    with open(OUTPUT, "a", newline="") as f:
        writer = csv.writer(f)
        if new_file:
            writer.writerow(["origin_time", "magnitude", "trace_id", "distance_km", "peak"])
        for tr in stream:
            distance = tr.stats.geodetic["geodetic"][0]
            writer.writerow([event.get("origin_time"), event.get("magnitude"), tr.id,
                             round(distance, 1), float(abs(tr.data).max())])
    print(f"[peak] {len(stream)} traces of the event at {event.get('origin_time')} added to {OUTPUT}")
    return stream

Run it with the first config file, in automatic mode (-a), cutting a window around the S waves with --vel:

surfquake processing -p ./tutorial1/project/andorra -i ./tutorial1/metadata/inv_all.xml -e ./tutorial1/events/events.txt -c ./tutorial1/configs/typical_config.yaml --vel 3.4 -cs 5 -ce 15 -ch HHZ --post_script ./tutorial1/peak_table.py -a

Open peak_amplitudes.csv. The peaks of the first event go from about 2 × 10⁴ (VALC) to 1.4 × 10⁸ (PAND): numbers without physical meaning. The traces are in counts, and every instrument has a different gain, so their amplitudes cannot be compared.

Now create ./tutorial1/configs/velocity_config.yaml, which removes the instrument response and converts the traces to ground velocity (m/s):

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'remove_response'
    water_level: 60
    units: 'VEL'
    pre_filt: [0.05, 0.1, 40, 45]
  process_4:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 1.0
    fmax: 10.0
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True

Delete peak_amplitudes.csv and run the command again with -c ./tutorial1/configs/velocity_config.yaml. Now the peaks are ground velocities in m/s:

Station Distance ML 3.49 ML 1.11 ML 0.48 PAND 7 km 2.2 × 10⁻³ 2.1 × 10⁻⁵ 1.6 × 10⁻⁶ CEST 20 km 4.1 × 10⁻⁴ 6.1 × 10⁻⁶ 3.0 × 10⁻⁷ GENF 37 km 5.8 × 10⁻⁵ 6.7 × 10⁻⁷ 1.9 × 10⁻⁷ FNEB 69 km 2.9 × 10⁻⁵ 1.9 × 10⁻⁷ 8.2 × 10⁻⁸

The physics appears:

  • The amplitude decreases with distance, about 100 times between 7 and 69 km (geometrical spreading and attenuation).
  • The amplitude grows with magnitude: at the same station, the ML 3.49 event is about 100 times larger than the ML 1.11 event. Two magnitude units, a factor 100: the local magnitude is a logarithmic measure of the amplitude.

Note

The processed traces of the three events can also be saved with -o ./tutorial1/output. Since the three events are on the same day, their files have the same name: the second and third events are written with the suffixes _1 and _2. To keep them separate, run one event file per output folder.

docs.title: Using Bash script
docs.text:
Finally, the whole workflow in a bash script file. Create a file named run_events.sh:

#!/bin/bash
set -e

# Activate your conda environment
eval "$(conda shell.bash hook)"
conda activate surfquake  # Replace with the name of your environment

BASE=./tutorial1

surfquake project -d $BASE/data -s $BASE/project -n andorra

rm -f $BASE/peak_amplitudes.csv
surfquake processing -p $BASE/project/andorra -i $BASE/metadata/inv_all.xml \
    -e $BASE/events/events.txt -c $BASE/configs/velocity_config.yaml \
    --vel 3.4 -cs 5 -ce 15 -ch HHZ --post_script $BASE/peak_table.py -a

To save the record sections automatically instead of displaying them, set show_plot: false and a plot_output_path in the plotting configuration, and add --plot_config to the processing command.

chmod u+x run_events.sh
./run_events.sh

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text:
• A project indexes the data once, and an event file describes the earthquakes: processing combines them to cut every station around every event.
  • The cut is centred on the first theoretical arrival (default), on a wave speed (--vel), or on the origin time (-r, no location needed).
  • The event information stored in the headers enables record sections, sorting by distance or back-azimuth, and alignment on theoretical phases.
  • For local events, include both p,s and P,S in --phases.
  • Amplitudes are only comparable after removing the instrument response.

docs.title: Time-Frequency Analysis Tutorial 2
docs.text:
In this tutorial, we will learn how to work with the commands: quick and specplot to compute, save and plot the spectrum, the spectrogram and the Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) of your seismic waveforms.

In this tutorial we will follow this structure:

  • Seismic files: tutorial2/data
  • Metadata: tutorial2/metadata
  • Config Files: tutorial2/configs
  • Folder for the tutorial output: tutorial2/time_freq, this will be created by surfquake.
--tutorial2
    --data
        --CA.ARBS..HH1.D.2022.32
        --CA.ARBS..HH2.D.2022.32
        --CA.ARBS..HHZ.D.2022.32
        ......
    --metadata
        --inv_all.xml
    --configs
        --typical_config.yaml
        --spectral_config.yaml
        --plotting_config.yaml

For this tutorial you need to download the seismic data here. Optionally, download the corresponding metadata.

All the commands of this tutorial are run from the folder that contains tutorial2.

Please, first open a terminal, activate your environment and type the following command to overview all surfquake capabilities:

surfquake -h

docs.title: Generate Config Files
docs.text:
As in the Basic Signal Processing tutorial, let's prepare the necessary files. This time we also need the template for the spectral analysis.

surfquake make_config -h
surfquake make_config -c spectral_config -o "./tutorial2/configs"
surfquake make_config -c typical_config -o "./tutorial2/configs"
surfquake make_config -c plotting_config -o "./tutorial2/configs"

The plotting configuration is commented to explain the functionality. The parametrization for signal processing can be found here for traces and here for streams.

docs.title: Process your waveforms
docs.text:
Now that the set up is done, let's compute a spectrogram interactively and then save it.

Please review the following documentation:

Trace processing and plotting

surfquake quick -h
surfquake quick -w "./tutorial2/data/*" -c "./tutorial2/configs/typical_config.yaml" --plot_config "./tutorial2/configs/plotting_config.yaml"
  • In this step you can select a time window: place the mouse on a trace and press u (start time), then move it and press i (end time). The spectral analysis will be computed only inside this window. If you do not set a window, the full traces are used.

docs.title: Interactive
docs.text:
We are going to compute the spectrum, the spectrogram and the Continuous Wavelet Transform.

  • Open an interactive prompt pressing v. The directions for interacting with the traces are printed in the terminal.
  • The traces are referred to by their position on the current page: 0 is the first trace, 1 the second... and all means all the displayed traces.
help spectrum
spectrum all loglog --mode fft

help spectrogram
spectrogram 0 5.0 50 --method fft --dates

help cwt
cwt 0 cm 6 0.5 10 -80 --dates
  • spectrum all loglog --mode fft: amplitude spectrum of all displayed traces, in log-log axes.
  • spectrogram 0 5.0 50 --method fft --dates: spectrogram of the first trace, with windows of 5 s and 50 % overlap, and dates on the x axis.
  • cwt 0 cm 6 0.5 10 -80 --dates: CWT of the first trace with a complex Morlet wavelet (cm) of 6 cycles, between 0.5 and 10 Hz, clipping the colour scale at -80 dB.

Before going back to picking mode, let's save the spectrogram. The command save_tf needs the product, the trace index (or all) and the output folder:

help save_tf
save_tf spectrogram 0 --win 5.0 --overlap 50 --method fft --folder_path ./tutorial2/time_freq
p

The file is saved as <trace_id>.D.<year>.<julday>.spec. If you selected a time window with u and i, only that window is saved. The plotted traces are not modified.

You can save the other products in the same way, for example save_tf spectrum all --folder_path ./tutorial2/time_freq or save_tf cwt 0 --wavelet cm --param 6 --fmin 0.5 --fmax 10 --folder_path ./tutorial2/time_freq.

docs.title: Automatic
docs.text:
In this section we compute the same Time-Frequency objects, but using a config file. The advantage is that we can automate big processes and save these objects for later use.

Please review the section related to Time-Frequency Objects to understand the output files and take advantage of their design.

Let's prepare the processing config file spectral_config.yaml. Below you can see that we chain the typical processing and the computation of the spectrogram:

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 0.01
    fmax: 45.0
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True
  process_4:
    name: 'spectrogram'
    win: 5
    overlap: 75
    method: 'fft'
    output_path: './tutorial2/time_freq'
  • win: window length in seconds. Longer windows give finer frequency resolution (about 1/win Hz) but coarser time resolution.
  • overlap: overlap between consecutive windows, in percent.
  • method: fft (fast) or multitaper (smoother, slower).
  • output_path: folder where the results are written, it is created if missing.

The template spectral_config.yaml also contains commented examples for spectrum, cwt, cross_spectrum, cepstrum and cepstrogram.

In the terminal run the quick command in automatic mode (-a). The command will filter the traces, compute the spectrograms and save the time-frequency objects in your output folder:

surfquake quick -w "./tutorial2/data/*" -c "./tutorial2/configs/spectral_config.yaml" -a

docs.title: Plot your Time-Frequency objects
docs.text:
Finally, we are going to open one of the files with the command specplot. It recognises the type of object from the file extension (.sp, .spec, .cwt, .coh, .cep, .ceps).

surfquake specplot -h
surfquake specplot -f "./tutorial2/time_freq/CA.ARBS..HHZ.D.2022.32.spec" --split --smooth -d
  • --split: split the plot into low and high frequency panels (default cutoff 1 Hz, for example --split 0.5 to change it).
  • --smooth (-s): smooth the time-frequency plane (slower, but prettier).
  • -d (--dates): dates on the x axis instead of seconds.
  • -c (--clip): minimum power displayed, in dB (for example -c -100).
  • --cmap: Matplotlib colormap (default rainbow).

To save the figure instead of only showing it, add --save_path:

surfquake specplot -f "./tutorial2/time_freq/CA.ARBS..HHZ.D.2022.32.spec" --split --smooth -d --save_path "./tutorial2/time_freq"

docs.title: Using Bash script
docs.text:
Since every time-frequency object is a file, you can loop over them and save all the images at once. Create a file named plot_spec.sh:

#!/bin/bash

# Activate your conda environment
eval "$(conda shell.bash hook)"
conda activate surfquake  # Replace with the name of your environment

for file in ./tutorial2/time_freq/*.spec; do
    surfquake specplot -f "$file" --split --smooth -d --save_path "./tutorial2/time_freq"
done

Open a terminal in your working directory and run it:

chmod u+x plot_spec.sh
./plot_spec.sh
